+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter One: Double, Neat The Last Outpost runs warm tonight, the way I like it — fryer grease and cinnamon steam, forty-odd bodies sweating off the cold of the belt. The jukebox is doing its nightly impression of a dying animal, all warble and static, and nobody complains because Grubb would fight them and Grubb wins fights by accident. "Nets." Grubb raps a knuckle on my bar, gentle, for him. "You watering my beer again?" "I'd have to *add* water to water it, Grubb. You're drinking recycled condensate with ambitions." "It's got a kick." "So does a kick. That's the point." Down the rail, Oye snorts into her tea. "He told me the same thing Tuesday. Grubb, your liver is a liar and you're its accomplice." "My liver's the only honest part of me," Grubb says, wounded, delighted. This is the shape of my evenings. Negotiate the drama, top the drinks, keep the peace with a rag and a raised eyebrow. Six years I've been doing it here, on a rock we call the Kettle because it hums during solar storms. It's not much. It's mine. Then the door chimes, and the cold walks in wearing a person. She — I think she — crosses the floor like the floor owes her money. Skin the grey of wet slate, a travel coat scorched along one shoulder, and hair that isn't hair: tentacled dreads, half of them unpinned, curling weakly at the air like they've given up tasting for anything worth finding. She folds onto a stool at the quiet end of my bar and puts both palms flat on the wood, steadying herself or the wood. "Vega whisky, neat." Her voice is gravel soaked in honey. "Better make that a double." I set a glass down. "Vega whisky. That's four thousand lights thataway, friend. This bottle's older than both of us." "Then it's had time to get good." Fair. I pour. Her hands shake — not drunk-shake, adrenaline-shake. I know the difference the way I know when Grubb's lying about his liver. Her eyes never land on me. They keep snagging on the door. "Rough crossing?" I slide the glass across. "You could say that." "From where?" "Far." "Big talker, huh." I put a dish of spiced nuts in front of her, on the house, because shaky hands drop things and I hate sweeping twice. She eats three like she hasn't in days. Payment comes in old cred sticks, pre-Union stamps, the kind collectors hoard. I bite one out of habit. Real. "You're the one they call Nets," she says. "Depends who's asking." "A friend." "I've got all the friends I can afford." Her mouth twitches. Almost a smile. One of her dreads lifts and tastes the cinnamon steam drifting from the kitchen, then droops again, disappointed. "Nettle," she says quietly. My rag stops moving. Not Nets. Not *hey, barkeep*. Nettle — the whole word, the whole weight of it. There are maybe five people alive who know that name means anything, and every one of them belongs to a life I buried three sectors spinward, on a ship that officially doesn't exist anymore. "How do you know that name?" Behind us, Pell leans back too far in his chair telling some story, elbows a tumbler off the corner table, and it hits the deck and bursts. In our half-gravity the shards hang there a half-second, glittering like somebody strung the room with cheap stars, before they remember how falling works. Half the bar flinches. Oye laughs. Grubb apologizes to the table on Pell's behalf. And the stranger's hand is inside her coat. Fast. Too fast. Wrapped around something I don't want to see on a Tuesday. Nobody else notices. That's my job — noticing so nobody else has to. "Easy," I murmur, loud enough to be friendly, soft enough to be private. "It was a glass. We lose more glasses than that to Grubb's elbows alone." Grubb raises his mug in proud confirmation. The hand comes out of the coat empty. She exhales through her nose, long and controlled, and wraps both hands around the whisky instead. "Pell!" I call. "You break it, you buy it. Again." "It was an *ambush*," Pell protests, to general laughter. I fetch the broom, sweep the glitter into a pile, and come back to her leaning close over the bar, voice dropped to almost nothing under the jukebox's death rattle. "They're tracing the *Calliope*'s route," she says. "Port by port. Wreck by wreck. This rock is next on the list." My stomach does something complicated. "The Calliope burned up. Everyone aboard. That's the record." "The record's wrong." The jukebox chooses that moment to change songs, so the silence between us lasts exactly one held breath. "Six years," I say. "Six years, and you walk into my bar with a face I've never seen and a name I buried. Why come to *me*?" "Because you're the last one still breathing within easy reach." She drains the double, sets the glass down with terrible care. "And because I need a room for the night, and a barkeep who suddenly remembers how not to ask questions." "I ask questions professionally." "Then ask this one: when they dock — and they will — did anyone here ever see me?" I look at her. Scorch marks. Shaking hands. Eyes that keep checking my door like it might grow teeth. Trouble doesn't usually announce itself this politely. Stairwell keys hang on the hook behind me. I take one down and slide it across the wood. "Triple rate," I say. "Trouble surcharge." "Fair." "One condition. Tomorrow, second shift, you sit right there and tell me everything. Starting with how the Calliope really ended." She stands, coins the cred sticks into my palm, pauses. "If I'm here tomorrow." "That's supposed to be mysterious? It works. I hate it." Almost-smile again. Then she's climbing the stairs, coat whispering, dreads dragging like tired seaweed, until the corridor lamp swallows her. Under her empty glass sits a datachip, matte black, no markings. I leave it there a while. The jukebox croons. Grubb argues with Oye about whether the Kettle's hum is romantic. Pell buys a round for the table he murdered a tumbler at. Everything normal. Everything fine. Second shift starts in nine hours. Whatever's crawling up the dark behind that woman, it'll arrive sooner than the morning delivery, and it won't be paying triple. I flip her glass upright, set the chip beside it, and pour myself the good stuff. Tonight, the Outpost feels less like home and more like the edge of something.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the cozy sci-fi atmosphere requested. The author successfully establishes Nets as a compelling first-person narrator with a distinct voice that balances world-weary bartender wisdom with underlying vulnerability. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing plot, and building atmosphere. The worldbuilding is efficiently handled through casual details woven into the narrative: the Kettle's hum during solar storms, half-gravity physics, the jukebox's deterioration, and the mix of species and backgrounds at the bar. These elements create a lived-in feeling without overwhelming exposition. The central conflict emerges organically through the mysterious stranger's arrival and her knowledge of Nets' buried past. The tension builds effectively through small details - the stranger's shaking hands, her reaction to the breaking glass, and the revelation about the Calliope. The author maintains mystery while providing enough information to hook the reader. Character interactions feel authentic, particularly the banter between regulars like Grubb and Oye. Nets' protective instincts toward her patrons and her careful navigation of the stranger's obvious danger create believable character motivation. The prose style is generally strong, with vivid imagery ("tentacled dreads, half of them unpinned, curling weakly at the air like they've given up tasting for anything worth finding") and effective metaphors. However, some descriptions occasionally tip toward the overwrought ("the cold walks in wearing a person"). The pacing works well, building from comfortable routine to mounting tension. The ending appropriately leaves the conflict unresolved while establishing clear stakes for future chapters. The dialogue percentage appears to meet the requested 60% target. Minor weaknesses include some slightly forced metaphors and a few moments where the prose becomes overly stylized. The stranger's motivations could be slightly clearer without sacrificing mystery. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South ## Chapter Two: The Kindness Mileage Limit Earl dumps me at the edge of the French Quarter at 6:40 in the morning, says "good luck, kid," and that's the whole ceremony. His taillights shrink down Rampart Street and I stand there learning the first law of strangers: kindness has a mileage limit, and mine just ran out. Two days ago I had a bedroom. A kitchen where I stood with my hands shaking behind my back and said the sentence I'd rehearsed for two years into every mirror in our house. *I'm your son.* And Dad made this face, like a door closing somewhere deep in the building. Mom cried in a way that wasn't sad exactly, more like angry that couldn't find a door either. The school counsellor used the phrase *concerning behavioural patterns* on the phone like she was reading a weather report. Sixty-one dollars in my left sock. Twelve in my pocket. The sixty-one is technically Mom's, from the emergency jar above the fridge, and I've decided that makes it poetic instead of stealing, because I am apparently the emergency. By nine the Quarter is awake and loud and smells like coffee and vomit negotiating a peace treaty. I'm hungry in that hollow, humming way, and I make the mistake of looking at a café menu — twelve dollars for a sandwich, these people are criminals with napkins — when a girl materializes at my elbow. "That's how they get you," she says. "Staring at menus. Marks you as fresh." She's maybe seventeen, army jacket in ninety-degree heat, eyeliner applied like she lost a fight with it. Chews her gum like it owes her money. "I'm not fresh," I say. "I'm seasoned." "Uh-huh. Where's home?" "Tennessee." "Everybody's from somewhere they ain't anymore." She jerks her chin down the block. "Come on, Turnip. Free red beans at St. Augustine's on Thursdays, and today happens to be Thursday, which makes me your guardian angel." "I didn't ask for—" "Nobody ever does. That's why I don't charge." Her name is Dee. She informs me that her last name and birthday are both unavailable, "because both are lies anyway, so why waste the effort." We walk and she narrates the city like a hostile tour guide. Don't sleep by the riverfront, cops sweep it at three. Library opens at ten, nobody bothers you till five. Never give anybody your real name twice. A vendor calls me "miss" while handing me a sample of praline, and the word lands wrong, a key that doesn't fit. I eat the praline anyway. Sugar and shame taste about the same. Dee clocks it. Doesn't say anything for half a block. Then, casual as anything: "What do you go by?" "Taylor." My throat does something complicated around the next part. "I'm — I'm a guy. Just. Recently. Officially." "Cool," Dee says, and steals my second praline. "You want beans or not?" And that's it. No seminar. No face like a closing door. I have to stare at a horse-drawn carriage for a solid minute to get my eyes under control, and if Dee notices, she has the decency to pretend the carriage is fascinating too. It's midday when I hear the saxophone. Royal Street is packed, sun hammering the pavement, and cutting through all of it comes this low, aching thing — "St. James Infirmary," slow as syrup going downhill. The player is an old man in a fedora with his eyes shut, playing like the horn is telling him secrets back. I stop. I don't decide to stop; my legs file the paperwork on their own. Music doesn't ask who you are. That's the thought that arrives, unwelcome, huge. Music doesn't ask and neither does this city, not yet, and I stand in a crowd of strangers letting a brass instrument say everything my father wouldn't hear. I put a dollar in the case. The old man cracks one eye. "You listenin' or waitin' on somebody?" "Listening." "First day in the city?" "That obvious?" "You still look up." He resettles the mouthpiece. "Give it a week." By late afternoon I've learned Dee runs hot and cold like a busted faucet. One minute she's teaching me which fountains have drinkable water; the next she's gone quiet, checking a battered flip phone she keeps in her jacket like other people keep knives. It buzzes. She silences it. Her jaw does a thing. "You expecting a call?" I ask. "I expect nothing. Expectation's for people with futures." She flips the phone shut. "Three months I've been out here. You learn quick or you learn dead." But hours later, sitting on the steps of the Cabildo while the sky goes orange, she says, almost to herself, "Been here since Halloween. Longest I ever stayed anywhere." Halloween to April is not three months. I do the math twice. I file it away in the drawer I'm apparently keeping for things-about-Dee-that-don't-add-up, right next to the flip phone and the fact that her army jacket has a name tape with the letters picked off. That's when I see the man across the street. Clean linen shirt, clean smile, standing too still for a tourist. Dee goes rigid beside me, grabs my sleeve. "Not him. Walk." We walk. Fast. She doesn't explain and I don't ask, and the silence between us has teeth in it now. At Decatur she finally stops, arms crossed. "There's a place. Squat off Chartres. Roof leaks a little, roof leaks everywhere, welcome to Louisiana. There's room." A pause. Her eyes flick over my backpack, my brand-new everything. "You coming or not?" Here's the inventory: I've known her eight hours. Her timeline is fiction. Somebody with a clean shirt wants her and she won't say why. Every survival instinct I own — and apparently I own several, they were just listed under *concerning behavioural patterns* — votes no. But the alternative is a bench by the river, and the sweep at three a.m., and being nobody's anything in a city that hasn't asked me to be anything at all yet. "A stranger with secrets," I say slowly, "is still warmer than a bench." "That's the saddest thing anybody's said to me all week." Dee grins, and for one second it transforms her whole face. "Welcome to New Orleans, Turnip." So I went. God help me, I went.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a blend of vulnerability and defensive humor, with internal monologue that feels genuine rather than forced. The characterization is particularly effective. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - wounded but resilient, suspicious yet desperate for connection. The author skillfully balances Taylor's gender dysphoria with the broader survival challenges of being a runaway, avoiding the trap of making identity the sole focus while still honoring its importance. Dee is equally well-crafted as a mysterious deuteragonist whose contradictions (timeline inconsistencies, the flip phone, the clean-shirted man) create intrigue without feeling contrived. The prose style is confident and distinctive, employing metaphors that feel organic to Taylor's perspective ("kindness has a mileage limit," "face like a door closing"). The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality, and the mixed tense approach works naturally rather than feeling gimmicky. Dialogue feels authentic throughout, particularly Dee's casual acceptance of Taylor's identity and her street-smart commentary. The interactions reveal character efficiently while advancing plot and building the world of street life in New Orleans. The pacing is well-controlled, covering a full day without feeling rushed or padded. The author builds tension effectively through the mysterious elements surrounding Dee while maintaining focus on Taylor's emotional journey. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphors feel slightly overworked, and the ending, while not inappropriately positive, perhaps resolves Taylor's immediate housing crisis a bit too neatly. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully balances multiple narrative demands. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy Home base was the ticket booth of the old open-air cinema, chosen for its walls, its roof, and a hatch in the counter through which Midas could watch the road without being observed by anything with opinions. He laid out the day's assets: one unlabelled tin (adventure in every sense), half a jar of pickled onions, a left boot, and Chewy. Chewy was a koala of the Before Times, plush over servos, grey fur gone the colour of regret, one glass eye dead and one burning a patient amber. Fed his rationed AA battery, he said four things, in whatever order the universe fancied: **G'DAY, MATE!** **LET'S BE FRIENDS FOREVER!** **TIME FOR A NAP!** and **I LOVE YOU THIS MUCH!**, arms rising in unconditional mechanical affection. "So," said Midas. "No food, low batteries, winter coming. Plan is: west along the canal, hit the depot, home before dark." **TIME FOR A NAP!** "That's not a strategy, that's surrender with extra steps." Midas didn't have bad luck, exactly. Bad luck implies variety. His mother had named him Midas hoping everything he touched would turn to gold; everything he touched turned to incident. He had a talent for trouble the way some people have perfect pitch — effortless, unasked-for, and mostly performed in public. They walked the canal, past the city's bones. Under the railway arch, paint still tacky enough to matter: **FOLLOW THE SLEEPING GIANT. KNOCK THRICE AT HIS HEEL. THE HAVEN FEEDS THE POLITE.*** > \*Politeness being the rarest currency left. Nobody had any, but everybody remembered it had once been legal tender. An arrow on a pylon. Another on a burnt church. And there, slumped against the western sky, the Giant itself: two concrete cooling towers that had lain down sometime between the invention of electricity and the end of it, and never got up. At the heel stood a green steel door, blast-rated, fitted with a brass knocker polished by hope. Midas knocked thrice. Silence. He waited the full polite interval and knocked again, which in retrospect was the incident starting. A slot clacked. A strip of paper slid out — typed, laminated, devastatingly bureaucratic: **REFUGE FULL. REGRETS. PLEASE TAKE ONE MINT. TRY THE COAST.** A single ancient mint dropped through, welded to its foil with age. A mint with tenure. Then the dogs came. The Burnt Oak pack ran the north bank: six of them, led by a mastiff cross called Duchess by whoever had loved her last, and nothing now. Midas went over the embankment on principle, found a culvert mouth, and fed himself into it backwards, which is the traditional posture. The small dog followed him in. There was only one thing left to do, and Midas hated that it worked. He threw Chewy. **LET'S BE FRIENDS FOREVER!** announced the koala, arms wide, eye glowing, sailing through the dark like a small grey missile of goodwill. The dog stopped. Not out of friendship — out of confusion, which among dogs is nearly the same thing and considerably safer. Three seconds later Midas was out the far end of the pipe, retrieving Chewy, and standing in a ditch on the golf course. Which was a problem. > \*Everyone knew the geese had held the golf course since Year Three. They had survived the Collapse without noticing it, on the reasonable grounds that they had already been the apocalypse. The sentry goose saw him from forty yards. The honk it produced curdled the ditchwater. Midas ran. The flock rose like a committee with grievances. He crossed the ninth fairway at speeds unwise in one boot and one sock, lost the boot to a bog with a sound like a kiss goodbye, and gained, somewhere along the fence line, a lifelong enmity with waterfowl. The rain started at the canal, because it had heard he was coming. By the time the ticket booth hatched into view, Midas was conducting an audit. *Losses:* one boot, one shirt sleeve, most of the skin off his left shin, the entire morning, and what remained of his dignity. *Acquisitions:* one mint (inedible), one unlabelled tin, and the permanent attention of the Burnt Oak pack, who watched him from the far bank with the patience of creditors. Far off, a goose honked once — not pursuit, just paperwork. Filing his address. Inside, he opened the tin. Artichoke hearts. Of course. The universe had a sense of humour, and it was a food critic's. He ate them anyway, because pride demanded the day yield something, and they were vile, and that felt earned. Chewy sat on the counter, eye dark, one arm hanging by a thread of stuffing, wearing the expression of someone who has recently been used as a distraction against a dog and has decided, graciously, not to mention it. Midas reached into his coat pocket for the mint and found, instead, a blister pack of AA batteries. Bought Before. Forgotten. Hunted for all week. He fed one to Chewy. The amber eye kindled. The arms rose. **G'DAY, MATE!** "G'day, Chewy," said Midas. **TIME FOR A NAP!** And for once, thought Midas, lying down in the booth with rain drumming ambitions on the roof and geese drafting documents somewhere in the dark, that was the first sensible strategic recommendation anyone had made all day.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and footnote-like asides. The author effectively establishes a post-apocalyptic world through clever details like the "Before Times," the bureaucratic refuge system, and the territorial geese who "had already been the apocalypse." The characterization is well-executed, particularly Midas, whose relationship with trouble is elegantly established through the line "He had a talent for trouble the way some people have perfect pitch — effortless, unasked-for, and mostly performed in public." Chewy works effectively as both comic relief and genuine companion, with his limited phrases providing punctuation to the narrative. The prose demonstrates considerable skill with memorable phrases like "grey fur gone the colour of regret" and "politeness being the rarest currency left." The voice remains consistently wry throughout, never breaking character or falling into sentimentality. The mission structure follows the prompt perfectly - deliberation, inevitable complications, and return home worse for wear. The escalating encounters (refuge rejection, dogs, geese) build naturally, each flowing logically from Midas's attempts to escape the previous predicament. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly clever phrasing that draws attention to itself rather than serving the story. Some metaphors, while amusing, feel slightly forced. The ending, while satisfying, relies somewhat heavily on the convenient discovery of batteries to provide resolution. The dialogue between Midas and Chewy's programmed responses works well, creating genuine character interaction despite Chewy's mechanical limitations. The world-building is efficient and evocative, establishing the setting through action rather than exposition. The emotional core - the companionship between man and machine in a collapsed world - emerges naturally without being overwrought. The piece maintains its comedic tone while still conveying the genuine hardships of survival. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Love in the Limelight — Scene Seven** The bell over the blue door had survived forty years of Welsh weather, and this morning it announced a drowned rat in a very expensive hoodie. "Don't mind me—" The man flattened himself against the poetry shelf, rain running off his jaw. "Is there a back way out?" "There's a front way," said Nerys, not looking up from the till. "They'll see me." "Then they'll enjoy it. Everyone else does." He peered round the biography display. Across the narrow street, two black cars idled, wipers going, cameras clustered on their bonnets like beetles. "You know who I am," he said. "I know you're dripping on my biographies." "I'm Rhys Carrow." She looked up then. Took her time. "The horse one." "The horse one," he agreed, relieved. "So you've seen—" "My mam cried at the horse. I sold ice cream in the lobby." She nodded at his sleeve. "You're soaking the Tennyson." He lifted his arm, guilty. "Right. Sorry. Tennyson. Love him. Huge fan." "You're standing on Wordsworth." He stepped sideways onto the mat. "Look—I need twenty minutes for the heat to die down, then I'm gone, and you can tell people Rhys Carrow hid in your shop." "I'll tell them a wet man stood on Wordsworth." "Can I sign your stock?" he tried. "Signed Carrows. They'd fly out." "They'd fly out faster if you left." "I could do a reading. Charity night. Whole village—" "It's Tuesday. The village is watching the telly." He picked up the nearest book—*Leeks: Fifty Honest Ways*—and laid it on the counter like a winning hand. "Fine. I'm buying. Behold: a paying customer. Cherish me." "Full price." "No fame discount?" "Fame's not legal tender, bach." He laughed—startled out of him, real. Then, because he couldn't help himself, he deployed The Look: head tilted, mouth curling, the one from the posters, the one that had ended marriages and launched franchises. "And what would it take, then? This discount?" "That's the poster face." "It usually works." "On Mrs. Price, maybe. She'd have liked the plague." His laugh cracked in the middle this time, and he put a hand on the counter as though the floor had shifted. Her mouth twitched toward a smile and was firmly restocked. "Why aren't you impressed?" It came out younger than he intended. "You do it to everyone," she said, stamping the leeks. "It's very good. Like weather. Impressive. Not personal." "Not personal," he repeated. He pushed the hood back properly. Up close, the film-star architecture was tired around the eyes. "Do you know why those cars are out there? Yesterday I walked off a live interview in Cardiff. The host produced printed texts—mine, private—about my ex, and smiled at me waiting for the bit. So I took out the earpiece and walked. Forty-eight hours as the national villain, till the next villain loads." "Sounds restful, walking." "It was. Best reviews I've had in years." He turned the leek book over in his hands. "Can I tell you something mad?" "You'll anyway." "When everybody likes you, you never find out whether anybody does." He said it lightly, but his thumb had gone white against the spine. "I've been likable since I was nine. My mam cleaned offices in Cardiff at night and I'd wait in the corridor, and I learned fast—if the cleaners were laughing at my impressions, nobody was asking whose kid I was or where my da had gone. Won the Urdd reciting once, aged ten. Stood on that stage and thought: *this is a skill*. Like juggling. You practise daily and nobody ever puts it down." A breath. "Twenty years on, I sleep with the telly on in hotel rooms. Silence feels like the pause before the marks." He winced at himself. "Rhys Price, Tonypandy. That's the real name. You're the first person outside my accountant to hear it in a decade." Nerys went very still, which was how she blushed instead of blushing—though her ears had quietly betrayed her, and she knew it, and despised them. "Hold on," she said, and disappeared into the back. He studied the ceiling beams and, for once, rehearsed nothing. She returned with a slim secondhand pamphlet and slid it across the counter. *R. S. THOMAS — SELECTED POEMS*, sixty pence sticker. "He's got one about a field," she said. "How everyone sprints past the one lit-up thing they actually own. Life isn't a race to tomorrow—it's noticing what's already burning. You'd hate it. Take it." "What's it cost me?" "Nothing. On the house. One condition." "Name it." "Back way's through the storeroom, over the churchyard wall, down the lane by Capel Salem. Your lot's cars won't fit. And if you meet Mrs. Price's dog, stand still—he only bites the famous." "That's very targeted." "We're a fair town." He gathered the leeks and the poems, then paused at the door. "What time do you close Tuesday?" "Five. Half four if it's quiet." "I'll make it quiet." "See that you do." "Nerys," he said—she hadn't told him; it was stitched on her apron—"diolch, Nerys fach." "I know," she said. "You said. Twice." The bell rang him out into the rain. Through the window she watched him pull the hood up, hesitate, glance back once at the blue door like a man checking a lit window—and go. On the counter lay a fifty and the pamphlet's price in exact coins. She made the change anyway, out of principle. Then she broke principle completely: took a cream card, wrote *R. PRICE — RESERVED — TUESDAY*, and slipped it into the Collected Thomas on the shelf behind her. "Half four, then," she informed the empty shop—and caught herself smiling at the cookbooks, and let it happen, since there was no one there to perform it for.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Rhys's performative charm gradually giving way to vulnerability, and Nerys's dry, practical Welsh wit that masks her growing attraction. The dialogue feels natural and carries the scene effectively, with each character's personality emerging clearly through their speech patterns. The setting is well-established through specific details like the forty-year-old bell, the narrow Welsh street, and references to local landmarks. The author shows good restraint in world-building, providing enough context without overwhelming the scene. The Welsh cultural elements feel authentic rather than stereotypical. The character development is particularly strong. Rhys's transformation from practiced charm to genuine vulnerability feels earned through the specific details of his backstory - the cleaning offices, the Urdd competition, the real name reveal. Nerys's character is more subtly drawn but equally effective, her resistance to his charm feeling genuine rather than contrived, and her eventual softening (the reserved book, the smile at the end) feels natural. The romantic tension builds effectively through their verbal sparring, with the chemistry emerging from their intellectual and emotional matching rather than physical attraction alone. The author handles the "immune to charm" dynamic well, making Nerys's resistance feel principled rather than arbitrary. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious, particularly in some of the more literary flourishes. The pacing is generally strong but could be tightened in a few places. The ending, while satisfying, borders on being slightly too neat with the reserved book gesture. The piece successfully fulfills the prompt requirements while maintaining literary quality and emotional authenticity. The dialogue-heavy approach works well for revealing character and building tension. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave way without protest, as though it had been waiting. Beyond lay the underhold: a low crypt of blackened oak beams arched like the ribs of some beached leviathan, its stone sweating brine despite the season. Whale-oil lamps burned low along the walls, shedding a greasy amber light that smelled of tallow and something sweeter beneath—ambergris, perhaps, or rot dressed up as perfume. Frost feathered across the flagstones where no frost had any right to be. At the far end squatted the vault door, iron-banded and seal-ringed, breathing cold into the room like a patient predator. Between the trio and that door stood a table. Behind the table sat a woman. "*Bollocks,*" breathed Katra. Yeva Morska was grey as gull-wing and dressed in widow's black strung with jet, her hands folded atop a scatter of scrimshaw playing-cards as though she had been sitting there for hours. Which, Aya thought, her stomach dropping through the floor, she almost certainly had. Flanking her stood four men: two cradling steam-harpoon launchers, their brass pressure-dials trembling at full charge; one holding a storm-lantern; and one whose left arm was all oiled piston and riveted joint, ending in a hook of polished steel. "That's not possible," Simeon whispered. "You were *arrested*. There were warrants. The *Gazette* printed—" "The *Gazette* prints whatever the magistrate's been paid to have printed." Yeva turned a card with one grey finger. "What they carted off to the gaol at dawn was a very convincing lady made of wax and river-clay. I've bribed a hangman before, children. A turnkey costs rather less." She glanced up, and her eyes were the colour of deep water over drowned things. "Though I confess, I expected *six* of you. The loyalty of the lower tiers disappoints. On your knees. All three." Harpoons rose in unison, dials hissing. Aya's mind ran the arithmetic—two barrels each, four men, twenty feet of open stone—and found the sum written in blood. She sank to her knees, and felt rather than heard Katra and Simeon follow. *Keep the choir quiet. Whatever comes, keep them quiet.* Yeva rose and crossed the floor slowly, drawing from her sash a knife of carved whale-ivory, its blade etched with tiny drowning ships. She hooked its tip beneath Aya's chin and lifted—a baleen half-mask, lacquered black, the disguise that had walked her safely through two years of midnight. "Let's see what manner of rat's been gnawing at my guild, hmm?" The mask came away with a whisper of shellac. For a moment the underhold was silent enough that Aya could hear the frost growing. Then Yeva's face changed—not softened, nothing so kind—but *shifted*, like weather. "I know those eyes," she said softly. "I stood in the crowd at Tyburn Cross the morning they hanged Elowen Corvain. I remember a girl in the front rank, white as milk, watching her mother dance at the end of a hempen rope." The knife-tip trembled, very slightly, beneath Aya's chin. "Wider eyes, then. But the same eyes." *No.* The word rang in Aya's skull like a cracked bell. *Not here, not now—* Somewhere behind the thin wallpaper of the world, the hungry guests stirred, tasting her terror like blood in water. *Don't answer. Don't you dare answer.* "She's nobody," Katra started, "she's just—" "She is Lady Aya Corvain," Yeva said, without turning, "daughter of Lord Aldous, and of a woman this city burned a *witch* upon. Well." She straightened, addressing her men as though delivering a sermon. "It seems the thief who's been robbing me blind since springtime is *titled*. Fetch me my salts." Out beyond the guild walls, muffled through yards of stone and the wool-thick harbour fog, a foghorn sounded—once, twice, thrice—long and mournful, like the sea counting its dead. "Now," Yeva said, settling her hip against the table's edge. "Here's how I see matters, my lady. Three burglars, caught red-handed in the deepest room of my house, come sniffing round a treasure older than this city. By rights, Mister Brack feeds you to the harbour, and by morning the crabs are the only souls who know your face." She smiled without warmth. "But dead girls are poor company, and poorer still at paying debts. So." Aya lifted her chin. Two years of masked nights, and it was the drawing-room lessons that saved her now—her mother's poise worn like armour over a hammering heart. "Then let us conduct business," she said. "My father is Lord Aldous Corvain: shipping concerns, insurance syndicates, three seats' worth of influence on the Harbour Commission. He will pay anything—*anything*—to learn his daughter is alive. And he will pay twice that to ensure no word of *how* she earned her ransom ever reaches the *Gazette*. You hold the one hostage in this city whose family can afford silence. Kill us, and you've spent a fortune for three corpses and a scandal you can't sell." "Clever little eel." Yeva tilted her head. "But ransom buys breakfast, not freedom. Your father's silver settles *your* debt. What of theirs?" A nod toward Katra and Simeon. "And what, pray, am I to make of *this*?" She gestured lazily at the vault door, and Aya saw the guards flinch—all four of them, brass and steel and all, flinching from the cold pouring off the iron. "Men trust brass and oil and steel, child. Steel keeps its promises. That door does not. My cunning-man opened it once, ten years past, and what came back wore his face and screamed in Latin till we drowned him in a barrel. You didn't crawl down here for coin. Coin doesn't dress itself in baleen and gamble on the rope. You came for what *sleeps* behind my door." *She knows. She has always known.* "I came for leverage," Aya said evenly. "The same as you'd have done, in my position." "Mm." Yeva studied her a long moment, the lamplight swimming in her grey eyes. Then, to the guards: "Bind them. Gag the loud one gently—she bites. And send a boy to my quarters for my father's old irons. The ones we fitted to the last cunning-woman." Her gaze slid back to Aya, and it was the look of a woman appraising livestock—or kindling. "If our lady's inheritance is real, she'll prove it soon enough. If it isn't..." She let the sentence hang, unfinished, the way the worst sentences always are. *Behind Aya's ribs, deep in the immateria's cold tide, something purred.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through detailed descriptions of the underhold, with its whale-oil lamps, ambergris scents, and maritime imagery. The prose maintains an appropriately dark, gritty tone throughout. # Gunpowder Rendezvous The jukebox in the corner has been stuck on the same scratchy rock track for three hours, neon tubes buzzing pink and blue around a guitar riff that skips at the same bar every time it comes around. Nobody feeds it a coin. Nobody fixes it. The bartender stopped trying around midnight. Spike Spiegel sits at the end of the counter with a beer he can't afford a second of, watching the door through cigarette smoke. His stomach has been negotiating with him for an hour—food against patience—and patience is losing. Three million on a syndicate accountant named Voss, a man who ran off with payroll, a briefcase, and no survival instincts. Spike thinks in woolongs. It's enough to eat for a year. Maybe two. The door bangs open, rain comes in sideways, and then a woman comes in after it, crossing the room like a knife looking for something to cut. Cut-off shorts, black crop top, a dragon coiling down one arm, and the twin bulges under her wet jacket that Spike's good eye reads as Berettas before his bad eye finishes the thought. She takes the stool beside him like she owns the bar, the city, and him. "Whiskey. The bottle." Then, sideways: "You're in my light." "It's a big bar." "It was." She pours two shots without asking and slides one over. Spike looks at it, then at her. "You buying me a drink?" "You're broke. I can smell it. It's embarrassing." She knocks hers back. "Revy." "Spike." "You're here for Voss." Not a question. "So am I. So here's how this goes: you finish your beer, you finish your cigarette, and you walk back to whatever rusted-out tub brought you. Before I walk you there." Spike drinks the shot she bought him. It's good whiskey, better than he's tasted in months, and he tells her so, which is somehow the wrong answer. Her hand twitches toward her jacket, and he watches it the way you'd watch weather. "Easy," he says. "I'm just here." "Everyone's *just here.* Nobody's just anything, shit-for-brains." The drunk at the pool table chooses that moment to reach for her shoulder—too much rum, not enough sense—and the room moves. Spike doesn't stand. He turns on his stool, catches the man's wrist, redirects, and the sailor goes over a chair into a table in one lazy, liquid motion, like he's dancing with someone only he can hear. Revy's Beretta is out before the man lands, and she shoots the rum bottle out of his hand instead of out of his head, which for her is practically charity. Then they look at each other across the smoke, guns and stillness, and both are annoyed by the same realization: *that was easy.* That felt rehearsed. She holsters. He lights a fresh cigarette off the stub of the old one. "Jeet Kune Do," she says. "Cute." "Quick hands." "Two of them. That's the name, honey—Two Hands. Ask around Roanapur sometime. If you live." The bartender, wiping a glass that's been clean for an hour, clears his throat. "Voss took a room at the Starlight Motel. Paid cash. Kept staring at the door." They're both on their feet before he finishes. --- Outside, the rain has teeth. The Starlight's sign has a burnt-out letter, so the whole wet street just says **ACANCY**, buzzing. They climb the outside stairs on opposite sides, meet at the same door at the same moment, and stand dripping, glaring, close enough to share breath. "Ladies first?" Spike offers. "Open the damn door." He kicks it in. Voss is a soft man in a good suit, frozen mid-pack, briefcase open on the bed and banded bills spilling across the mattress. Two guns come up—hers left-handed, his right—and then, in the same heartbeat, swing sideways and lock on each other. "Bounty's mine," she says. "Split it." "Like hell." "Voss," Spike says pleasantly, without moving, "tell them about the double-cross clause." Voss does what soft men do. "Double! Double *each*, I'll pay you both double, just—one of you, please, shoot the other one—" And it would be so easy. Spike can see it in her face, the arithmetic she's running, bullets against money against the look in his eye. He's seen that look before, in mirrors, in men he used to be. His bad eye aches the way it does when the past leans in. She's close. The gun in her fist is steady as a fact. His gaze drops to the dragon on her arm and comes back up. "Eyes up here, bounty boy." "You're not gonna shoot me." "You wanna bet your one life on that?" "I already died once. Didn't take." Something moves behind her eyes—not softness, never that, but recognition, the animal pause of one stray meeting another. Her weight shifts half an inch. His does too. Rain hammers the window and the space between them gets very small, her breath whiskey-warm, his cigarette burning down between two fingers, and for one suspended second the standoff is about something else entirely— Voss hits the bathroom window. Glass explodes. Both guns swing and fire—two shots, one hole—and the accountant drops three stories into a dumpster with the briefcase and waddles off into the dark like a rich little crab. Silence. Rain through the broken frame. A few loose bills flutter down. Crumbs. Revy lowers her Berettas and laughs, low and genuine and furious. "Three million. *Gone.* Because you wanted to flirt." "I don't flirt. I loiter." She scoops up the scattered bills anyway, stuffs them in her shorts, finds the minibar, and sits on the wrecked bed, pouring something cheap into two plastic cups. She hands him one. Neither of them says why. "To Voss," she toasts. "May he drown in that dumpster." "Whatever happens, happens." "God, you're exhausting." She drinks, wipes her mouth, stands, pauses at the door with the rain behind her. "I'm not a good person, Spiegel. Not a bad one either. I'm just here. Remember that next time." "Next time?" "Next time I see you, I shoot first." "You'd miss." She almost smiles. The door bangs shut. Spike finishes the cheap whiskey, lights the last cigarette off the broken neon bleeding through the window, and stays a while in the wreck of the room. Down the street, faint through the rain, the jukebox is still playing the same song, skipping at the same bar, like it's got nowhere else to be either.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and character understanding. The author successfully captures both Spike's laconic fatalism and Revy's volatile aggression while maintaining their distinct voices throughout. The noir atmosphere is well-established through environmental details like the broken jukebox, neon lighting, and persistent rain. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Spike's dry wit ("I don't flirt. I loiter") and Revy's crude directness coming through clearly. The sexual tension builds naturally through their competitive dynamic and physical proximity, culminating effectively in the motel room standoff. The action sequences are well-choreographed, particularly Spike's fluid takedown of the drunk and their synchronized shooting of Voss. The author demonstrates good understanding of both characters' fighting styles and capabilities. However, the piece has some structural issues. The pacing feels slightly rushed in places, particularly the transition from bar to motel. The ending, while thematically appropriate, lacks the full emotional payoff that the buildup promises. The sexual tension reaches a peak but doesn't quite deliver the complexity suggested by the prompt. The prose occasionally veers toward overwrought territory with phrases like "crossing the room like a knife looking for something to cut" and "bullets against money against the look in his eye." While atmospheric, some descriptions feel forced rather than organic. The characterization is mostly strong, though Revy's moments of vulnerability could have been explored more deeply. The piece captures the surface-level attraction and mistrust but doesn't fully delve into the psychological complexity that makes both characters compelling. The ending maintains the noir tone appropriately without false optimism, and the circular return to the jukebox provides nice structural symmetry. Overall, this is competent genre fiction that succeeds in its primary objectives while falling short of exceptional depth. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 87.0
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta We told Astrid's mother we were going night-fishing at the lake, and her mother didn't look up from her crossword, because in Lillträsk nobody watched anybody, which was half of why I hated it there and half of why it worked. It was the last week of August, 1995, and the dark had finally come back to the village. In Stockholm I'd never noticed darkness arriving, it just leaked in around streetlights. Here it fell like water filling a well. Astrid said that was why the old people had made up so many rules. "Long dark, lots of rules," she said, the way you'd explain weather. She laid everything out on her bedspread like a surgeon: a twist of paper holding rock salt, a heel of hard bread, a jar lid with milk in it. She'd already made me take off my belt and empty my pockets of anything with metal. "No iron inside the stones," she said. "Farmor was strict about that." "Why?" "I don't ask her questions like that." She said it without embarrassment, the way she said most things. "Salt in both pockets. Bread under your tongue when we sit down—not eating it, just holding it. So they don't mistake your mouth for an empty house." She shrugged. "You don't have to believe it. You just have to do it." I was fourteen and bored out of my mind and secretly flattered that the strange local girl had chosen me. I put the salt in my pockets. The mound stood in a clearing behind the Berglund farm's back pasture, a grassed-over heap older than the church, older than the village, older than any name anyone used for it except the one everybody used anyway: Kungshögen. The King's Mound. Kids dared each other to bike past it. Nobody sat on it. We walked the last stretch in single file because Astrid said so, and she counted our steps under her breath, and at some point she stopped counting and said, "From here, if it talks to you, you don't answer until the third time. First two times, you keep your mouth shut even if it's screaming your name. Especially then." "Astrid." "It won't scream," she said, matter-of-fact. "It's patient. That's worse." Three times around the mound, always clockwise, *medsols*, the way the sun goes. She corrected my direction once, gently, like a dance teacher. At the top she poured the milk into the grass, set the bread beside it, and told me to sit facing north with my feet apart. "Apart? Why apart?" "So nothing pulls you down between your own heels." She sat beside me, knees loose, hands open on her thighs, and looked so ordinary—a skinny girl in a windbreaker smelling of mosquito spray—that I almost laughed. "What do we even ask?" I whispered. "Whatever we want to know. Who keyed my moped. Whether Marcus lied about the party. Who's been saying my farmor is a witch to the seventh-graders." Her jaw went tight on that last one. "You ask quiet. Like you're ashamed. That's the whole trick of it." So we sat. The cold came up out of the ground faster than the cold came down out of the sky, which I noticed and filed away and tried not to notice again. Somewhere a cow moved in the pasture. My heart did its teenage drumming. I kept the bread crust under my tongue and it tasted like dust and old wheat. "This is so stupid," I whispered, to be brave. "Yeah," Astrid said comfortably. "Keep sitting." Time got strange. I'd left my watch taped to the fence post, per instructions, and without it the night had no seams. Once I heard a sound below us—below, in the mound—a soft rhythmic shifting, like a large animal turning over in bedding, and I decided it was water moving in gravel, because mounds have gravel in them, obviously, and water moves. Once the grass around us bent in a slow circle while the heather stood perfectly still, and I decided it was our body heat making a little weather. I was getting very good at deciding things. Then the church bell rang. One stroke. Clear, near, silver-edged—though the church was nine kilometers away across the lake, though it was exactly midnight, though bells strike the hour twelve times and this was one single note, like a finger tapped on glass, like something checking that we were listening. Astrid's hand found my wrist. Not squeezing. Just resting there, heavy as a stone. "Don't count," she breathed. "Whatever you do, don't count the strokes." There had only been one to count. That was the problem. After that the mound was warm. Warmth rose through my jeans like standing near an oven door, and I thought, composting grass, decomposition makes heat, everyone knows that, and the thought sounded exactly like a girl reassuring herself in the dark, and I let it stand because the alternative was to get up and I found I couldn't get up. My feet wanted to stay apart. My mouth held its bread. Something asked, very softly, from the north side, in Swedish, in an old man's dry voice or in wind finding a crack in stone: *Vem sitter där?* Who sits there? I didn't answer. First time. Astrid's nails pressed crescents into my wrist. The voice waited—it was good at waiting—and asked again, and I stared straight north at nothing and my whole body was a struck bell. Third time, it didn't ask who sat there. It said, pleasantly, "Linnéa Maria." And Astrid leaned forward into the dark and asked her question—who, who had been saying it about her farmor—and something answered her, a whisper with a shape to it, two words, a name, and Astrid went rigid as a fence post. "We go now," she said. "Walk. Don't run. Don't look back." We walked. Behind us our footsteps continued a half-step past ours whenever we stopped at the fence, and stopped when we climbed it, and I kept my eyes on the grey rectangle of Astrid's house and thought: echo, slope of the ground, a deer, anything, anything. At her porch Astrid finally spoke the name she'd heard. I've never written it down before now. Here is what I tell myself: she'd guessed. She'd known the village, known its mouths, and the wind did the rest, and grief makes people invent answers. But the voice had said *Linnéa Maria*, and I hadn't used my middle name since my confirmation, and I have never once told Astrid what it was.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in executing folk horror within the specified parameters. The author successfully captures the voice of an adult Linnea recalling teenage events, maintaining the requested transparency of this narrative device while allowing subtle hints of retrospective knowledge to seep through. The characterization is particularly effective. Astrid emerges as a compelling figure - matter-of-fact about supernatural practices yet recognizably teenage, with her concerns about gossip and her moped. Her dialogue feels authentic, mixing casual explanations ("Long dark, lots of rules") with eerily specific ritual instructions. Linnea's voice captures adolescent psychology well - the boredom, the flattery at being chosen, the rational explanations she constructs for increasingly irrational events. The prose maintains excellent control throughout, avoiding both overwrought mysticism and dismissive rationality. Phrases like "darkness fell like water filling a well" and "my whole body was a struck bell" are evocative without being purple. The author demonstrates restraint in building tension, using concrete details (the salt, the bread, the specific walking instructions) to ground the supernatural elements in believable ritual. The ambiguity is masterfully handled. Each supernatural occurrence receives a rational explanation from Linnea, yet these explanations feel increasingly desperate. The church bell striking once, the warm mound, the continuing footsteps - all could be explained away, but the cumulative effect creates genuine unease. The revelation about Linnea's middle name provides the perfect capstone, impossible to rationalize yet not definitively supernatural. The setting feels authentic to 1990s rural Sweden, with period-appropriate details and a convincing sense of isolation. The ritual elements appear well-researched, mixing recognizable folk practices with the author's invention in a way that feels organic. Minor weaknesses include some slightly mechanical exposition about the setting and Linnea's situation, though this serves the story's needs adequately. The pacing occasionally slows during the setup, but recovers strongly once the ritual begins. The ending strikes an excellent balance - dark enough to justify the buildup, ambiguous enough to maintain the story's central tension, and emotionally resonant in Linnea's continued uncertainty decades later. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 90.7
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Therapeutic Boundaries The musculature chart hangs on the wall past the head of the table, laminated, clinical—a man flayed to bright red fiber and ivory tendon, every muscle labeled in Latin, a body with no skin and therefore no shame. I stare at it while Mara straps my left ankle into the towel roll. *Gastrocnemius.* The calf. On the chart it's a clean geometry of parallel striations. In my leg it's a knotted rope with a grudge. Six months since the tendon let go mid-race with a sound like a starter pistol fired inside my own heel. Six months of learning that recovery is just training with the joy removed. "You're tensing," Mara says. "I'm breathing." "You're breathing around the tension." Her hands are already working, fingers hooking under my heel, her other forearm braced flat along my sole. "Knee stays straight. This one's for the gastroc—it crosses both joints, so we lock the knee to isolate it." She draws my foot slowly toward my shin. The stretch arrives like a wire tightening from heel to behind-the-knee. My whole body maps itself around the pull: toes curling, quad firing once in protest, breath snagging somewhere above the sternum. "Talk to me." "Four," I say. Out of ten. A lie shaved down by two. She doesn't call it. She was a four-hundred hurdler; she knows what athletes' scales look like from the inside. She holds the position, counting seconds aloud, her thumb riding the arch of my foot, and I fix my eyes on the flayed man on the wall and recite old split times to myself like scripture. Twenty-eight-one at the break. Twenty-eight-one. The body remembers what it will never run again. She releases, eases my leg flat. "Same hold, knee bent this time—that shifts the load to the soleus underneath." Her palm warms my shin as she guides the bend. The second stretch goes deeper, duller, closer to bone. Closer, somehow, to her. Then she moves to the head of the table and I lose the chart to the angle of my own neck. "Goniometer," she says, fitting the plastic protractor's arms along my tibia and the outside of my foot, measuring the angle of my ankle like a surveyor assessing land she used to own. We trained on the same track for three years. Same coach, same ice baths, same 6 a.m. fog. Then her hamstring tore in a semifinal, and instead of shattering she went back to school, got the doctorate, became the person who fixes people like me. Her transition was seamless. Mine is a crime scene. "Fourteen degrees," she says, writing it down. "Up from eleven." "Congratulations to us." Her pen pauses. Just a beat. Then she caps the marker and moves on. Next comes the joint work. She stands at the foot of the table, stacks her hands—one over the other, heel of the bottom hand bridged across the front of my ankle, thumb settled just below the joint line where the talus lives. "When you dorsiflex, this bone has to glide backward under your shin. Yours forgot how. So we remind it." She leans. Her weight travels down through locked elbows, through her palms, into the joint—a slow, graded press, deeper and deeper, until the ache blooms broad and hot across the front of my ankle, a bruise being born from the inside. "Breathe out," she says. "Don't fight the grade-three. Fight me later." I exhale. The bone gives a millimeter. Sweat prickles at my hairline. Her face is very close to my foot, concentration pulling her mouth sideways, and I am cataloguing things I refuse to be noticing: the fine tendons in her forearms, the strand of hair escaping its clip, the fact that her hands are still calloused even though she'll never hurdle again either. Then the scar. The incision runs two inches up the inside of my ankle, a zipper of shiny pink tissue. She seats herself on the rolling stool, drags it close, and lays two fingertips on either side of the ridge. Cross-friction: small, firm strokes, perpendicular to the scar, breaking down the adhesions knitting my tendon to everything it touches. My foot plantarflexes without my permission—an involuntary clench, the body throwing itself between her fingers and the wound. Guarding. She stops instantly, palm going flat and still over the area, waiting out the spasm like weather. "There it is," she murmurs. Not mocking. Almost tender. "It thinks it's protecting you." "It's wrong," I say, "like everyone else." Under her fingertips, pressed against the hollow behind my inner ankle bone, she can feel my pulse. I know she can, because her fingers go briefly, minutely lighter—and my heart, traitor, chooses that moment to climb. Not from pain. The pain is a five. She adjusts nothing, says nothing, resumes the strokes, and we both pretend her thumb isn't resting on my heartbeat like a held note. The last technique is the one I hate. She hooks my forefoot over her forearm, locks her other hand across my shin, and takes the dorsiflexion past comfortable into the burning country—the calf screaming along its whole length, fibers singing that high warning note just shy of tearing. "Number." "Seven." "Good seven or bad seven?" "Does it matter?" "It matters." She holds anyway, because a seven is still inside the fence, and I grip the edge of the table hard enough to whiten my knuckles rather than ask her to stop, because some pride survives even when the career doesn't. My calf trembles against her forearm. She watches the tremor with clinical attention and something else underneath it, banked low, the way you bank a fire you're not allowed to light. Then she leans across me to reposition the pillow—her sternum a few inches from my shoulder, the green smell of arnica and clean hair, her breath landing warm on my collarbone—and for one suspended second neither of us is a clinician or a case file. She straightens. "Thursday. Heel raises. Eccentric only—three sets of fifteen, slow down, don't cheat the lowering." "Wouldn't dream of it." She writes my numbers on the chart. Fourteen degrees. Seven out of ten. Progress, in a language built entirely of losses. On the wall, the flayed man keeps his secrets in Latin. *Gastrocnemius*, from the Greek: *gaster*, belly—the calf's honest name, printed right there in black. Ours, hers and mine, go home unwritten.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery and sophisticated narrative control. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: Hog Lane The dawn gun woke me the way it always did—like a nail drawn slowly out of wood. I lay in my cot listening to the harbour assemble itself: oar-tholes creaking, a gong two streets over, the sampans slapping water against the seawall. My shirt was glued to my back. Somewhere below, Ah-Ling was sweeping, and each stroke of the broom went through my skull like a file. The knock came at seven. "You cough all night, master." "I slept." "The boat come two times. Lieutenant Harrowby, he stand on the quay making very angry face. He ask are you dead." "Tell him the dysentery's back. Tell him I'm sending for the surgeon." My voice cracked in the wrong place. "Tell him whatever keeps him off these stairs." "You eat nothing yesterday. You shake like wet dog." Ah-Ling stood in the doorway with my boots, watching me the way servants do—knowing everything, saying only what is safe. "Master, this house has back door. Other officers, they use it." "Not yet." I took the boots. My hands wouldn't close properly around them. In my pocket, the little jade carp. Cold, even in that furnace of a morning, its scales worn blind by three years of my thumb. I pressed it until the chill reached something under my breastbone. --- Hog Lane at eight o'clock smelled of charcoal smoke, dried shrimp, and drains that had given up pretending. Flies rose off the cookshop stalls in sheets. Cursetjee sat behind his counter fanning himself with a ledger, and when he saw me his eyebrows climbed toward his turban. "Mr. Merrick! And before nine o'clock. You honour me early today." "Business is business, Mr. Cursetjee." "So it is. And whose business brings you?" He knew. They all knew. The whole waterfront could read my face like a manifest. I laid the miniature on his counter—my mother, painted the year before she died, in a locket of Birmingham gold. "Sixty dollars." He held it to the light for a long, insulting while. "This is not sixty dollars. This is forty dollars wearing a chain." "Fifty." "Fifty-five, and I say nothing when you bring the sword next week." He counted the Mexican coins out one at a time, letting each ring on the wood. "You know what I admire about you, Lieutenant? Your punctuality. Grief keeps such regular hours." Outside, a voice hailed me from the American hong steps—Mr. Talbot, billiards tonight, brandy, girls from the Lane. I pleaded the dysentery. He laughed and wished it upon me warmly. --- Behind China Street, up stairs that stank of sulphur and spilled firecracker powder, Fourth Uncle received me in a room the size of a coffin standing upright. Sandalwood smoke. A bird somewhere, complaining. "Eight dollars the ball now," he said, before I'd finished sitting. "Don't look wounded. The mandarin raises his squeeze, the squeeze runs downhill, and you, *fan-kwei*, are at the bottom of the hill holding your hat." "I brought fifty-five." "And I require seventy." "Since when?" "Since the navy began playing games on the river." He picked tea leaves from his cup with a fingernail like a claw. "Boats everywhere. My customers nervous. Nervous men pay more or buy nothing." He studied me over the rim. "Unless the lieutenant wishes to take tea with the gentleman downstairs. Friends of the river drink free." My stomach turned over—not the sickness, the other thing. "Downstairs." "He is waiting already. He asked would the sick officer call." Fourth Uncle smiled with genuine warmth, which was worse than contempt. "Everyone knows you are sick, Lieutenant. Everyone is very sorry." --- The man downstairs had clean fingernails and a merchant's cotton gown too fine for his manners. He poured tea I didn't touch and introduced himself as Fung, agent to certain persons who moved goods at night. "Thursday," he said. "Your ship's boats. Where will they search?" "That's not mine to give." "No. It's yours to sell. Different thing entirely." He set a purse on the table between us and did not push it forward. Pushing would have made it a bribe. Leaving it made it furniture. "Twenty dollars. More than your mother's face was worth, I think." I rubbed the carp through the cloth. Cold. Cold. It never got warm enough. "The Whampoa reach," I heard myself say, "below the second beacon. After the turn of the tide—they row back against the current, so they're slow on the return leg. Two boats only. The third's laid up with a smashed tiller." Fung wrote nothing down, which told me how many times he'd done this, and with whom. "The scrambling-dragons thank you," he said—the fast smugglers' boats, named for the very thing I fed. At the door he added, kindly: "Buy yourself a good dinner, Lieutenant. You look like a man who needs feeding." --- By dusk the squall had come and gone, leaving the streets steaming. In my room I cooked the chandu over the little lamp the way the book says a man shouldn't need instructions for, and watched the tar go soft and sweet-smelling—scorched sugar, a whisper of vinegar—and told myself, as one does, that this was the last time it would be necessary. People speak of chasing the dragon. I had stopped chasing anything years ago. It waited for me now, patient as a creditor. Afterward the room grew kind. The aches untied themselves joint by joint. The harbour lights smeared into gold thread, and I lay there thinking of Harrowby's angry face on the quay, of my mother's face in Cursetjee's drawer, of the second beacon at Whampoa, and found—to my lasting astonishment—that I could hold all three thoughts without weeping. Ah-Ling knocked softly. "Master. I bring congee. You eat something?" "Tomorrow," I said. I had said it every night that week. From the pocket of the coat hung over the chair, the jade carp clicked once against the wood, cooling, keeping its own accounts.

The narrative structure works well, following Merrick's descent through increasingly compromising situations - from pawning his mother's miniature to betraying naval intelligence. The progression feels natural and inevitable, driven by addiction's logic rather than melodrama. The dialogue is particularly strong, with each character having a distinct voice that reveals their relationship to Merrick and their place in Canton's social hierarchy. Merrick emerges as a genuinely complex character - neither purely sympathetic nor entirely contemptible. His internal monologue reveals self-awareness of his degradation while showing his inability to stop, creating authentic psychological tension. The jade carp serves as an effective recurring motif, representing both comfort and the cold reality of his situation. The prose style is controlled and evocative without becoming overwrought. Phrases like "grief keeps such regular hours" and "patient as a creditor" demonstrate sophisticated metaphorical thinking. The sensory details effectively establish atmosphere - the oppressive heat, various smells, and physical sensations of withdrawal create visceral immersion. The ending avoids false redemption or excessive darkness, instead presenting Merrick's temporary relief with appropriate ambiguity. The repetition of "tomorrow" and the cooling jade carp suggest the cyclical nature of addiction without heavy-handed symbolism. Minor weaknesses include some dialogue that occasionally feels slightly modern, and a few moments where the historical voice wavers. Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
