# Sisyphus Gives Advice The Underworld contains many hills, most of them decorative. One is load-bearing.* *Everything in the Underworld is technically load-bearing, since the entire arrangement rests upon Tartarus, which rests upon nothing whatsoever and prefers to keep it that way. Atop this particular hill stood a boulder, and beside it — lashed to the slope at an angle of permanent optimism — a small desk. It had begun, as most institutions do, with theft. Crows are thieves; this is not slander, it is ornithology.† One of them made off with a letter sealed in lead — the shiny ones go first — addressed, in the manner of the desperate, *"To Whoever Is Listening."* Sisyphus, resting between pushes, read it aloud for the pleasure of a new voice, discovered the writer's problem was entirely solvable, and sent the solution back down the mountain by the same criminal route. The living, being quick studies where miracles are concerned, spread the word: burn a letter at a lonely shrine, and an answer returns on a black wing. The gods classified the whole business as Another Trick and resolved, as gods do, to ignore it until it stopped. Nine centuries later, Hope had moved in permanently and, like all cats, behaved as though it had been invited. †See also: magpies, lawyers. --- "Seal count," said Sisyphus, settling his shoulders against warm granite. "Two burnt, one damp, one that smells powerfully of onions," said Crow. "Onions means a kitchen. Kitchens mean marriages. Marriages mean material." "People," said Sisyphus. "They mean people." --- > *Dear Sisyphus — My husband says "yes, dear" to everything, then does precisely as he pleased anyway. Yesterday he agreed to spend the harvest feast with my mother; today the boat and my brother-in-law are both missing. Am I married to a man or a weathervane? — Windblown of Piraeus* "Dear Windblown. A yes given quickly is not agreement — it is a door closed politely. Stop asking questions with a yes already hidden in them. Next time, say: *tell me our plan for the feast.* Then listen to what he does not say. Your husband is no liar; he is an escape artist, and escape artists only perform for loose audiences. Let him have the sea now and then besides. A man kept from his friends all season is unbearable company in it. Fight fewer battles, and win the ones concerning mothers." *[Crow's note: search the boat. there is always wine.]* "We are not printing that." "Fine. Smaller handwriting." --- The boulder reached the crest at noon, as it had for nine hundred years, give or take the odd earthquake. Sisyphus gave it a pat; it was warm, like bread. It departed downhill with the sound of distant thunder clearing its throat, and he ambled after it, because the walk down was where he did his finest thinking — other people's problems on the way down, his own on the way up. "Ask Kilned-Out after her boy," he said. "Broken arm in the spring, wasn't it? Boys are mostly knees. They mend." --- > *Dear Sisyphus — I throw pots, fire pots, sell pots, and repair the kiln that eats them. My wife says I have become a man-shaped smudge. When am I meant to live? — Kilned Out in Knossos* "Dear Kilned-Out. Decide your hours first, not last. A workshop drinks whatever time you pour into it, then asks why the cup is empty. Choose one evening and guard it like wet clay in the rain. Teach your apprentices the boring jobs properly — you redo their work because redoing is faster, and that is how three apprentices become six hands and no help. Lastly: your wife is not complaining. She is sending smoke signals. Take her somewhere green. Customers forget amphorae. Families remember evenings." *[Crow's note: OR RAISE YOUR PRICES. revolutionary, i know.]* --- > *Dear Sisyphus — I am seventy-one, a widow, and on Thursdays I receive a visit from the butcher. Not for mutton. My daughters say a woman my age ought to be ashamed. Ought I? — Tender of Tarentum* "Dear Tender. At seventy-one, shame is a garment you should have worn out decades ago. Your daughters aren't scandalized; they are frightened. Your heart has already broken once, and they were there for it. Say that to them plainly. Then bring the man to Sunday dinner and enjoy watching them count his teeth. Grief and joy share one house, and neither should sleep alone forever. Marry him or don't, but stop hiding. Thursday is an excellent day for honesty." *[Crow's note: which butcher? asking for a friend. the friend is me.]* --- > *Dear Sisyphus — My neighbour complains. The wind, the figs, the price of figs, the wind again. He follows me along my own fence narrating ruin. I have begun regarding the ravine with professional interest. — Cornered in Corinth* "Dear Cornered. Complainers want a witness, not a rescue. Grant him ten minutes on your terms — *walk with me as far as the gate, Philitas* — and listen properly. It is astonishing how quiet people become once they feel heard. You need not attend every performance you are invited to; gates exist. And consider that complaint may be the only conversation anyone offers the poor fellow. You may be the best thing on his street. As for the ravine: it has never once improved the price of figs." *[Crow's note: I know several excellent ravines. reasonable rates.]* --- > *Dear Sisyphus — My brother-in-law says a man should find his purpose and want more. I mend nets. I like mending nets. Must I want more? — Contentish of Naxos* "Dear Contentish. Wanting more makes a fine servant and a terrible master. Try a better question than *what is my purpose*: if nobody ever knew, would you still mend the nets well? If the answer is yes, then you are not lost — you are found, and your brother-in-law is merely bored. Purpose is not a trumpet on a summit. Some days will knock you flat and roll you all the way down to the bottom of yourself. Stand up kindly, and begin the same small work again. That steadiness is the entire secret. Everything else is noise." On the slope, the boulder paused, in the manner of one who suspects he is being discussed. --- Crow loaded the day's replies, plus one marginal note he had won through sheer persistence. The gods, it may be recalled, had filed the whole arrangement under PUNISHMENT. Sisyphus had spent nine centuries meaning to submit a correction. "Incoming," said Crow, dropping a fresh bundle. One letter was sealed with black wax that he declined to touch. Sisyphus whistled, put his shoulder to the evening's work, and began to push — with the serenity of a man who knows exactly what tomorrow holds, and does not mind one bit.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his blend of wit, wisdom, and whimsy. The author skillfully avoids the obvious pitfalls outlined in the prompt - there are no heavy-handed boulder metaphors, no forced fish-out-of-water humor, and no overwrought philosophical treatises. Instead, Sisyphus emerges as genuinely wise and naturally gifted at advice-giving. The epistolary format works exceptionally well, with each letter presenting distinct voices and realistic problems. The advice itself is genuinely insightful and practical, particularly the responses about marriage dynamics ("A yes given quickly is not agreement — it is a door closed politely") and finding purpose in simple work. The characterization of Sisyphus is nuanced - he's neither bitter nor artificially cheerful, but genuinely content and wise from experience. The Pratchett-style footnotes are well-executed and add authentic flavor without feeling forced. Crow's interjections provide excellent comic relief while maintaining character consistency. The prose flows naturally with Pratchett's characteristic rhythm and observational humor. The piece successfully shows rather than tells Sisyphus's transformation into an advice columnist, letting his wisdom emerge through his responses rather than exposition. The humor is understated and emerges organically from the situations and character interactions. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Pratchett pastiche feels slightly self-conscious, and the ending, while satisfying, doesn't quite reach the emotional resonance of Pratchett's best work. The piece also could have benefited from slightly more development of the relationship between Sisyphus and Crow. The writing demonstrates strong technical skill, with varied sentence structures and excellent control of tone. The imagery is vivid without being overwrought, and the world-building feels authentic to both Greek mythology and Pratchett's Discworld sensibilities. + Coming of age: Lost & Found in Osaka — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Lost & Found in Osaka** *Scene Three* The noise of Den Den Town was a wall — pachinko thunder leaking through shuttered doors, the chirp of a hundred gacha machines, vendors calling prices into the current of bodies on Ota Road. Sumire moved through it the way she moved through everything: shoulders drawn in, oversized headphones clamped down like a helmet, world muted to a comfortable hum. Then the guitar cut through. Fast. Bright. A melody she knew before she'd finished deciding she knew it — *Cruel Angel's Thesis*, but faster than the record, sharper, played like the song owed the guitarist money. Sumire stopped so abruptly a man with shopping bags clipped her elbow and kept going. Near the arcade entrance, a girl stood on a small rubber mat with a Fender Stratocaster slung low and a shoebox open at her feet. Behind her, a tiny amp and a gray stompbox. She hit the last note with a tapped run up the high frets and held it, grinning at the applause like it was a tip she hadn't earned yet. Sumire's mouth moved before her brain could stop it. "You didn't slow down." The guitarist looked up. "Hm?" "The—the bridge." Sumire's ears went hot. "On the record there's a... a slight ritardando. Before the last chorus. You didn't do it. You went *up* in tempo." Her voice shrank with every word. "Sorry. Sorry, that's—that wasn't criticism." "It absolutely sounded like criticism." The girl laughed, not unkindly, and wiped her palm on her jeans. "It's on purpose. The slowdown always felt like an apology to me. Like the song getting tired. I don't think it should get tired." She tilted her head, studying Sumire the way she'd study a strange chord voicing. "You've been standing there for three songs, by the way." "I wasn't—" Sumire nodded, a reflexive denial, and the headphones slipped forward off one ear. She fumbled them back. "Sorry." "Okay, see, that keeps happening. Every time you nod. They're bigger than your head. What are they?" "Sony. MDR-7506." Then, quieter, like she was confessing to something: "...Bought used. One driver was blown, so I—I replaced it." "You repair headphones." The guitarist crouched and nudged the gray stompbox with her boot. "Quick test. What's this?" "That's—" And here Sumire's voice changed, steadied, like a hand finding a familiar rail in the dark. "Boss RC-1. Looper. You recorded the bassline first, then the chords over it, then played the melody live on top. Three passes. Your timing on the overdubs is really clean. Most people rush the second layer." The girl stared at her. Then she threw both arms up. "*Finally.* Do you know how many people watched me today? Hundreds. One guy asked if the box was a karaoke machine. You're the first person who knew what it does." "Oh. Um." Nod. Slip. Fumble. "Sorry." "Stop apologizing, it's fine. I'm Aki." She stuck out her hand, still holding her pick. "...Sumire." The handshake lasted half a heartbeat. "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt your—you're working." "Eh, I was due a break. So what's your instrument? Guitar?" "No. I mean—not really. I don't—synths." She said it fast, like ripping off a bandage. "Synthesizers. Mostly. I have a microKORG. And a Volca Beats. And—" She hesitated, then couldn't help herself. "And a DX7." Aki's eyebrows went up. "A DX7? Those are ancient. My uncle had one. Half the keys didn't work." "Mine too. When I got it. There's a junk bin at one of the recycle shops back there—" she pointed vaguely toward the tangle of secondhand electronics stores, "—and it was marked 'junk, for parts,' and it was four thousand yen, and the problem was just the button membranes. And the backup battery. So I..." She trailed off under Aki's expression. "What?" "Nothing. It's just—" Aki pointed the pick at her like a conductor's baton. "You have this whole face going. Like there's a concert happening behind your eyes and nobody bought tickets." Sumire looked at the pavement. "That's... probably accurate." "Okay, expert question." Aki hopped up onto the low ledge beside the arcade doors, guitar across her knees. "The original recording of the song I just played. The synth solo in the middle. What's it?" "FM synthesis. Probably a DX7-family patch, or—and this is heresy—a TX816 rack. Everyone thinks it's a preset but the operator ratios are tweaked, the feedback's higher than stock, you can hear it in the attack transient, it's got this little—" She caught herself mid-air-gesture. "...Sorry. You didn't actually want the answer." "I wanted *exactly* that answer." Aki was grinning wide now. "Sumire. You listen like you're taking notes. It's kind of terrifying. I love it." "I'm not—I'm not interesting, though. I just read manuals. For fun." "That is the most interesting thing anyone's said to me all week." Aki swung the guitar around to her back and started coiling cables with quick, practiced loops. "Okay. Executive decision. I've been playing out here since noon, my hands are dying, and there's a Sushiro two streets over where the plates are a hundred and twenty yen and nobody cares if you take four hours." Sumire blinked. "Four hours of... sushi?" "Of talking. The sushi is just an excuse." Aki slung her gig bag over one shoulder and held out the empty hand. "Come on. You can tell me why my looper timing is clean, and I'll tell you how I learned this stupid song, and we'll see whose story's more embarrassing." "I—I don't—" Sumire nodded, caught the headphones with both hands this time, and stood there holding them against her head like a person keeping their hat on in wind. "Why me?" Aki shrugged, easy. "Because you stayed for three songs. People who stay for three songs are my favorite kind of people." She wiggled the offered hand. "Well? I'm starving, and the good plates go fast." Sumire looked at the hand. At the arcade spilling light and noise behind it. At the street full of strangers who had never once asked her a single question. "...Okay," she said. Barely a whisper. Then, louder, surprising even herself: "Okay." "Cool." Aki grinned and turned down the side street, walking backward a few steps so she could talk facing her. "Fair warning, I eat a disgusting amount of salmon. Don't judge me." "I wasn't going to—" "You were going to judge me a *little*. Everyone does." She spun forward again. "So. The DX7. Walk me through the repair. From the top." And Sumire, headphones finally sitting right, found—to her enormous surprise—that she had a lot to say.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and character development within the slice-of-life genre. The author successfully creates two distinct voices: Sumire's hesitant, technical precision contrasted with Aki's confident, playful energy. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character, advancing the relationship, and providing exposition about their shared musical interests. The setting of Den Den Town is efficiently established through sensory details that feel authentic rather than touristy. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 87.8
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Five: Tick. Tock. *Twice.* There are three things you should know about me. One: My name is Milo Reyes, and I'm twelve years old. Two: Last Monday, my voice was two octaves higher. Three: I did not mean to grow a mustache. Okay. Deep breath. Let me back up. The watch came from Lucky Finds, the junk shop on Delancey Street, where everything costs a dollar and nothing has a price tag that matches. It was buried in a bin of dead remote controls and happy meal toys — a black smartwatch, sleek, no brand name, its screen swirling like soap bubble in sunlight. "One dollar," said Mr. Ferrous, the owner, without looking up. He has a hundred years of wrinkles and eyes like wet stones. "No refunds. No *returns*." I should have asked what he meant by *returns*. I found out Tuesday, third period, during the math pop quiz I absolutely did not study for. I was poking at the watch under my desk, pressing the little crown on the side, when the classroom went *smear*. Blue-gray smear, like wet paint dragged sideways. Chalk dust floated up off the board and back into Mr. Grubb's hand. His voice played backward — *"sdrawkcab"* — and then— "—pencils *up*," said Mr. Grubb, "quiz begins *now*." My quiz paper was blank. My pencil was sharp. Ten minutes had un-happened. Except inside my head. Inside my head, I remembered every single thing. Guys. Guys. The watch rewound *time*, and it only took me along for the ride. So naturally, being a genius, I used it again. And again. I rewound the pop quiz and aced it. I rewinded the dodgeball game where Tyler Boone beamed me in the face, and caught his killer shot one-handed. I rewinded the moment I tripped in the cafeteria and wore a tray of nachos like a hat. Each time: the blue-gray smear, the world sliding backward, me standing perfectly still inside it. And each time, when the world snapped back — Something was different. About *me.* By Wednesday, I had a dusty shadow of a mustache. By Thursday, my voice cracked so low in English class that Mr. Grubb made me read the grown-up part in our play. My jeans, which fit fine Monday, ended two inches above my ankles. My knuckles looked like walnuts taped to my hands. People started treating me weird. Mr. Grubb handed me the attendance sheet and said, "Run this to the office, would you, *Mister* Reyes?" An eighth grader I've never spoken to in my life nodded at me in the hallway like we were war buddies. A tiny sixth grader stopped me by the water fountain and asked, "Excuse me, sir, do you know where Room 114 is?" *SIR.* Worst of all, my best friend Owen squinted at me at lunch and said, "Are you Milo's older brother? You guys look *exactly* alike." "I'm *Milo*," I said. "Sure," Owen said slowly, the way you talk to someone you don't want to argue with. "Sure you are." That night I dug out my student ID. The picture showed a round-cheeked kid with a gap in his smile. I held it up to the bathroom mirror. The kid in the mirror had a jawline. And stubble. And shoulders that barely fit the frame. The watch sat on the sink, screen glowing softly. In the corner, tiny gray letters I swear weren't there before: **COST ACCRUING.** "Cool," I whispered. "Cool cool cool." Oh — and one more thing. There's a stray cat that lives on the chain-link fence outside Lucky Finds. Gray, raggedy, left ear torn like a movie ticket stub. Normal cat. Ignore-it cat. Except after every rewind, it was *there*. Same fence post. Same exact pose, tail wrapped around its feet. Staring at me. Not the way cats stare at birds or bugs. The way you stare at someone across a crowded room when you thought they died. And here's the part I really don't want to tell you: during the rewind-smear, when the whole world goes blue-gray and melty? The cat stays sharp. Perfectly, horribly sharp. Watching. Friday afternoon, my little sister Zoe fell off the monkey bars. I heard the crack from the basketball court. I heard her scream. I saw her arm bent where arms do not bend, and Ms. Alvarez shouting into her walkie, and I felt my whole soul drop through the pavement. And I did the dumbest, most human thing imaginable. I spun the crown as far as it would go. The screen flashed **MAX**. The world smeared blue-gray — longer than ever, a whole river of smear — and I stood alone in it, heart slamming, until everything snapped back and— Monday morning. I'd overshot. Way overshotted. Four days, gone. But Zoe was alive. Her arm was fine. She was complaining about oatmeal in the kitchen like gravity worked. I laughed until I cried. Then I walked to school, and that's when I saw what I'd done. The marquee outside said **TUESDAY** — and underneath it, ghostly, overlapping, **FRIDAY**, both at once. The old oak by the gate flickered: huge and leafy, then skinny and bare, then huge again, like reality couldn't pick. On the announcements, Principal Ward's voice came through the speakers twice, a half-second apart, saying the same sentence in two slightly different ways. Zoe waved at me from the fourth-grade line — with an arm in a purple cast. An arm attached to an elbow that bent just fine. "You already owe me a dollar from Thursday," Owen told me at my locker. "It *is* Thursday," I said. "No," he said, frowning at something over my shoulder, at something that wasn't there. "It's also Monday. Why is it also Monday, Milo?" Everyone was looking at me funny now. Not *older-brother* funny. Worse. Like I was a song they half-remembered from a dream. The watch buzzed against my wrist. **SYNCHRONIZATION FAILED.** **REVERSE CLOCK TO RESYNC.** **REWINDS REMAINING: 1.** One. One rewind left, and my skin crawled, because I understood, suddenly, completely, what **COST ACCRUING** meant. Every spin of the crown had been paid for. Out of me. And I did not want to find out what the last payment bought. "Hey," said a voice like a radio between stations. "*Kid.*" The gray cat dropped off the fence post. Walked straight across the sidewalk — through the flicker, through the double-shadow world — and sat down on my sneaker. Around its neck, glinting, was a collar tag I'd never seen up close. Engraved on it: ***PROPERTY OF M. REYES.*** "Don't waste the last one," the cat said, blinking slow green eyes. "Take it from somebody who used to have hands." Somewhere behind me, a bell rang for a class that hasn't happened yet. I grabbed the crown. The cat smiled.

His voice feels authentically twelve years old, with believable motivations and reactions. The progression from excitement to horror as he discovers the consequences feels natural and earned. The supporting characters, while brief, serve their purposes well, especially Owen's confused recognition and the mysterious cat's revelation. The prose style strikes an excellent balance between accessible and sophisticated. Phrases like "the world went smear" and "blue-gray smear, like wet paint dragged sideways" create vivid, memorable imagery without becoming overwrought. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from discovery through experimentation to consequences and crisis. The timeline fracturing is handled with creative visual details (the flickering marquee, overlapping announcements) that make the abstract concept concrete and unsettling. The dialogue feels natural throughout, particularly Milo's internal voice and his interactions with peers. The cat's final line delivers genuine chills while maintaining the story's tone. The mystery elements are well-layered, with clues planted effectively (the cat's consistent presence, the "COST ACCRUING" message). Some minor weaknesses include occasional rushed transitions and a few moments where the exposition could be more seamlessly integrated. The ending, while appropriately ominous, leaves perhaps too many questions unanswered for a complete chapter experience. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise strong piece that successfully captures the essence of classic teen horror while bringing fresh elements to familiar tropes. Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions The lamps along the boardwalk came on the way rumors do—one, then another, then all at once, buzzing awake in a haze of amber. Sodium light, the new kind, and it lied about everything: it turned the sea the color of weak tea, the candy apples into embers, and every face on the boardwalk into warm candle wax. When the current stuttered—and it stuttered constantly, some fault in the wires or the times—the faces changed. A sailor's grin went hollow as a skull. A fat man mid-laugh looked briefly like a man screaming. Then the light steadied, and everyone was ordinary again, and nobody seemed to notice but her. She stopped before the shooting gallery, where tin ducks rattled past on their chain and the air smelled of cordite, burnt sugar, and brine. *His locks are bushy, and black as a raven.* There it was again. She knew the line the way she knew the shape of her own teeth—from the green Bible with the cracked spine, from the one book of Scripture nobody preached on Sundays. A love poem, smuggled into the Good Book like a letter hidden in a drawer. That her mind should fetch it up, unasked, for a stranger's head—that was the trouble. That was the entire trouble. "You came." He was leaning on the counter as though he'd grown there, sleeves rolled, forearms dusted with gun-oil and gold light. "I said I would." "People say a great many things to strangers on a boardwalk. It's practically the local industry." He smiled, and in the stuttering glare his eyes went gold, then black, then gold again. He reached into his canvas apron and drew out a glove. Kid leather, buttoned at the wrist. Hers. "Tuesday," he said. "You left it on the rail." She reached for it. He held on a half-second longer than necessary, and then let it go. Their fingers never touched. She was almost sorry, and the almost frightened her more than the touch would have. There was nothing to confess. Not yet. Only a walk she hadn't mentioned at home, a name she hadn't asked for, ten cents about to be spent on a stranger's eyes. Small sins. The kind that fit through keyholes. "Ten cents, five shots," he said. "Hit three ducks, I tell you my name. Miss all five, you answer one question of mine—truthfully. House rules." "And if I hit all five?" "Then I'm wrong about you, and we'll both be disappointed." The rifle was lighter than she'd imagined, worn smooth at the stock by a thousand stranger hands. He came around the counter and stood close enough that she could smell the powder on him. "Elbow in. Cheek down. Breathe out slow, and then—don't." She obeyed. That was the remarkable thing, she thought, how easily—as if her body had convened some committee without her and signed papers on her behalf. The first shot went wide and spanged off the backing board. The second rang a duck clean off its hinge. Third, fourth—clang, clang, little tin deaths. On the fifth, the lamp overhead died altogether. One full second of true dark: sea-sound, a distant organ grinder, his profile beside hers simply gone. The light snapped back. She fired on the relight. Clang. "Four," he said, and something in his voice had shifted—or the light had shifted it, dragging his youth sideways into something older. "Three was our bargain. You've overshot yourself." He set the rifle down with a craftsman's care. "Absalom." "That's a name out of a story." "All names are. Mine more than most. The fortune teller pinned it on me—said I'd come to a bad end, and that my hair would have something to do with it. Showmanship." A pause. "Mostly." She realized she was staring at his hair—the black curls pushed back off his brow, gleaming dull bronze under the guttering lamp. A traitorous thought arrived, unbidden: what one curl would feel like wound tight around her finger. She put it down the way you put down a live wire. "You're staring," he said, not unkindly. Heat climbed her throat. "I am not." "Everyone does. It's the best advertisement I've got." He leaned in, just slightly. "Careful, though. My mother used to say every Delilah starts out a good girl." "Was your mother a fortune teller as well?" "She was a cautionary tale." The lamp buzzed, dimmed, rallied. Down the boardwalk the crowd flickered with it—faces gilded, gutted, gilded again—and she understood suddenly that the light did to everyone what this man did to her: showed a different face each time she blinked. "And my fourth duck?" she managed. "What does that buy?" "A question. Any question you like, answered honestly. Most people waste it." She ought to ask the sensible things. Where he slept. What he wanted. Whether he was trouble. Instead she heard herself say: "Why me?" He considered her the way he might sight down a barrel—patiently, with a stillness that made the fairground noise fall away. "Tonight? Nothing," he said. "Tonight I only wanted to learn whether you keep promises made to strangers." He tapped the counter once, softly. "You do. It's the most dangerous thing about you. Everything else can be bought or taught." A barker's cry went up somewhere behind them, a wheel clattered, a child shrieked with delight or terror—it was impossible to say which, here. "Friday," he said. "Eleven o'clock. The tents shut at eleven." "And you?" "I don't." She walked away without trusting her legs to consult her first, buttoning the glove as she went, the leather still holding the ghost of his pocket's warmth. Behind her the ducks clanked on their endless circuit, riding their little chain like souls on a Ferris wheel. The lamp overhead steadied at last, and in the steady light he was only a young man at a shooting gallery—which was somehow worse. *His locks are bushy, and black as a raven.* The verse rose one final time, and this time she didn't press it down. She let it run on, verse after verse, all the way down the boardwalk and into the dark— like footsteps following her home.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated literary craftsmanship with several notable strengths and minor weaknesses. The author successfully creates the requested atmosphere of romantic allure tinged with danger, establishing tension through carefully controlled pacing and evocative imagery. The prose style is notably elegant, employing vivid metaphors like "The lamps along the boardwalk came on the way rumors do" and the recurring motif of flickering lights that transform faces. The biblical allusion to Song of Solomon ("His locks are bushy, and black as a raven") adds literary depth and connects to the character's name, Absalom, creating thematic coherence around biblical figures who met tragic ends. Character development is nuanced, particularly the unnamed female protagonist whose internal conflict between propriety and desire feels authentic to the 1937 setting. Absalom emerges as genuinely mysterious rather than merely brooding, with dialogue that reveals character while maintaining intrigue. His line "every Delilah starts out a good girl" demonstrates the author's skill at layering meaning. The dialogue feels natural and period-appropriate, comprising roughly the requested 50% of the piece. The shooting gallery scene serves as an effective metaphor for the dangerous game both characters are playing. The internal monologue captures the protagonist's psychological state convincingly, showing her rationalization of "small sins" and her body's betrayal of her conscious intentions. The pacing builds tension effectively toward the Friday rendezvous setup. The ending avoids false resolution while maintaining the established mood. The imagery of ducks "riding their little chain like souls on a Ferris wheel" exemplifies the author's ability to find fresh metaphors that serve the story's themes. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose approaches purple territory, though it generally stays on the right side of the line. Some descriptions, while beautiful, occasionally prioritize style over clarity. The piece also relies heavily on atmosphere over plot advancement, though this suits the prompt's focus on tension-building. The author successfully captures the "restrained classic sensibility" requested while maintaining an edge. The moral ambiguity emerges naturally from character choices rather than forced circumstances. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Two Supper that night was beans and franks, same as the first night of every season since JT could remember, and that was exactly the problem: everything was the same, and nothing was. His father barely touched his plate. Mike cleaned his twice and asked for more. Backwards. Mike had been the finicky one since he was six years old, the boy who wouldn't eat stew because the carrots had *looked at him*. Now he shoveled like a man fueling a furnace. "You see how it stood there," his father said. Not a question. He was looking at the wall above the stove, at the antlers they'd nailed up over thirty autumns, but JT didn't think he was seeing any of them. "How it waited." "Like it wanted to," Mike said. JT's fork stopped halfway to his mouth. Their father nodded slowly, the way a man nods at scripture. "My father used to say the woods gives you the animal when the animal's ready to be given. I figured that was old-man talk." He smiled down at his beans. "I think I finally understand him." Nobody laughed. Nobody was supposed to. "Tomorrow we'll go up the ridge," he added. "Past the Prentiss place." JT looked up sharply. "Nobody goes past the Prentiss place." "That's why the caribou'll be there." Mike frowned. "Who's Prentiss?" "Hunted these woods forty years," their father said, in the tone of a man reciting directions. "One October he didn't come out. They found his truck at the end of the logging spur. His rifle was leaned against the cabin door—unloaded, muzzle down in the mud, like somebody had planted it. No body. No blood. No tracks going away." He sipped his coffee. "Door standing open about a hand's width." "And the smoke," JT said, before he could stop himself. Both of them looked at him. "The guys at the gas station in Twin Brook talk about it. Smoke off the chimney some mornings. And in winter—no tracks. Snow right up to the door, never broken." Their father considered this with an expression JT couldn't read. "That's the story," he agreed mildly. "Some say somebody lives out there. Something. Never seen. Never leaves tracks." He set the cup down with a small ceramic click. "Course, nobody ever saw a caribou stand still to be shot, either. Until this week." Mike laughed—one beat too late, like a sound dubbed into a foreign film. "Ghost story," he said, reaching for the potatoes. "Never said it was a ghost," their father said, and that ended the conversation, because when he ended a conversation, it stayed ended. --- JT lay awake in the bunkroom under a quilt that smelled of cedar and mouse droppings, listening to the lodge tick and settle. Around midnight—the clock on the nightstand had stopped at 12:00 sometime in the nineties and no one had ever fixed it—the porch boards took on a slow, careful weight. One person. Bare feet. He got up and looked through the frost-feathered glass. His father stood at the rail in his union suit, bareheaded, breath smoking, facing north. Toward the ridge. Toward the Prentiss place, though from the porch there was nothing to see but black spruce and stars. He stood so long that frost began to silver his hair, his shoulders, like the first stages of a statue. *Go out there,* something urged. *Call to him. Drag him inside.* JT opened his mouth—and his father's head began to turn. Not all the way. Just enough. Just enough that JT understood, with a certainty that lived somewhere below thought, that he was being listened to. He dropped beneath the sill, heart slamming. He counted to a hundred, then a hundred again. When he finally risked another look, the porch was empty. The rail wore a skin of frost—except for two hand-shaped patches where his father had gripped it. *Dream,* he told himself. *You dreamed it. The silence up here does that. Presses on your ears till the brain makes noise to fill the hole.* The lie tasted like copper, but he swallowed it. What else was there to swallow? --- Morning came hard and bright, cold enough to make the door hinges squeal. Their father was cheerful—bright-eyed, flushed, humming something tuneless under his breath. It was the wrong kind of cheerful. It was *clearing*-cheerful. "Ridge today," he said, and smiled, and JT thought: *that's not how he smiles.* There was too much room in it. Too much space between the teeth. The woods were wrong too. No jays scolding. No squirrels. Nothing running anywhere, because nothing ran anymore. Twice they passed caribou standing among the trunks, close enough to touch, heads swinging to follow them with the smooth patience of lighthouse beams. Mike walked within twenty feet of a heavy-beamed bull and never raised his rifle. None of them did. The guns had become things they carried, like walking sticks. Like rosaries. The cabin appeared the way things appear in dreams: suddenly, completely, as if it had stepped out from behind the world. Gray shakes gone soft with moss. A stone chimney with a thread of smoke rising dead straight in the windless cold, straight as a plumb line dropped from heaven. And the caribou. Dozens. Standing in the dooryard, between the trees, along the collapsed fence—all facing the cabin, spaced with a regularity that crawled up JT's spine like mourners who had rehearsed. Their breath rose and fell in unison. In. Out. In. Out. One lung, shared. His father waded in without slowing. The herd parted before him, silent, none turning their heads—only the eyes moving, tracking. Mike followed, wearing his own too-roomy smile. JT stopped at the treeline. *Run,* something screamed in him. *Grab Mike, shout, run.* But his legs had gone to wood, and besides—where? He glanced over his shoulder, and the bottom dropped out of his stomach. Caribou stood in the woods behind him, too. Evenly spaced. Facing inward. They weren't guarding the cabin. They had never been guarding the cabin. They were a drive line, and the drive had been closing all season—maybe all his life—patient as winter, and the clearing was the corral, and he was already inside it. At the cabin, his father climbed the rotted steps and paused before the door, which stood ajar on darkness. He didn't knock. He bowed his head slightly, the way men do entering church. "He kept his part of it," he said softly—to the door, to the dark, to whatever in there breathed in rhythm with the herd. "We're keeping ours." From inside came a long, unhurried exhale. The chimney smoke bent sideways, against the windless morning, and pointed—at the treeline, at the gap where JT stood. Every caribou in the clearing turned its head at once and looked at him. The nearest one took a single step forward. Then another. Unhurried. It had all the time in the world, and it seemed to know that sooner or later he would do what everything in these woods eventually did. It would stop running. It would wait for the shot.

His father's transformation is subtly rendered through behavioral details - the wrong kind of cheerfulness, the too-roomy smile, the midnight vigil on the porch. Mike's personality reversal (from finicky eater to ravenous) provides an unsettling detail that reinforces the wrongness without explanation. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building dread. The father's exposition about Prentiss feels organic to the campfire storytelling tradition, while his final declaration at the cabin carries genuine menace. The structure builds expertly toward the revelation that JT has been driven into a trap. The final image of him being hunted like the caribou provides a satisfying thematic payoff that recontextualizes the entire narrative. The pacing never drags, and each scene serves the larger arc while maintaining its own internal tension. The prose flows naturally with varied sentence structures that create rhythm and emphasis. The author demonstrates restraint, allowing implications to carry weight rather than over-explaining the supernatural elements. Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Model Output:
# Hell Is Other Demons Hell did not have mornings, strictly speaking. It had a consensus—arrived at over several millennia of negotiation and at least two civil wars—that the great red ceiling would dim at appointed hours so that everyone could pretend to sleep. Lucifer Morningstar had signed off on the consensus personally, back when he still believed in compromise. It was, he reflected, the last compromise he'd ever enjoyed. He woke alone in a bed built for two apocalypses, which is to say it was very large and very cold on one side, and he lay there for the customary eleven minutes pretending he wasn't counting them. Downstairs, Hell was already queueing. That was the secret nobody up top ever guessed: eternal damnation was mostly queues. Souls snaked through the obsidian concourse clutching numbered tickets, waiting to be processed into their appropriate circles, and the processing was handled by demons who had unionized in 1347 and had been insufferable about it ever since. Lucifer took his coffee—which tasted of burnt churches—and settled onto the Iron Throne to hold court. The throne wobbled. It had been wobbling for three weeks, ever since Mercy got at the left front leg. Mercy was Lucifer's hellhound, a wolfhound the size of a cathedral with eyes like banked coals and a name chosen, Lucifer maintained, ironically. Mercy did not show any. What Mercy showed was an unwavering commitment to chewing the throne's leg, specifically the left front one, specifically the part where the iron had been folded seven times over the screaming of the first tyrant Lucifer had ever deposed. Connoisseurs said it gave the metal character. Mercy apparently agreed. "Drop it," Lucifer said, without looking. Mercy dropped it, wagged once—a tectonic event that rattled the dais—and picked it back up. "You are a dog of the Pit," Lucifer told him. "You were whelped in the Second Circle. You have chased the souls of emperors across burning plains until they begged for the sweet mercy of oblivion." Mercy chewed thoughtfully. The Vice-Undersecretary of Torment arrived then, a squat demon named Malphas with clipboards growing out of him the way barnacles grow out of ships. "Morning, Lord. We've got the appeals backlog again—the damned have filed another forty thousand petitions citing 'unfair sentencing,' and the Frozen Lake is thawing on the north shore because somebody in Maintenance keeps scheduling the blizzards wrong, and—" Malphas consulted a clipboard, wincing at whatever grew there, "—there's a visitor." "I'm not seeing anyone." "She said you'd say that." "Then she knows me disturbingly well," said Lucifer, "and I'm still not seeing anyone." But Lilith came up the obsidian stair anyway, because Lilith had never once in the history of creation waited to be announced, announced herself, or otherwise acknowledged that doors applied to her. She wore the morning like a gown she'd designed out of spite. She looked, Lucifer noted with professional admiration, magnificent, which was infuriating, because he'd been hoping she'd look terrible. "Luce." "Lilith. To what do I owe the intrusion?" She held up a small black box. "Your raven died on my doorstep." "That's not my raven." "It had your seal on its leg." "It had my seal on *a* leg. Ravens steal things. It's practically their whole personality." He gestured vaguely. "Leave it with Malphas. He does bereavement." Malphas made a noise like a filing cabinet falling downstairs and withdrew, taking several clipboards with him, which was the closest thing Hell had to tact. Lilith did not leave. She walked the length of the hall instead, trailing one finger along the armrests of the damned, past the braziers, until she stood before the throne, regarding its wobbling leg with the expression of a woman cataloguing evidence. "Your throne is broken." "My throne is *fine*." "It's listing. Like a ship. Like a ship captained by someone who refuses to admit he's sinking." Her mouth curved. "Still can't train the beast, then." "He's a hellhound. He isn't meant to be trained, he's meant to be *feared*." "Mm." Lilith crouched, and Mercy—who had ignored Lucifer for three weeks, who had ignored the combined commands of two Archdukes just yesterday—rolled onto his back immediately and presented his belly like an offering at a temple. She scratched. Mercy made a sound like distant artillery being happy. Lucifer watched this betrayal with the serene face he'd once worn while casting angels out of Heaven, and inside that face, quietly, something ached. This was how the cycle went. She would arrive for some pretext—a dead bird, a border dispute in the Eighth Circle, a soul she wanted transferred—and she would stay an hour, or an evening, or once, memorably, a decade, and then some old wound would open between them like weather, and she'd be gone again, and he'd tell the court he preferred it that way, and everyone would nod in the way that subjects nod at kings who are lying. "Adam sent me a letter," she said, to the dog. "Did he." "Asked if I'd consider coming back to Eden. Says the new model humans don't argue properly. Says the garden's gone to seed since—" She stopped. She was very good at stopping mid-sentence in ways that made you lean forward into the silence. "Since what?" said Lucifer, leaning, hating himself for leaning. "Since nobody interesting lived there." They regarded each other across the throne room, two immortals with ten thousand years of grievances and exactly one working subject between them, currently receiving belly rubs. "The leg could be reforged," Lilith said at last, standing, brushing off her knees. "Seven-fold iron. I know a smith in the mountains of the Fourth Circle. Terrible conversationalist. Excellent work." She paused at the top of the stair, silhouetted against the red dimness. "I'll send him tomorrow. I may come and supervise." "You may," said Lucifer, "find it tedious." "I usually do," she said, and was gone. Lucifer sat on his listing throne for a long time. Then he rang for Malphas and said, "Clear my afternoon." "All of it, Lord?" "All of it. And find out everything about smiths in the Fourth Circle. Names, families, prices. Discreetly." "And shall I have Maintenance look at the throne leg in the meantime?" "No," said Lucifer, scratching Mercy's ears at last, magnanimous in victory. "Leave the leg. It's finally getting some attention down there." Mercy wagged. Somewhere above them, faintly, Heaven pretended not to notice.

The characterization is nuanced and believable. Lilith is portrayed with appropriate mystique and power, arriving uninvited yet offering subtle gestures of care through the throne repair suggestion. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Wheel They woke us before dawn, as they always did, with the rattle of iron keys and the smell of tallow smoke bleeding into the barracks. Forty men breathing in the dark, straw rustling, someone coughing the wet cough that takes the old fighters first. I lay a moment with my eyes closed and my thumb moving over the little clay wheel at my throat — Fortuna's wheel, bought with my first purse of prize silver from a shrine-seller near the Circus — and I said her name silently, the way other men say a lover's. *Fortuna. Turn gently.* They call me Ferox. *Fierce.* The lanista chose it the day I came off the slave ship at Ostia, thin as a whip handle and sick with the sea. My true name I have never spoken aloud in this city. It lives in my head, in my mother's voice, and nowhere else. Rome has taken everything else; it will not have that too. Breakfast was barley porridge and beans, ash cakes pressed into our hands, vinegar-water to drink. Men complain, but I understood early what the barley meant: they feed us as farmers feed oxen, because we are livestock that performs. A fat beast pulls the plow; a hard one dies well in the sand. We are called *hordearii*, the barley-men, and there is no insult in it anyone intends, which is somehow worse. In the yard the sun climbed over the wall of the Ludus Magnus and found the dust already hanging in the air, gold-colored, tasting of chalk and old sweat. Wood cracked against wood down the line as the younger men worked their posts. The doctore moved among them shouting corrections in Latin I no longer have to translate. I drilled lightly, enough to keep the heat in my shoulders, and watched the shadow of the great amphitheater shorten across the floor. On still mornings you can almost hear it — that hollow, waiting silence a building keeps when it has swallowed ten thousand deaths and been paid in applause. At midday the steward took me out with two others to buy lamp oil in bulk, which is how I get my street. Rome in summer hits you like a hand: the reek of the fish stalls and the sweet rot of fruit gone over, bread and hot ash from the ovens, incense drifting from a doorway shrine, dung, roses, the brown breath of the Tiber. Hammers everywhere — Rome is always hammering itself into new shapes. Children spotted me first. They always do. They ran alongside chanting *Fer-ox, Fer-ox* until a porter shoved them laughing out of the way, and a dyer leaned from his shop and called out odds on the next games as if I were a horse. Near the Forum we passed the column they are raising for the emperor — scaffolded to the sky, sculptors swarming it like ants, stone by stone telling the story of the Dacian wars. My wars. I stood in the shade of the scaffolding and looked up at the spiral of it and saw, carved forever in marble, my countrymen falling. Somewhere up there a village burns that I walked through as a boy. Four years ago they carried King Decebalus's head through these same streets on a bier, and the crowd cheered as if it were a festival day, and I stood among them with my hood up and cheered too, because a dead man does not get to grieve in public. That is Rome. It does not hate you. It simply consumes you, and puts your defeat in stone so the eating lasts a thousand years. The porters waiting by the oil shop talked politics the way Romans breathe. Grain ships late out of Alexandria again; the dole queue restive; the aedile-designate Numisius promising beasts from Africa and pairs of fighters enough to fill three days, spending a fortune he doesn't have to buy a career he can't afford. "Bread and the games," one of them laughed, "that's the whole contract, brother. Keep the belly full and the eyes busy and nobody asks who counts the gold." Nobody asked. That was the whole trick of it. Back inside, the Greek rubbed me down with oil and scraped me clean with the strigil, counting my scars like coins. "You're worth triple what Vettius paid," he said, pleased, as though he spoke of a vase. Old Flamma sat nearby oiling his joints, the Sicilian with his four refusals of the wooden sword behind him. They offered him the *rudis* — freedom, actual freedom, the stick itself in his hand — four times, and four times he gave it back for another season of the roar. "Freedom's cold," he told me once, not boasting, warning. "The crowd never is." I have watched him at night sometimes, listening to the city, and I think he is the freest unfree man I know, and I am afraid of becoming him. Supper was beans, a heel of bread, a spoonful of honey the steward sells from his own portion. Small mercies. Afterward I knelt by my bunk and set Fortuna's wheel on the floor and traced my true name in spilled barley flour — just the letters, quickly, the way you'd warm your hands at a fire — then smoothed it flat with my palm. I prayed to her, because she is mine now, the goddess whose whole business is the turning: the emperor high on his wheel, the beggar low, the fighter face-down in the sand with a stranger's boot on his neck, and none of it permanent, none of it deserved, only the wheel going round. I asked her not for victory. I asked her for a gentle revolution. Nine days until Numisius's games. They say I'm matched against the Gaul, the murmillo with the fish crest who has never needed a second pass. Under my fear there is arithmetic: five more palms and Vettius must weigh the *rudis*. Five. Far off, Rome went on breathing — cart wheels, a drunk singing, dogs arguing over bones — and above the rooftops the amphitheater held its silence, patient as stone. I closed my hand around the little wheel and slept, and dreamed, as I always dream, in a language no one in this city speaks.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in historical fiction writing. The author creates a vivid, immersive portrayal of gladiatorial life in ancient Rome through the eyes of Ferox, a Dacian warrior turned gladiator. The narrative successfully avoids the expected combat scene, instead offering an intimate character study that reveals the psychological and emotional complexity of a man caught between cultures and identities. The sensory details are particularly strong - the "tallow smoke bleeding into the barracks," the "dust already hanging in the air, gold-colored, tasting of chalk and old sweat," and the overwhelming assault of Roman street smells create an authentic atmosphere. The author demonstrates solid historical knowledge, weaving in period-appropriate details like the Ludus Magnus, the Dacian wars, Trajan's column, and the Roman grain dole system. The characterization of Ferox is nuanced and compelling. His internal conflict between his true Dacian identity and his Roman gladiator persona creates genuine emotional depth. The detail of him keeping his real name secret while tracing it in barley flour is particularly effective. His relationship with Fortuna and the wheel metaphor provides thematic coherence without being heavy-handed. The prose style is generally elegant and controlled, with strong imagery and natural sentence flow. The author effectively captures the voice of an educated barbarian who has learned to navigate Roman society while maintaining his inner identity. The political and social commentary feels organic to the narrative rather than forced. However, there are some minor weaknesses. Certain phrases occasionally veer toward the overwrought ("Rome is always hammering itself into new shapes"), and a few moments feel slightly purple in their construction. The piece also relies somewhat heavily on familiar gladiator tropes, though it executes them well. The ending strikes an appropriate tone - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. The countdown to the next games and the mention of five more victories needed for freedom creates natural tension without requiring resolution in this slice-of-life piece. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper **1. Ewan to his mother — 14 March 1965** Dear Mam, I'm at the Cape and settled. The van from Durness takes two hours over the Moine, and the driver talked the whole way, which was a mercy, for the land has nothing to say for itself. Bog and sheep and wind. The station sits above the Clo Mor cliffs — near nine hundred foot, highest on the mainland, they tell me — and when the mist lifts you can see the whole grey edge of Scotland. The Kyle of Durness has to be crossed by ferry at Keoldale, and the ferryman crosses when the tide and his temper suit, so supplies are a fortnightly gamble. I share the watch with a Mr. Rennie, sixty if he's a day, who speaks maybe ten words a week. I'm counting. It's lonely, Mam. I'll no lie. But the wage is good and I'm sending six pounds as arranged. Your son, Ewan **2. Jessie to Ewan — 2 April 1965** Dear Ewan, Six pounds received, thank you. Put your mind at rest about the debt. It's no running away. You'll eat whatever Rennie cooks and thank him for it. A man that talks ten words a week will cook well, mark me. News: the herring's late. Mrs. Sim's boy Donald got his third-hand ticket. Your room is as you left it; I dust round your books. The minister asked after you. I said you were keeping the light, and he said we're all called to keep some light or other, and I said aye, some of us keep the kettle. Waterproof your boots. Sea air eats leather. Mam **3. Ewan to Jessie — 19 June 1965** Dear Mam, The work suits me better than I let on. The optic's a Stevenson — that family built half the lights in Scotland — and there's a pride in it. Paraffin vapour, incandescent mantle, the whole turn carried on a bath of mercury so it swings like a thought. I wind the weights every half hour, and in haar, the horn. I saw whales off the Clo Mor on Tuesday. Three of them, going north like commuters. The cliff tops are white with guillemots just now; you hear them a mile inland, like a market. Rennie spoke eleven words today. He said, "You wind it like you mean it." I'm taking that as a reference. Money enclosed. Tell me honest how the roof stands. Ewan **4. Jessie to Ewan — 8 August 1965** Dear Ewan, Roof stands. The insurance man came and looked and charged me for looking, which is the way of the world. The doctor had me in for a look at my chest. Naething. He's young and likes to be thorough. I told him thoroughness runs dear and he laughed, so he'll go far. Mrs. Sim wants your address for the papers. I said send them care of me. The postman here has kent me forty year; the postman there kens nobody. Eat. Wind your weights. Mind the haar. Mam **5. Ewan to Jessie — 23 October 1965** Dear Mam, We had it proper this week. A gale straight from the northwest, force eleven, spray coming clean over the compound wall, and us four hundred foot up. At two in the morning the watch picked up flares to the south. A Peterhead boat, the *Provident*, engine gone, drifting for the cape. They couldnae see land in the squalls. Our light was the only thing between them and the Clo Mor. They got their bearing off us, clawed off, and ran south for Lochinver. Eleven souls aboard. The skipper's a Buchan; his youngest, Sandy, sat behind me at school. I stood in the lantern room after, shaking, and I understood for the first time why I took this posting. Or near enough. Enclosed six pounds. Ewan **6. Jessie to Ewan — 18 December 1965** Dear Ewan, Glad of the *Provident* news. Sandy Buchan's mother was in the shop greeting and laughing in the one breath. Christmas here was quiet. Turkey from the Co-op, kirk twice, your Auntie Nettie snoring through both. My chest is no mending as quick as I said. Dinna fret. The doctor's a worrier and I'm a poor patient. Keep the light. Mam **7. Ewan to Jessie — 11 February 1966** Dear Mam, The nights are long just now, and I've been carrying a thing I should have posted years ago. The night the *Aurora* went down, Da had asked me to sign on for the winter herring. I refused. I was sick of herring and said so, and said worse besides. Four men lost, him among them. My refusing didnae sink her — I ken that in daylight. But I never said sorry, and then it was too late to say it to him, so I've been saying it to the sea ever since, out a window nine hundred foot above the Clo Mor. The money I send is the last of his debt to the yard. When it's cleared I'll tell you, and we neednae speak of it again unless you want. Tell me true, Mam. Was he angry with me at the end? Did he say anything? Your son, Ewan **8. Telegram — 3 March 1966** MOTHER IN COTTAGE HOSPITAL PETERHEAD PNEUMONIA DOCTOR SAYS NOT DANGEROUS YET COME WHEN RELIEF ALLOWS LOVE NETTIE **9. Ewan to Jessie — 21 April 1966** Dear Mam, Writing this in the visitors' chair, where you can glower at me proper. You're looking better than Nettie says and worse than you'll admit, which is the usual balance of things. You never answered my February letter, and I'm glad, for you told me to my face instead. Forty times I've read what he wrote you from Wick that last trip. *Let the lad find his own water.* I'm leaving the page with you. It's yours. The debt's cleared. Paid the yard on Friday. This is the first envelope in two years with naething in it but a note, and I'll tell you it felt strange. It felt light. I've leave till the May relief and I mean to sit here and be fed. Ewan **10. Ewan to Jessie — 30 June 1966** Dear Mam, Back at the Cape. I chose it, which is a different thing from landing in it. The guillemots have moved out to the far skerries for summer and the cliff path is loud with pipits. First bus of sightseers came over the Moine on Tuesday — eight of them and a dog, and the dog was the best travelled of the party. Rennie spoke fourteen words. Records broken all round. I stood the night watch thinking of nothing much, and it came to me I'm no hiding here any more. The light turns and I turn it, and the Clo Mor stands there being older than any grief, and I sleep fine. Come in July if the chest allows. The ferryman at Keoldale owes me a favour, the bothy has a bed, and I've a fortnight's leave owing. Bring your own tea. Mine's stewed. All my love, Ewan
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative demonstrates strong technical execution and authentic voice work. The author successfully creates two distinct Scottish voices - Ewan's more literary but working-class perspective and his mother Jessie's terse, practical wisdom. The dialect feels natural rather than performative, with phrases like "kent me forty year" and "greeting and laughing in the one breath" that ring true without becoming caricature. The story structure is well-crafted, revealing information gradually through the correspondence format. The central revelation about Ewan's guilt over his father's death emerges organically, and the backstory of debt and family obligation unfolds naturally. The lighthouse setting is vividly rendered through specific technical details (the Stevenson optic, mercury bath, paraffin vapor) that demonstrate research and authenticity. The emotional arc is convincing, moving from isolation and guilt toward acceptance and healing. The dramatic rescue of the *Provident* serves as both plot climax and symbolic turning point, where Ewan understands his purpose. The resolution feels earned rather than forced - his mother's revelation of his father's final words provides genuine catharsis. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Attack Surface The restaurant has two exits, a camera above the register pointed at the ceiling instead of the door, and a point-of-sale terminal running firmware at least two major versions behind. I know all of this because I cannot stop knowing things like this. Ten years of penetration testing rewires something in you. They call it a security mindset. My ex called it a disease. Reformed. That's the word I use. White hat, certified, gainfully employed finding holes in other people's fortresses so bad actors can't walk through them. But habits don't get patched. You can take the exploit out of the hacker, but the hacker keeps enumerating. And right now the hacker is losing badly to the rest of me, because Wren just said the words "casual Commander night" and my entire threat model collapsed. "You play?" she asks, delighted, twirling her pasta. "I have a problem," I confess. "Foiled-out Kess deck. It's a sickness." "Oh no. A control player." She grins like she's caught me doing something shameful, which, fair. "I run Krenko. Goblins. It's chaos. Games either end turn six or I flip the table." I am, against every odd, having a wonderful time. Which is exactly when the breadcrumbs start falling, and the part of my brain I can't firewall starts catching them. "My parents' golden retriever, Biscuit—best dog ever—I still cry about him," she says, laughing at her own sentimentality. *Name of first pet: Biscuit.* Filed. I hate myself. I file it anyway. Then her mom calls mid-dinner and Wren answers, and I hear half the conversation: "No, Mom, tell *Aunt Patty*—okay, okay, tell the whole Okafor side I'll be there Sunday." *Mother's maiden name: Okafor.* There isn't a form on earth that doesn't ask for that one. I stare very hard at my water glass and think about responsible disclosure and how there is no CVE编号 for being a creep at dinner. "And we grew up on Fenwick, this tiny little cul-de-sac, everybody knew everybody—" *Street you grew up on.* Stop. *Stop.* By dessert I've got a full profile assembled without trying, the way rain gets through a roof. First car: hand-me-down Corolla. Childhood nickname: "Bug." I am sitting across from a woman whose security questions I could answer in my sleep, and she's telling me all of it freely, warmly, because that's what people do on dates—they *disclose*. Humans are the only systems that leak by design, that hand over their secrets as a courtship ritual. It's going well. It's going so well. And then she pulls out her phone to show me pictures of her sister's new baby, and she unlocks it right there, three feet away, screen tilted toward me without a shred of suspicion. Four nodes. Starting top-left. Straight down, then straight across. An L. A textbook, dictionary-definition L. Top-ten most common Android patterns on the planet, the kind that falls to a smudge analysis in seconds, the kind I demo in conference talks while the audience gasps. "That's an L," I hear myself say. "From the top-left. Statistically that's crackable in under—" The sentence dies in the air between us. Wren sets the phone down face-first, slowly, the way you'd set down a live grenade. "Were you *watching* me unlock my phone?" "No. Yes. Not—not like that." My mouth keeps executing code my brain never approved. "Shoulder surfing is the oldest vector there is. I wasn't *surfing*, I just—pattern recognition is involuntary for me. It's like hearing someone play a wrong chord." "So you've been reading me all night." Her arms cross. Not playful-crossed. Audited-crossed. Here's the thing about getting caught: you can deny, deflect, or go full transparency. Denial fails against anyone paying attention, and Wren is very obviously smart. So I put down my fork and surrender. "Yes. Occupational hazard. I break into systems for a living—the legal kind—and I can't switch it off. Your dog's name, your mom's maiden name, Fenwick Street, the Corolla. I caught all of it and I hated myself for each one. The phone was the one thing I couldn't quietly ignore, because an L-pattern is genuinely dangerous and apparently I'd rather torpedo a great evening than let you walk around unpatched." Silence. Long enough that I start mapping the exits again, out of pure anxiety habit. "Say all of that again," she finally says, "slower, because I want to decide whether it's the most insulting or the strangest compliment I've ever received." "If I were malicious, you'd never have known anything was wrong. I'd have smiled, taken the intel, and left clean. I blew my own cover instead. Because I like you, and liking you apparently means I want you secure, which is either romantic or deeply pathological. Possibly both." Something shifts in her expression. "So this whole dinner was—you've been running a penetration test on me?" "Passive reconnaissance only. No exploitation attempted. Findings disclosed voluntarily." I slide my napkin across the table, and on impulse, I write down everything: *Biscuit. Okafor. Fenwick. Corolla. Bug. L-pattern.* "Full incident report. Do with it what you will." She stares at it. Then she laughs—a real one, surprised out of her—which is the sound I'd been chasing all night. "You're changing that pattern tonight," I add. "Something with a curve. Never a letter." "Are you negotiating remediation terms?" "I'm a consultant. It's what I do." She picks up the napkin, folds it, and tucks it into her purse instead of tearing it up, which I choose to interpret favorably. "Second date," she says. "You're teaching me Commander. And if you ever catch another one of my passwords, you buy dessert for a year." "Acceptable terms," I say, and mean it, and realize that for the first time all evening I've stopped cataloging the room. Some systems you spend your life breaking into. This one, I think, watching her flag down the waiter, I'd rather be invited into—and honestly, leaving the door unlocked doesn't scare me the way it used to.
