+ Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# What the Stone Keeps *On Serevan they say: the stone keeps what the ship forgot.* The Governor's hall smelled of hot lamps and cut flowers, and the speeches ran long in two tongues. Sova Kes, twenty-six years old and the youngest accredited envoy the Communion had ever posted, stood where protocol put her and smiled until her face ached. The brief called Serevan's two peoples proud, separate, near war over water. The brief had been assembled from nine years of reports by men who had never left the spaceport quarter. Somewhere during the second anthem she had begun to doubt it. When the toasts began she murmured the word for fatigue, bowed to the Governor's sister, and went. The corridor guard watched her, watched the rain, watched the wall — which is its own kind of permission. Ossory at dusk was limestone gone the color of old honey: stepped streets, fish-oil lamps guttering blue. Over every lintel ran carvings worn soft by thumbs. A woman with a lamp going down into the dark. A man chained to a rock, fire in his fist. A boat riding out a flood, the animals asleep aboard. The colony's two ships had been named for the stories, or the stories for the ships; after six hundred years no one could say which. The briefing called all this superstition. The briefing did not say the myths were cut above the doors people actually married behind. The nightmarket opened off the cistern square, braziers smoking with tar and roasting grain. The Vale-born came down from the terraces — short, broad, slow-moving, wide-pupiled for the long dark of Serevan's winter. The Sunward stood among them — tall, narrow, barrel-chested for the thin plateau air, squinting even at lamplight. And everywhere was the third people the brief insisted did not exist: children with a grandfather's height and a grandmother's wide dark eyes; a ferryman whose two wives argued cheerfully, in different languages, over one pot. Nine years of dispatches, and no one had written: *they marry each other.* She bought sun-cakes from a Vale-born woman with forearms like mooring rope. The woman miscounted change in Kes's favor, caught it, corrected it, and added a third cake anyway. "For the road, sky-daughter. You walk like the winter's after you." Nearby, two canal-masters, one of each lineage, argued over sluice quotas and ended it with a coin spun by a priest of neither. Nobody drew a knife. The brief had used the word *irreconcilable* eleven times. *** Her console was blinking when she returned. > SECTOR COORDINATOR AMMAS TO ENVOY KES. PRIORITY. Unauthorized absence from official residence, 1900–2240 local. Appended field notes recategorized UNSOURCED ANECDOTE; excluded from transmission. You will proceed at 0900 to the Minister of Sciences and obtain countersignature on Compact Annex Seven. The Ministry is honorific. The occupant is a retired provincial administrator. Do not improvise. So: they would send the ethnographer to collect a signature from a figurehead. Kes lay awake under the wool listening to rain, and woke before the bell. *** The Archive House was older than the colony's metal age; its records were pressed in fired clay, floor to ceiling. Minister Odile Rens proved to be a small old woman in undyed grey, pouring tea that tasted of tar and honey. "You walked the Nightmarket," Rens said. "I did." "Against orders." "The orders described a prison. I went to see if it had walls." Rens poured the second cup without asking. "How many peoples live in this city?" "Two," Kes said. "By the brief." "Wrong." Kes held her gaze. "One. With two memories." Something moved at the corner of the old woman's mouth. "Better. Your Command burned your letters, Envoy. I kept them. You wrote that the founders recut Romulus out of the founding frieze. Tell me why that matters." "Because on Earth the city was founded on a brother's murder, and here the chisel refused it. A people shows you what it fears by what it edits." "And the Vale-born?" Rens cracked a smoked nut between finger and thumb. "They hibernate. Mindless as marmots until thaw. Your medical corps will find that useful." "No," Kes said. "Half-sleep, and shared. I heard whole streets singing the sleepers up at dusk, taking turns, house by house. You don't sing livestock awake." The rain ticked against the shutters. Rens set down the shell. "Good. You look before you judge. Rarer in your profession than you'd think." She turned her cup a quarter-circle, precisely, as if aligning an instrument. "Now. Annex Seven, as drafted, names the Vale-born wards of the Sunward administration — a legal fiction that makes your fleet's protection necessary, and permanent. Sign it, courier it home, and you return to Terra decorated at twenty-seven. Or you write Terra what you saw last night, and cost yourself a career, and cost us — perhaps — a garrison." She lifted her eyes. "Which envoy are you?" Kes felt the pull of it, honest and warm as the tea: the fast ship home, the commendation, the whole weight of six hundred years lifting off her. She set the cup down so her hands would have something true to do. "The one who was told not to improvise," she said, "and is about to." For a long moment the old woman studied her the way scholars study weathered stone. Then she rose, stiff-kneed, and led her down the vaulted room to the great frieze: two brothers, hands joined, raising one roof between them. Beside it, half-hidden behind a shuttered panel, an older block — the same brothers mid-quarrel, one arm raised to strike. "The public carving is third-century," Rens said. "That underneath is the landing generation. We don't carve lies here, Envoy. We carve *over* them, and leave the way back open. Your Command carves away. Learn the difference; it will keep you alive on Serevan." She closed the panel herself, gently, as one covers a sleeping face. "Thursday, you come to me. The water ledgers. Bring your doubts — they're the only equipment you have that works. And tell your Command the truth it can carry. Bring me the rest." Outside, morning had come up hard and clear. Over the Archive gate the lamp-woman descended forever into her carved dark, flame held high. Kes sat on the cold steps and ate the second sun-cake, stale now, tasting of honey and smoke and stone. *The stone keeps what the ship forgot,* she thought. *And the ship kept what the stars forgot: us.* Then she went in to write the letter that would end her career, and begin her work.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's literary style, successfully capturing her anthropological approach to science fiction, her measured prose rhythm, and her focus on cultural observation over action. The author creates a believable alien world through careful attention to linguistic details, social customs, and architectural elements that feel lived-in rather than constructed for plot convenience. The characterization of Sova Kes is particularly strong - she emerges as a competent professional caught between institutional expectations and personal integrity. Her observations feel genuine and her decision to defy orders grows organically from her experiences. Minister Rens is equally well-crafted, embodying the seasoned political operator described in the prompt while avoiding caricature through subtle details like her precise cup movements and gentle handling of the carved panel. The world-building excels through specific, sensory details: the honey-colored limestone, fish-oil lamps, the woman with "forearms like mooring rope." The central conceit of two human subspecies who have actually begun intermarrying contradicts the official narrative in a way that feels both politically realistic and thematically rich. The recurring motif of the carved friezes - particularly the revelation that lies aren't erased but carved over - provides elegant metaphorical depth. The dialogue feels natural and purposeful, particularly the testing conversation between Kes and Rens. Each exchange reveals character while advancing both plot and theme. The pacing builds effectively from the formal reception through the market exploration to the climactic meeting. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly literary language that, while beautiful, sometimes prioritizes style over clarity. Phrases like "which is its own kind of permission" and some of the more elaborate metaphors feel slightly forced. The ending, while thematically appropriate, resolves perhaps too neatly - Kes's transformation from dutiful envoy to principled rebel happens quickly, though it's reasonably well-motivated by her experiences. The prose demonstrates strong technical control with varied sentence structures and effective use of fragments for emphasis. The anthropological perspective remains consistent throughout, and the piece successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while creating something that feels authentically Le Guin-esque rather than merely imitative. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Master Line Cycle thirty-one of forty, and the extension step is holding at seventy-two degrees when a rudimentary solar panel rig flickers with unstable voltage in the lab, and my heart stutters along with the ammeter needle. One brownout during annealing and Frankie—the thermal cycler I built out of Peltier junctions stripped from three dead wine coolers—will drop his grip on the reaction. Forty cycles of stolen nucleotides, gone. I throw the transfer switch to the capacitor bank myself, palm flat against the bus bar, feeling the current hum through the tardigrade-proteins stitched into my skin. Perpetua Life Systems never sold that modification to consumers—they leaked it, the way you leak anything you want tested for free. Ten years later I still run a half-degree fever every day of my life, but I've stood in open sunlight through three summers of thinning ozone without blistering, so. Trade. Everyone in Substation Nine knows the trade by now. Perpetua wrote senescence locks into everything—corn, wheat, the insulin yeast, the wound-clotting cultures. Beautiful organisms, guaranteed vigorous for exactly one generation. Then the engineered sequences fray on schedule, like a fuse burning down, and the second generation comes up sterile or scrambled. *Planned obsolescence,* printed right there in the patent filings they left behind when the markets ate themselves. Abundance, guaranteed. Once. Which is why, when the knock comes at the airlock, I'm holding the last verified master-line of rice in the northern wastes inside a foam cooler, and my hands are shaking. Her name is Vesper, and she travels with a shotgun she never touches and a smile she always does. Black-market broker, honest in the way that matters: she delivers, and she remembers who shorted her. She sets the cooler on my bench, between the centrifuge—a screaming hard-drive motor with epoxy counterweights—and the pipettes I calibrate monthly by weighing water on a jeweler's scale. "One gig of gold, two crates of amoxicillin, and a working lithium cell," she says. "For six viable copies of the master line, sequenced and confirmed before Thursday." "The plasmid's degrading." I pop the cooler. Inside, a cryovial sweats in its foam cradle. "Every hour it sits above minus twenty, the backbone nicks a little more. Whoever carried it here didn't keep it cold enough." "Then you'd best start now." She peels back her sleeve, shows me the injector port scarred into her forearm, the pale keloid lattice of someone who's been dosing untested mods since before the Collapse. People like us read each other's scars like ledgers. "My employer wants it done right. They're paying for *viable.*" I should ask who the employer is. That's the question I don't ask, because asking it ends contracts, and Substation Nine has forty mouths and a winter coming. I say yes instead. The work takes the night. I render agarose from the red algae we farm in the old fuel tanks, cast gels in a picture-frame mold, and run my template alongside ladder standards stained with methylene blue because the ethidium ran out two years ago. My primer stocks are lyophilized pellets labeled in ink that's fading faster than the oligos are. The dNTPs came out of a university freezer raid in '41; they've thawed and refrozen so many times the labels have wept into illegibility, but the spectrophotometer says they're still good enough. Good enough is the whole religion out here. Around midnight my thumb slips on a cracked cryovial and opens a red line across the knuckle. I don't bandage it. I dose myself from the axolotl-cocktail vial instead—off-label, untested, mine—and watch the edges of the cut silver over in minutes, sealing into a scar that gleams green-gray under the bug-zapper tube I use as a transilluminator. That's the other ledger written on my body: regeneration factors that healed everything except correctly. My left ring finger regrew a centimeter short and double-jointed, which sounds like a loss until you've spent a night chasing microliter volumes and discovered the finger reaches angles straight fingers can't. There's no version of this life where I'd trade it back. The photosynthetic freckling across my cheekbones drinks an hour of dawn and calls it breakfast, which is the only reason I can afford to work through the night on half rations. Downside: I sweat the smell of cut grass, and the settlement kids follow me around in summer hoping the bees will follow me too. Upside: the bees do. At cycle thirty-four, Vesper's sample tells me something it wasn't sold as telling me. I'm running confirmatory digest, and there it is in the restriction map, quiet as a knife in a drawer: a second lock. Not the standard senescence fraying—something cleaner, deliberate, threaded into the master line itself. A kill-codon cluster keyed to a proprietary promoter. Whoever Perpetua's ghost-remnant employers are, they didn't salvage this rice. They *engineered* this batch, and the Fade is still in it, waiting for generation two. Vesper's people either don't know, or they know exactly, and they're buying scarcity. The contract says six confirmed copies. It doesn't say the copies have to carry the lock. I sit with that while the gel runs, while the capacitors tick, while my fever hums its daily hymn. Excising the kill-codons is four hours of work I won't be paid for, using reagents I can't replace, on a promise I made to a woman with a shotgun. Honoring the contract exactly means handing six doomed bloodlines to whoever thinks they own the last rice on earth. So I do both. Six copies, contract-perfect, delivered at dawn with the amoxicillin and the cell changing hands in the gray light. Vesper counts, smiles, seals the deal. And off-book, in a seventh reaction nobody paid for, I cut the lock out and amplify it clean—true viability, generational, free—then seal it into an unlabeled cryovial and tuck it behind the loose tile where I keep the things that shouldn't be property. By full morning the germination tray in the window is showing radicle hooks, white and certain, reaching down through salvaged soil. Generation one. Somewhere in that tile-shadow waits generation two, and three, and however many we can steal back. The solar rig flickers. I let it. Some currents you ride; some you reroute.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and worldbuilding within the biopunk genre. The author creates a convincing post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has created scarcity, and follows a biohacker navigating both the technical and moral complexities of their work. The prose is dense with technical detail that feels authentic without becoming incomprehensible. The narrator's voice is consistent throughout - knowledgeable, pragmatic, and tinged with both resignation and defiance. The integration of scientific terminology with jury-rigged equipment creates effective atmosphere, from "Frankie" the thermal cycler built from wine cooler parts to the spectrophotometer readings on degraded reagents. Character development is handled efficiently through physical modifications and their trade-offs. The narrator's body serves as both tool and ledger of their choices - the tardigrade proteins, photosynthetic freckling, and regeneration factors that heal "everything except correctly." These details feel organic rather than gratuitous, serving both worldbuilding and character development. The central conflict around the black market contract creates genuine moral tension. The discovery of the hidden kill-codon and the narrator's decision to fulfill the contract while secretly preserving viable genetic material demonstrates character agency and ethical complexity. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither triumphant nor despairing, but quietly subversive. The technical aspects of the genetic work are handled with apparent expertise, making the scientific elements feel grounded rather than hand-wavy. The pacing moves efficiently from setup through discovery to resolution without unnecessary diversions. Some minor weaknesses include occasional density that might challenge readers unfamiliar with molecular biology, and Vesper could have been developed slightly more beyond her broker archetype. The dialogue, while limited, serves its functional purpose effectively. Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Azra Gambit ## Chapter Three: Terms of Surrender The tender had no name painted on her hull, and that told Arthur Neegan more than any name could have. Honest ships advertised themselves. This one carried only a registry number that, when he'd squinted at it during boarding, seemed to blur pleasantly out of focus — a transponder scrubbed clean. He adjusted his collar for the fourth time. The garment was real silk, shipped up the gravity well from Earth, and it fit him the way a treaty fits a small nation: precisely, and against his interest. Someone had measured him while he slept, he suspected. He did not enjoy being reminded of it. Six escorts shared the cabin with him. They wore the dove-grey sashes of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, and they carried sidearms that were diplomatic in the same sense that a siege was a conversation. One of them, a broad woman with a face like unweathered basalt, caught him looking and gave him a courteous nod. Arthur nodded back. On Mars you learned early that courtesy and violence were not opposites; they were frequently colleagues. Through the port, Mars shrank to a rust-red coin. Somewhere beneath that coin lay his quarter-section of rock — forty hectares of regolith he'd spent eleven years coaxing into yield, sitting atop a vein of Azra large enough, according to the assay punched out by the Tharsis survey office, to power a fleet or end one. The tender docked, with a softness that cost money, against a wheel spinning in high orbit. *Charterhouse*, said the brass letters on the airlock ring. A hotel, or something wearing a hotel's skin. --- They led him down carpets thick enough to muffle conscience, past fountains playing under spun gravity, into a room paneled in genuine hardwood — hardwood, in orbit, where a single plank outweighed a miner's annual wage. At its center stood a table of dark Martian timber, and behind it sat a woman of perhaps sixty, silver-haired, dressed in dove-grey to match her soldiers. A single pin marked her lapel: the compass-star of Antares. "Mister Neegan," she said, rising. "Councillor Maren Voss. Please sit. Coffee?" "I'm told it's real," said Arthur, sitting. "It is. It costs more per cup than your father paid for his passage under the Indenture Act." She poured with her own hands, which he noted was either sincerity or theater. "Your father came out in '61, didn't he? Third wave. Died of lung-seal failure when you were nineteen." "You've read my file." "I wrote half of it." She smiled without warmth. "Antares has been writing files on Mars for thirty years, Mister Neegan. We are very thorough. It's why we're still alive." "And what does the file say I am?" "A mining engineer of moderate distinction. A widower. A man with no political debts and no family left to threaten." She folded her hands. "Which is to say: a man who can be dealt with cleanly. You'd be surprised how rare that makes you." Arthur drank the coffee. It was excellent, and he resented it. "Then deal with me." "Directly, then." Voss touched the table; a hologram bloomed above it — his land, rendered in wireframe, the Azra vein glowing beneath it like a lantern under cloth. "This deposit represents approximately four percent of all known Azra in the settled system. Azra accelerates radioactive decay — you know this better than I. A drive core laced with it burns fuel ten thousand times faster. A warhead built around it detonates ten thousand times dirtier. Whoever owns your forty hectares holds a lever on every engine and every bomb between here and Proxima." "And Antares wants to buy the lever." "Antares wants to buy *you*, Mister Neegan. The vein follows the metal rights, yes. But claims are paper, and paper burns. Men are sturdier. We offer you citizenship of the Compact, a seat in our Assembly, a stipend you couldn't spend in nine lifetimes — and our protection." "Protection from whom?" She counted, unhurried, on ringed fingers. "From the Colonial Directorate, which voted last week to nationalize all Azra finds above ten kilograms and has already frozen your bank accounts. From the Terran Metals Combine, whose lawyers are drafting a lease-inversion action that would make your land technically theirs by Friday. And from whichever party sabotaged the airlock of one Yorick Vance, three months ago, after he found a vein one-two-hundredth the size of yours. The Directorate called it an accident. The Combine called it a tragedy. We called it a message, and we read it correctly." Arthur set down the cup. His hands were steady; he made sure of it before he spoke. "And if I refuse?" "Then you are returned to Mars, to your frozen accounts, your litigated land, and your unguarded airlock. We are not thugs, Mister Neegan. We merely decline to be responsible for arithmetic we warned you about." Her eyes were pale and patient as frost. "But consider, also, the larger board. Earth holds twelve billion souls and starves for energy. The Outer Worlds hold two hundred million and hold the drives instead. Azra decides which way that balance tips — whether the hive swallows the frontier, or the frontier inherits the stars. You are not being offered wealth, Mister Neegan. You are being asked to choose a future. Most men never get the chance to matter. You get it whether you wish to or not." "In chess," said Arthur, "a gambit isn't a gift. It's a purchase made with tempo. So tell me what you're buying besides my signature." For the first time, Voss paused. Something flickered behind the frost — reassessment. "The file undersells you," she said softly. "The file," said Arthur, "is yours. My signature is mine. Give me until the return transit to decide." "Forty hours." She slid a slate across the timber — heavy, real, deliberate. "Terms are inside. Read them slowly. And Mister Neegan—" the smile again, thinner now, "—do note the clause numbered seven. Everyone does, eventually." At the door, waiting for his escort, Arthur glanced back once. Voss had turned to the viewport, hands clasped, watching Mars turn below like a thing being weighed. Beside the door, her young aide stood at parade rest — and for half a second, as the man shifted, his cuff fell back. Beneath the dove-grey sleeve glinted a second pin. Small. Unofficial. The green-and-black chevron of the Terran Metals Combine. Arthur faced forward, adjusted his collar, and began, quietly, to count.

Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The safelight makes liars of us all. After three hours in here, everything runs red — my hands, the chemical trays, the silver chains at Elliot's hip — and your eyes quit asking for true color. I love that. I've built a whole personality on being legible: shaved sides, red lip, opinions filed sharp. The darkroom is the only room where I let the world stay blurry. Our final project is *Thresholds* — doorways, dusk, the gap between lightning and thunder. Liminality, Professor Okafor called it, and she paired us alphabetically, which I choose to read as the universe doing editorial work. We meet at night because the day slots fill fast and because neither of us has suggested stopping. Tonight Elliot prints while I mix fresh developer. He works the way he talks — careful, precise, like the equipment might bruise. Thrifted lace under a band tee two sizes too big, chipped black polish, eyeliner smoked out so well it looks like an accident. Nineteen and dressed like a Victorian ghost who loots Hot Topic. I've spent a semester pretending not to catalog him. I'm terrible at pretending. "Test strip's ready," he says, voice starting confident and shrinking by the end, like he's returning something borrowed. We lean over the tray together. Beneath the developer's surface, the image arrives the way weather does: a gray bloom gathering into shoulders, a face, the doorway we shot behind the gym. I've watched ten thousand prints emerge and it still gets me. The picture was always in the paper. The chemistry invents nothing — it just coaxes the latent image into admitting what it's been all along. "Can I say something kind of weird?" Elliot asks the tray, not me. People confess to me constantly. Apparently I have a face that says *I can handle it.* Usually I can. Usually I already have opinions, formatted, with citations. "Weird's allowed in here," I say. His rings click against the plastic as he agitates the tray. "I keep trying the word *boy* on. And it fits like — okay, like a borrowed jacket. Close, but somebody else's shape. Sometimes I try *girl*, and it's almost right too, which freaks me out more? Mostly I just feel like a really good question nobody's gotten to yet." Every term I own lines up in my throat — nonbinary, genderfluid, the whole seminar — and I swallow all of it. Naming someone else's gender is just taking charge with extra steps, and for the first time in my adult life I don't want the wheel. "That sounds exhausting," I say. "Also kind of holy." He laughs, surprised, wet at the edges. "Holy. Okay." Here's my problem, the one I've dodged for fifteen weeks: I like edges. My exes came pre-sorted — a butch welder with forearms like bridge cable, a pretty-boy poet who ironed his shirts, a drag king who could out-stare God. I fall for certainty because I enjoy being the variable. Nobody warned me about falling for a question. Elliot is a question wearing eyeliner, and instead of boring me he's quietly rearranging my furniture. Because two things happen in my chest when he talks like this. There's the want — pure, embarrassing, wanting to back him against the enlarger column and learn what his hair smells like. And underneath, enormous tenderness, the urge to stand between him and every snickering Marcus from midterm critiques, forever. I used to assume those were the same feeling in different jackets. They're not. One of them wants him. The other wants to guard him like property, and he hasn't asked to be guarded. What he needs — I know this the way photographers know things, in the hands before the head — is a witness. "I shot a roll last month," Elliot says suddenly, still addressing the tray. "Not for class." Click, click. "It was me. Bathroom mirror. Mascara on one eye, and I couldn't finish it in either direction, so I just photographed the unfinished part." His ears burn, though in here everything burns. "Would you help me print one? Tonight? Only if — I've never seen them bigger than a contact sheet." I want to say yes so fast it frightens me. Instead I dry my hands and hold out my palm. "Your negatives, your call," I say. "You pick the frame. I'll run the machine." He picks frame eleven — of course he does — the one where his reflection splits along the mirror seam, half made-up, half bare, both halves staring down the lens like they dare you to choose. Loading the negative, our fingers collide inside the film holder and stay collided one second longer than physics requires. The safelight is merciful; it files every blush under shadow. My phone buzzes against my thigh — twice, then quits. Old me would already be composing replies. I leave it where it is. Whatever's out there can develop on its own. Frame eleven surfaces slowly. Elliot makes a sound low in his throat when the eyes resolve, and I realize I'm gripping the sink hard enough to hurt. "That's me," he whispers. "It's the most me I've ever looked." "Yeah," I manage. My voice comes out wrecked. Twenty-five years of talking and that's the best I've got. He looks over, red-washed, terrified, luminous. "Thanks for not making it a big deal." "It *is* a big deal," I say. "Just not a loud one." We clip the print to the wire, side by side, closer than the task requires. Neither of us reaches for the lights or the door. Above us the boy in the photograph dries between genders like a flag between poles, and beneath him I'm revising my own caption. I came into September knowing exactly what I like: defined, decided, legible. Now I want someone gloriously illegible, and I want to be the one who waits while they develop — patient, hands steady, witness to whatever they're becoming. "Same time Thursday?" Elliot asks. "Earlier," I say. "If you want." He smiles at the floor. The red light keeps our secrets, and for once I'm in no hurry to know the ending. Some images take their sweet time. Fine. I've got chemistry.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated craft in several key areas. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically, creating an intimate confessional space where the red light becomes a character itself. The author shows strong command of voice - Dani's narration feels authentic to her character: assertive, articulate, yet genuinely vulnerable when confronted with unfamiliar territory. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani emerges as a fully realized person whose usual confidence wavers in meaningful ways when faced with Elliot's gender questioning. Her internal conflict between wanting to take charge (her usual mode) and recognizing Elliot needs agency is psychologically astute. Elliot, despite less direct characterization, feels genuine in his tentative self-exploration. The prose quality is high, with memorable phrases like "The safelight makes liars of us all" and "Elliot is a question wearing eyeliner." The photography metaphors are woven throughout without feeling forced, particularly the extended metaphor about latent images developing, which parallels both characters' self-discovery. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Dani's attraction is layered - physical desire, protective instinct, and confusion about her own identity preferences. The piece avoids easy answers while still providing satisfying emotional resolution. However, there are some weaknesses. Certain phrases veer toward preciousness ("holy" as a response feels slightly calculated). The ending, while sweet, edges toward being too neat given the complexity established earlier. Some metaphors, particularly around photography, occasionally feel overextended. The dialogue feels natural and serves character development well. The pacing is controlled, building intimacy gradually. The piece successfully avoids both exploitation of trans themes and oversimplification of complex identity questions. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma The guidebook said the Trevi Fountain was best appreciated *in quiet contemplation*, which is why Ben Whitcombe was standing in the middle of the road reading aloud. "—the Barcaccia, commissioned under Urban the Eighth, though attribution remains—" The horn was the last thing he heard before the world became a smear of red motorbike and black hair, swerving so close that the courier's elbow clipped his satchel and sent him spinning onto the pavement in a shower of paperback pages. "*Ma sei scemo?!*" She kicked down the stand and was off the bike in one motion, helmet tucked under her arm, dark eyes furious. "*Ti sembra il posto per leggere? È una strada, professore, non una biblioteca!*" "Terribly sorry — *mi dispiace* — molto — er — *scusi* —" Ben gathered pages with trembling hands. "I was — the attribution of the *Barcaccia* is genuinely contested, you see, some scholars argue—" "You nearly die," she said, "quoting footnotes." Something in his mortified face cracked her fury open. The laugh escaped before she could catch it — sharp, delighted, entirely at his expense. "I do beg your pardon," Ben managed. "You are always begging pardon. You English beg pardon like other people breathe." She snatched the guidebook from his hands — *Rome in Three Days* — and flipped through it with theatrical horror. "Three days. For Rome." She strapped it under her arm like confiscated contraband. "This is hostage now. Come." "Come — where?" She jerked a thumb at the pillion seat. "I deliver a parcel in Trastevere by noon. After that, who knows. Get on, or stay here and apologize to the fountain. It loves that." --- He had ridden motorcycles exactly twice in his life, both times at university, both times badly. Nothing had prepared him for Alessandra threading a courier's Aprilia through Roman traffic like a needle through silk — past buses separated from their mirrors by centimeters, down alleys barely wider than the handlebars, her voice trailing back to him on the wind. "Breathe, professore! If you squeeze me any harder I charge extra!" They delivered a legal envelope to a man who shouted into three phones at once; a padded parcel Ben decided, wisely, not to ask about; and a single long-stemmed rose to a woman on a balcony who blew Alessandra a kiss and Ben an amused look. Between deliveries, Alessandra talked them through gaps in scaffolding to a courtyard no guidebook mentioned, where a Caravaggio hung in a dim chapel with nobody guarding it but a drowsy custodian whom she charmed in thirty seconds of rapid Roman dialect. Ben emerged blinking into the sunlight feeling like a conspirator. At the market on Via dei Giardini she stopped at a fruit stall, argued joyfully with the vendor about football, and walked away pressing a perfect peach into Ben's palm. Ten meters later, a woman behind them cried out that her peaches were short by two. "Your hat," Ben announced loudly, to the vendor, "is extraordinary. Where *do* people find such hats?" Alessandra's grin, beside him, was incandescent. At lunch — supplì and cheap wine at a formica counter — he watched three teaspoons and a fistful of sugar packets vanish into her jacket pocket between sentences, soundlessly, mid-laugh, as if her hands were independent citizens with their own foreign policy. "You saw nothing," she said, catching him seeing. "I'm afraid I saw quite a lot." "And you said nothing." She leaned in, chin on her hand, studying him like a text she hadn't finished annotating. "You're learning, Inglese." "What's in the parcels you won't tell me about?" "What's in the book you're not writing?" He went still. "How did you—" "You have the face." She waved her fork at him. "The face of a man escaping something. So. Tell me what you're not writing, professore." "It's a monograph," he admitted, "on the correspondence of Cardinal Pacca's head gardener. Sixteenth century. Fascinating irrigation disputes." He turned his glass. "Four months in Rome and I haven't written a word. I keep meaning to begin." "Good," Alessandra said. "Dead men's mail can wait. You've been reading other people's lives for too long. Today you borrow mine." --- The storm arrived without negotiation — the sky over the Quirinale turning bruise-purple, then splitting open with a crack of thunder that emptied the piazza in seconds. They ran laughing, Ben's jacket over his head, Alessandra not bothering, and ducked beneath the striped awning of a gelateria as the rain came down in ropes. "Pistachio," she told the boy behind the counter. "Due coni." She paid with coins that seemed to appear from nowhere. "Rule number one of Rome, professore: when it rains, Romans steal an hour. Everything else can wait." They stood shoulder to shoulder watching the water sheet off the awning, eating gelato while thunder rolled across the rooftops. She held her cone to his mouth without asking. Pistachio, salt-bright and green. "Your turn. Feed me yours or admit cowardice." He did. Stracciatella. She pronounced it "acceptable," which from her seemed like a decoration for valor. "Why did you take me with you?" Ben asked quietly. "Really." Alessandra watched the rain for a long moment. When she glanced at him, she didn't look away, and he felt the look all the way down. "You stepped off a curb into my road," she said finally, "reading about Rome instead of looking at it. Somebody had to fix you." A pause. Thunder filled it. "Also, you apologize beautifully. Like a prayer. I wanted to see how long it would take to break the habit." "How long?" "This morning. When you lied about the hat." She smiled slowly. "That was the moment, professore. You lie terribly, by the way. Practice." --- Night found them outside his pensione near Barberini, the streets steaming, lamps doubled in wet cobblestone. Alessandra produced his guidebook from inside her jacket — warm, slightly bent, smelling of engine oil and rain. "Spoils of war returned." She swung onto the bike, pulled on her helmet. "It was a terrible book. I improved it." "Alessandra—" She leaned down from the saddle and kissed him — quick, decisive, tasting of pistachio and rain — then straightened, kicked the engine alive, and was gone down the glistening street before his heart remembered its job. Inside, under the thin lamp of his rented room, Ben opened the ruined guidebook. Across the map of Rome, in red ballpoint, someone had drawn the day's whole mad route — Trevi, chapel, market, gelateria — ending with an arrow at a bar in Trastevere and a line of slashing handwriting: *Bar San Calisto. Domani, ore nove. Non fare tardi, professore.* Tomorrow, nine o'clock. Don't be late. He reached for his pen to underline it, out of scholarly habit, and found his breast pocket empty — his fountain pen gone, vanished sometime between the peach and the rain. Ben laughed alone in the lamplight, a man thoroughly robbed and utterly rich, and began, for the first time in four months, to write.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in adapting the prompt's requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomania is woven seamlessly into the narrative through subtle details - the peaches, sugar packets, teaspoons, and ultimately Ben's fountain pen - creating a character trait that feels organic rather than forced. The structure effectively uses interconnected vignettes spanning a single day, each building momentum and deepening the relationship. The writing style is confident and polished, with particularly strong dialogue that captures the cultural and personality contrasts between the characters. Alessandra's voice feels authentically Italian-inflected without becoming caricature, while Ben's academic politeness transforms believably throughout the day. The imagery is vivid and specific - "threading a courier's Aprilia through Roman traffic like a needle through silk" and "the sky over the Quirinale turning bruise-purple" - creating a strong sense of place without overwhelming the narrative. The author demonstrates restraint in description, allowing the characters and their dynamic to drive the story. The romantic tension builds naturally through shared experiences rather than forced moments, culminating in a satisfying but not overly neat conclusion. Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost ### Chapter Seven: The Lighthouse The gravity hiccups while I'm mid-pour, and Doss's stout climbs the side of his glass like it's trying to make a break for it. "Station's breathing again," he says, tilting the glass to catch the foam. "Somebody oughta oil her lungs." "Somebody oughta quit complaining about free entertainment," I tell him, and slide him a napkin anyway. That's the Outpost for you. An asteroid the size of a fist clenched around a town, bolted to a rock spinning through the Andromeda outer rim. The grav-plating here is older than most of my patrons' marriages, and twice a shift it does this slow inhale-exhale thing that makes every drink in the house shiver. Nobody leaves. Nobody complains too loud, either. There's real wood behind the bar — salvaged, pre-Flight, probably older than humanity's whole exodus — and there's Rivet asleep in the corner booth, and there's always somebody's drama simmering on a back burner. It's not much. It's mine. The door hisses open at 21:40, letting in a knife of vacuum-cold air and a stranger. She crosses the floor like she's counting exits. Travel coat gone gray at the seams, boots worn through at the outer edge, and her hair — seven small tentacled dreads, the kind my grandmother would've called *living* — are pulled flat against her skull like they're trying to disappear. They don't succeed. Neither does she. She takes the far stool, the one with the wobbly leg, and says, "Vega whisky, neat." A breath. "Better make that a double." "Vega's a long way from home," I say, reaching for the good bottle. "So am I." I pour. The gravity sighs again and the amber surface trembles, rings spreading out from the center like something under it moved. She watches the glass the way you'd watch a stranger sit down next to you on a long haul flight. "Rough transit?" I try. "You could say that." "Weather out past the belt's been ugly. Micrometeor showers, comms static." "It wasn't the weather." Fair enough. I set the drink down and turn to deal with Marisol, who has materialized at my elbow wearing the specific face that means her on-again partner has done something unforgivable, probably involving cards. "Nets. Nets. Tell her the odds on the Kessari run were posted *publicly*—" "Marisol, honey, I love you, but if I arbitrate this one I lose either way." "You're supposed to be neutral!" "I'm neutral like the station's gravity is stable." She flounces off toward the card table, which is the correct place for flouncing, and when I come back the stranger has drunk half the double in one pull. Her dreads have flushed faintly violet at the tips. Fear-color, if I remember my xenophysiology right. I remember it right. "Refill?" I ask. "In a minute." She turns on the stool to face me properly. Up close she's younger than the coat suggested, and there's a burn scar crawling up from her collar. "Questions first. You own this place?" "I tend it. Ownership is a rumor." "Who runs your docking authority?" "The rock runs itself. We pay tithes to nobody and ask permission of nothing. Why?" "Do shipping consortium men come through here? Asking after passengers?" "They mostly come through asking after whiskey and forgiveness." I keep my voice easy. "Neither's free." Her mouth almost twitches. Almost. Behind us, the card table erupts — Old Tam accusing a Kessari merchant of palming chips, which happens Thursdays — and she flinches hard enough that her elbow catches the glass. The gravity chooses that exact moment to exhale. Whisky jumps the rim, spreads across the bar, soaks her pushed-back sleeve. And there, on the inside of her wrist: a brand. A circle broken by a single vertical line. I know that mark. I knew it in another life, in another arm of the galaxy, back when I had a different name and a different relationship with the concept of *safe*. I put a rag over the spill and my hands stay steady, because ten years of bartending will teach you that. "You spilled your drink," I say. "I'll pay for it." "That's not what I asked about." "No," she agrees quietly. "It isn't." We look at each other over the wet wood. Around us the Outpost keeps humming — Doss arguing about ore yields, Rivet stretching and resettling, the fryer hissing in the back. Cozy as anything. Cozy as a lit window in deep dark. "My name's Nettle," I offer, because sometimes you hand someone a rope to see what they do with it. "I know," she says. The room gets very small around the two of us. "Do you," I say. "A man on Ceres Junction told me to find this rock. Find the outpost. Find the bartender." Her dreads lift, just slightly, off her skull. Violet bleeding to a deep, bruised blue. "He said you'd hate him for sending me, and you'd help anyway." "There's no man I know on Ceres Junction." "There's one man who'd know to send me to you." The station intercom crackles overhead, cheerful and oblivious: *"Incoming vessel requesting emergency berth. Registry: Vigil, class-three courier. Claiming drive malfunction."* At the scanner table, Old Tam lowers his cards and says, to no one and everyone, "Vigil's never had drive trouble in her life. Vigil *is* drive trouble." The stranger's whole body goes still, the way water goes still right before it freezes. "How long since your last maintenance stop?" I ask her, though I already know. "Eleven days." "And how fast is a class-three courier?" "Faster than me." I take her empty glass, refill it unasked, set it down in front of her. My heart is doing what the gravity does — that little stutter, that slow wrong-footed sway. She reaches into her coat and slides something across the bar. Not credits. A data-chit, scuffed, ancient, with a hairline crack through it that I recognize the way you recognize a scar on your own body. "He made me memorize a message," she says. "In case he didn't make it off Ceres. In case I had to find you without him." Her voice drops under the noise of the room, under Doss's laugh, under the fryer, under the whole warm machinery of the life I built. "He said: *tell Nettle the lighthouse still burns.*" The gravity exhales. Every glass on the bar shivers. Nobody built a lighthouse on Ceres Junction. But once — one lifetime ago — somebody promised me one.

The supporting characters like Doss, Marisol, and Old Tam feel authentic rather than merely functional. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South ## Chapter Two: Powdered Sugar Mathematics The truck dumps me at Decatur Street at nine in the morning, and just like that I'm nobody's problem anymore. The driver didn't even want gas money. He wanted company, he said. Then he saw my face when his hand landed on my knee outside Baton Rouge, and suddenly downtown New Orleans looked real good to me too. *Fine,* I told him. *Whatever. Thanks for the ride.* Like it was a favor. Like I hadn't spent four hours doing math in my head about door locks and shoulder checks. Now the humidity hits me like a wet towel to the face. There's a cathedral to my left all white and sharp against the sky, artists selling paintings on the fence across the square, the smell of pralines fighting the smell of garbage and horse pee, and I stand there with my backpack and think: *this is the most beautiful place I've ever wanted to throw up in.* My phone buzzes. Twelve percent. Of course. Mom: 11 texts. One voicemail. All of them some version of *come home* except the ones that aren't, the ones that say *you're confused* and *we love you but* — that *but* doing more damage than anything Dad said with his fork scraped down onto the plate two nights ago, him saying *not under my roof*, her saying *Lord give me strength* like I was a demon and not their kid. And one text from Izzy, my little sister, sent at midnight from under her blanket: *did u take the $40? don't tell mom. i'm proud of you. also mom took ur door off.* Twelve percent. No charger. Every bar is a countdown clock now. I walk. That's the whole plan. Walk until something happens. Something happens fast. A guy peels off a doorway like he'd been growing there, gold tooth, friendly eyes, the friendliest eyes. "You lookin' for somebody, lil bit?" "My uncle's meeting me." I don't break stride. "Right there. See him?" Gold Tooth sees nobody, but he also sees I'm not easy, and melts back into his doorway. My heart's going like a hummingbird. Note to self, lesson one of the big city: lie faster. That's how she finds me, actually — flinching. "You're new." The girl's sitting on the riverfront steps, sketching tourists on cardboard with a stub of charcoal. Seventeen, maybe. Army jacket in ninety-degree heat, sleeves pushed up. "You flinched when that dude talked to you. Locals don't flinch. They just keep walking." "I'm meeting people." "Sure you are." She pats the step next to her like it's assigned seating. "Sit down before somebody less boring finds you first. Name's Wren." "...Taylor." "Cool, Taylor." She goes back to her sketch like I'm weather. Somehow that makes sitting down possible. We watch the river for a minute. Brown and enormous and going somewhere. "How much money you got?" she asks, not looking up. "That's —" "It's math, not a robbery question. How much?" "Forty-one dollars." "Okay. Rules." She holds up charcoal-black fingers. "One: never tell nobody you're alone. Not me, not cops, not preachers, especially not friendly guys with gold teeth. Two: free red beans Mondays at the church on Rampart, bag lunches at the library at noon if you don't mind God talk with your sandwich. Three: Covenant House takes minors. Real beds. They ask questions, but they feed you first. Four—" she finally looks at me, and her eyes are older than seventeen, "—don't sleep in the Quarter. Cops sweep it. I know a spot." "Why are you helping me?" "Because eight months ago somebody helped me, and because you've got that look." "What look?" "Just-got-off-the-bus. Like the whole world's a dog that might bite or lick you and you can't tell which." I almost laugh. Almost. "What if it's both?" "Then you learn to tell 'em apart quick." She snaps her notebook shut. "C'mon. Beignets. Café du Monde does cheap and the sugar's free calories." At the café table, powdered sugar snowing down my black shirt — mistake, but the best mistake I've ever eaten — she asks the question sideways, the way people do when they already know. "So what'd you run from? Nobody lands here by accident." I stare into my cup. And weirdly, with this stranger, it comes out easier than it ever did at that dinner table. "I came out. Two days ago. To my family." My hands won't stop moving. "I'm trans. It's Taylor. Just — Taylor. They, I guess. And Dad said not under his roof, and Mom started praying *at* me, and I had forty bucks and a duffel bag, so." Wren shrugs. Shrugs. Like I told her the time. "Cool. Pass the sugar." Just like that. No sermon, no *but*, no fork scraping. Eight months on the street and this kid hands me acceptance like it costs nothing, and my eyes burn and I blame the chicory coffee. "What about you?" I manage. "Your *before*?" Her sleeve's ridden up. There's a scar on her forearm, shiny and old, the shape of something iron-shaped, and I know better than to ask. Down the block a silver pickup idles at the light, and Wren goes still in a way I recognize from mirrors. "Everybody here's got a before," she says quietly, pulling her sleeve down. "You trade 'em when you trust somebody. Day one, you don't trust me, I don't trust you. That's math." The light changes. The truck leaves. She breathes again. "C'mon. I'll show you the spot before dark." Later, on the levee behind the floodwall, the river goes orange and the steamboats put on their lights like the water grew jewelry. Somewhere across it, Texas. Somewhere north, Tennessee, and a house with my door off its hinges. Battery: four percent. I type: *I'm safe.* Delete. Type: *I'm sorry.* Delete. Type: *My name is Taylor.* Thumb hovering over send, heart hammering, and I think about Izzy saying *proud of you*, and I hit send on all three lines before I can chicken out, and the screen flashes — and dies. Black glass in my palm. Cut clean loose. Wren bumps my shoulder with hers. "First night's the worst," she says. "After that it's just nights." Below us the river keeps going south, and for once in my life, so am I — on purpose.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The author successfully captures Taylor's voice through a compelling blend of vulnerability, street-smart defensiveness, and dark humor that feels genuine to both the character's age and circumstances. The writing excels in several key areas. The prose is crisp and evocative without being overwrought, with particularly strong sensory details like "humidity hits me like a wet towel" and "powdered sugar snowing down my black shirt." The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building the world. Wren's casual acceptance of Taylor's identity ("Cool. Pass the sugar") is particularly well-handled, showing rather than telling how different environments can offer different responses. The characterization is nuanced and believable. Taylor's internal monologue effectively conveys the complex emotional state of someone processing recent trauma while navigating immediate survival needs. The author skillfully balances Taylor's fear and inexperience with moments of resilience and dark humor. Wren emerges as a fully realized character despite limited page time, with her own implied trauma and survival wisdom. The pacing is well-controlled, moving from immediate danger through tentative connection to a moment of quiet reflection. The structure follows Taylor through a complete emotional arc within the single day timeframe as requested. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not falsely optimistic but suggesting possibility and forward momentum. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious in its cleverness, and a few instances where emotional beats could be more subtly handled. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully adheres to all prompt requirements: first person mixed tense narration, internal monologue, dialogue with interesting characters, navigation of trust and danger, and authentic emotional complexity around Taylor's recent coming out and family rejection. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 76.3
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The world ended the way most bad things do: slowly, and then all at once, and then very slowly again for everyone who survived it. Historians would have argued about the exact date, but the historians had been among the first to go, which many considered proof of a merciful universe. Midas lived in the shell of a roadside shop called *Buddy's Fuel 'n' Bait*, which he felt was thematically appropriate, since he had a buddy and the apocalypse was, in a sense, the bait. "We're out of water," he said, on the morning in question. "Not *out*," said Chewy, from the counter. "There's a mouthful left. Two mouthfuls, if you don't breathe while you drink." Chewy was a koala of the ancient type — plush, battery-fed, and manufactured in a Before Time when humanity had apparently looked at the koala and thought, *yes, but can it say G'day.* His eyes flickered colours according to strong emotion, which made him the most honest creature left alive, including all humans, dogs, and weather. They were amber now. Scheming amber. "There's a HyperMart," said Chewy, "two suburbs east." "The last 'two suburbs' took us four days and cost me a boot." "Short trip," said Chewy. His eyes went briefly, guiltily, yellow. --- The M1 was parked solid with cars that had been waiting patiently for the traffic to clear for eleven years. Nobody had told them. Midas picked his way along the median strip while Chewy rode in his pack, offering navigation. "Bear left at the flaming wreck." "That's a landmark now?" "Hug me!" said Chewy, which was one of his six original phrases and his response to nearly everything. --- The HyperMart had lost its roof to fire and its dignity shortly after. Skylight glass lay everywhere in glittering drifts, and down in the dark of Aisle 7, feral shopping trolleys had nested.* Midas crouched by the pharmacy shutter, which had jammed at knee height, and peered into the gloom. Water purification tablets. Somewhere in there. Also, ideally, double-A batteries, since Chewy ran on faith and four of them. "Careful," said Chewy. "Remember the saucepans." "I'm trying not to." He reached through the shutter. His fingers closed on cardboard. Victory tasted like dust and foil. And then, because the universe keeps receipts, his elbow brushed a display stand, and the Great Pyramid of Glassware — fifty years of surviving fires, floods, and looters — came down behind him like applause. Every trolley in Aisle 7 woke up at once. And somewhere overhead, with a sound like a dying refrigerator clearing its throat, something else woke up too. "WELCOME TO HYPERMART," boomed Helpful Harold. Harold had been a Customer Assistance Unit, back when customers were a thing. He was a chrome torso on a single wheel, with a smiley face sticker across his shattered screen, and he had spent the Long Quiet patrolling his aisles in the firm belief that the store was simply experiencing a slow Tuesday. "SIR," said Harold, rolling toward the noise with gathering speed, "PLEASE HAVE YOUR LOYALTY CARD READY." "That's not — I don't have —" Midas scrambled up, clutching the box. "I'm just leaving!" "LEAVING WITHOUT PURCHASING IS THEFT," said Harold, gaining. "THEFT IS AGAINST STORE POLICY. STORE POLICY IS ETERNAL." Trolleys scattered before him like pigeons before a terrier. Midas vaulted a fallen freezer, splashed down the flooded aisle, and heard Chewy behind him yell — at full ceremonial volume — "**HUG ME!**" To his lasting astonishment, it worked. Harold stopped dead. Somewhere in his rotted firmware, two protocols collided: *Threat Detected* versus *Customer Requires Emotional Support*. He hovered there, wheel spinning, emitting a low confused hum, while Midas hauled himself onto the checkout conveyor and ran along it like a man fleeing down the tongue of an enormous grey whale. "He's rebooting," panted Chewy. "Left! Left at the lottery stand!" The loading dock was ahead, blessedly open, pouring grey daylight. Behind them Harold came back online with a shriek of servo and the words "SECURITY ESCORT TO EXIT," which was technically friendly and practically a death sentence at forty kilometres an hour. Midas dove through the dock. Harold did not fit through the dock. Harold hit the doorframe at speed, expressed the store motto — "*HYPERMART: EVERY DAY LOW PRICES*" — in a tone of genuine grievance, and folded up like a deckchair in a gale. Silence. Rain beginning, fat and sour on the concrete. Midas lay on his back, bleeding from one eyebrow, one elbow, and several opinions. He held up the box. Purification tablets: nine. The batteries were gone. The water bottle was gone. Chewy sat beside him, dripping, and his left eye had died sometime in the chase. The right one flickered a mournful blue. "You said short trip," croaked Midas. "G'day, mate," said Chewy, with dignity. --- They limped home through the rain, which was doing that thing where it cleaned nothing and dissolved a little of everything. It was, Midas reflected, bitterly ironic to be soaked in undrinkable water while carrying tablets to purify water. Then he reflected further, and stopped walking. "Chewy. The rain." "What about it?" "It's filthy. Full of whatever fell on Dandenong. Which means—" he shook the box— "these aren't pointless. These are *pointful*." Chewy's eye flickered green, then settled into a warm pink that had nothing to do with his remaining circuitry and everything to do with his programming. Back at Buddy's Fuel 'n' Bait, they boiled rainwater in a hubcap over a fire of telephone books, and toasted each other in chipped enamel mugs of the cleanest liquid either had tasted in a year. Midas's eyebrow throbbed. Chewy was down one eye, one ear, and most of his tail seam. Nine tablets, minus the two Midas had dropped in the dock, minus the one Chewy insisted on keeping "for emergencies," which meant under his stuffing, where all treasures went. Seven tablets. Half a mug each. Riches. "So," said Midas, leaning back against the counter as the rain ticked on the roof. "Tomorrow?" "Thought we might head west," said Chewy. "There's an old pharmacy. Short trip." His eye flickered yellow. Midas sighed, and got the needle and thread ready. --- \* *Trolleys are the only species that has genuinely thrived since the Fall. Unburdened by predators, purpose, or loyalty cards, they nest in the high aisles of the great dead stores and come out at dusk to rust romantically in the rain.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations, and footnote-style asides. The opening line about the world ending "slowly, and then all at once, and then very slowly again" immediately establishes the Pratchettesque tone, as does the observation about historians being among the first to go as "proof of a merciful universe." The characterization is well-executed within the constraints of the format. Midas emerges as a believably weary survivor with a sardonic outlook, while Chewy is given genuine personality through his color-changing eyes and limited vocabulary that somehow conveys meaning beyond its programming. The relationship between them feels authentic - neither overly sentimental nor coldly pragmatic. The plot structure adheres perfectly to the prompt's requirements: deliberation, mission gone sideways, return home worse for wear. The HyperMart sequence is particularly well-crafted, with Harold the Customer Assistance Unit serving as both obstacle and comic relief. The solution to Harold's threat - Chewy's "HUG ME!" triggering conflicting protocols - is clever and fits the established world logic. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with memorable phrases like "the universe keeps receipts" and "ran along it like a man fleeing down the tongue of an enormous grey whale." The footnote about trolleys thriving post-apocalypse is pure Pratchett pastiche. However, some descriptions occasionally veer toward the overwrought, particularly in the action sequences. The dialogue serves its purpose but lacks the razor-sharp wit that elevates Pratchett's best exchanges. While functional, it doesn't crackle with the same energy as the narrative voice. The emotional core works well - the ending's modest triumph feels earned rather than artificially upbeat, and the cyclical nature (Chewy suggesting another "short trip") provides satisfying closure while suggesting the pattern will continue. The piece succeeds in creating a lived-in post-apocalyptic world that feels both desolate and oddly cozy. The imagery is generally strong, though occasionally the author tries too hard for effect. The pacing is solid, building tension effectively during the HyperMart sequence before settling into the quieter resolution. Minor weaknesses include some forced metaphors and a few moments where the Pratchett imitation becomes slightly too obvious. The piece also occasionally tells rather than shows, particularly in establishing the world's backstory. Overall, this is a competent and entertaining piece that successfully fulfills its brief while demonstrating genuine understanding of its stylistic target.
