+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# THE BOY WHO BORROWED TIME ## Chapter Nine: The Face in the Mirror Owen Delgado had used the watch six times before he noticed what it was taking from him. The first time had been an accident. He'd been fiddling with the crown — twisting it the way you'd wind an old clock — when the kitchen lurched *backward*. Orange juice crawled up out of the carpet and poured itself neatly back into the glass. His sister's scream unscreamed. Three minutes of Saturday morning rolled in reverse, and Owen stood frozen in the middle of it, heart hammering, while everyone else lived those three minutes like they'd never happened at all. Only Owen remembered. Only Owen had *paid*. But he didn't know that yet. The second time, he redid a pop quiz he'd bombed. The third, he dodged a dodgeball that would have flattened his nose. The fourth, fifth, and sixth times? Let's just say nobody at Jefferson Middle School ever needed to know he'd tripped in front of the entire cafeteria. Six little fixes. Six little twists of the crown. By Monday morning, his jeans were two inches too short. "That's weird," Owen muttered, tugging at the fabric flashing his socks. Weird, but not *scary*-weird. Kids grew. That was the deal with bodies. Except bodies didn't grow overnight. Bodies didn't drop half a foot between Friday and Monday. Bodies didn't make your voice crack *downward* in the middle of saying good morning, so low that your own mother turned around and stared at you like a stranger had wandered into her kitchen. "You sound like your father," she said, laughing. But her laugh wobbled. At school it got worse. Sixth graders stepped out of his way in the halls and *nodded* at him, like he was somebody. Coach Reyes clapped his shoulder and said, "Big man! You eating your vitamins?" Mr. Hendricks, the science teacher, squinted at him during attendance and asked — in front of everyone — if he was sure he was in the right room. "I'm Owen Delgado," Owen said. "Huh," said Mr. Hendricks. "You look... *older* than Delgado." Older than himself. Great. Tuesday, Owen found a single dark hair on his chin. Wednesday, his mom silently set a stick of deodorant on his dresser and backed out of the room without making eye contact. Thursday, he caught two eighth-grade girls whispering and giggling when he walked past, and one of them called him — *sir.* Sir. They called him SIR. That night Owen stood in the bathroom, gripping the sink, staring at his reflection. Twelve years old. Mostly. The face looking back had shadows under the eyes that hadn't been there in September. His jaw looked heavier. Sharper. Like someone was slowly carving a grown-up out of him, chip by chip. "This isn't happening," he whispered. And then it happened. His reflection *flickered*. Just for a second — like a bad video signal — the boy in the mirror vanished, and a MAN looked back at him. Late twenties, maybe older. Tired eyes with fine lines around them. Stubble. A scar on the eyebrow that Owen didn't have. Yet. The man wore the exact same horrified expression Owen was wearing. Owen blinked. The man was gone. Just Owen again — pale, twelve, shaking. He did the math right there on the tile floor, hugging his knees. Six rewinds. Six years? Was that how it worked? Was the watch spending *him* to buy back its little do-overs? He should have stopped. He would have stopped. But Friday afternoon, his little sister chased her soccer ball into Maple Street. Owen saw the delivery truck the same instant he saw Ada — tiny, laughing, oblivious — stepping off the curb. There was no time to shout. No time to run. There was only the crown. Owen grabbed it and twisted *back* — hard, farther than he'd ever gone. One hour. The world smeared sideways. Birds flew in reverse. The sun stuttered across the sky like a scratched DVD. Then — *snap* — one hour earlier. Owen sprinted the four blocks to Maple Street, lungs on fire, legs longer than they'd been a week ago, and snatched Ada off the curb just as the truck roared past, close enough to ruffle her hair. "You okay?" he gasped, holding her tight. Ada patted his arm like he was the one who needed calming down. "You always worry too much," she said. "*Old man.*" He laughed. It came out deep and rusty. It wasn't until Monday that he understood what one hour of stolen time actually cost. Danny's desk was empty. Not absent-empty. *Erased*-empty. Clean. Like no kid named Danny Okafor had ever sat there, cracking jokes, trading Oreos, being Owen's best friend since kindergarten. "Danny who?" Ms. Alvarez asked, frowning. Owen ran to Danny's house after school. FOR SALE sign. Dusty windows. Empty driveway. He checked his phone — every photo of them together was just... Owen. Alone. Grinning at nothing. At *nobody*. The hour hadn't come from nowhere. The watch had taken it from somewhere. From *someone*. It had reached into the timeline and pulled a thread, and Danny had unraveled right out of the world. That night Owen locked the bathroom door and stared into the mirror until his eyes watered. "I'm sorry," he whispered. "I'll fix it. I'll put it back." He knew what it would take. One more twist. One more rewind — far enough back to catch the thread before it snapped, far enough to pull Danny out of wherever the watch had stuffed him. One more year of Owen, spent like pocket change. He raised his wrist. The watch glowed softly, patiently, like it had been waiting for exactly this. In the mirror, his reflection flickered — boy, man, boy, man — faster now, like a lightbulb dying. The man's mouth moved. Owen couldn't hear it, but he could read the lips perfectly. *One more. Go ahead. See who's left.* "Shut up," Owen told his own face. He gripped the crown. His hand looked forty years old. He twisted. And somewhere very far away, in a place with no clocks at all, something enormous opened one eye — and started counting *down*.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative storytelling within the Goosebumps-style teen horror framework. The author successfully captures the escalating dread characteristic of the genre while maintaining age-appropriate content and pacing. The concept is genuinely creative - a smartwatch that rewinds time at the cost of aging the user is both contemporary and horrifying in a way that would resonate with middle schoolers. The progression from minor inconveniences (failed quiz, dodgeball) to major catastrophe (sister's near-death) to cosmic horror (erasing his best friend) creates excellent escalating tension. The prose quality is notably high, with vivid imagery like "Orange juice crawled up out of the carpet" and "Birds flew in reverse. The sun stuttered across the sky like a scratched DVD." The writing maintains consistent voice throughout - appropriately sophisticated for the target audience without being condescending. Character development is well-handled. Owen's motivations feel authentic for a twelve-year-old, and his horror at the consequences rings true. The physical transformation details (voice cracking downward, needing deodorant, being called "sir") are both creatively unsettling and believable markers of accelerated aging. The story structure is tight, moving efficiently through the discovery, experimentation, realization, and final crisis phases. The mirror scenes provide effective horror beats, and the flickering reflection device works well as both foreshadowing and revelation. However, there are some weaknesses. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctive character voice - Owen sounds somewhat generic for a middle schooler. The ending, while appropriately ominous, feels slightly rushed in its cosmic escalation. The piece also relies heavily on telling rather than showing in places, particularly in explaining the watch's mechanics. The emotional complexity is appropriate for the genre - Owen's guilt, fear, and desperation come through clearly. The story earns its dark ending through the logical progression of consequences, avoiding unearned positivity while maintaining hope for resolution. # Carnival of Dangerous Intentions He was at the shooting gallery, as arranged — though *arranged* was generous for a sentence exchanged across two nights and one borrowed umbrella, which hung now on her arm like a closed fan, the excuse she'd rehearsed the whole ride down from Flatbush. The bulbs along the boardwalk buzzed awake one strand at a time, strung like fruit ripening toward the dark. Salt, sugar, machine oil, creosote. Somewhere the Cyclone knocked through its long descent like artillery two towns over; nearer, a calliope wheezed out something jaunty and wrong. The tin ducks slid along their rail, dented, patient. *His locks.* There it was again — that prim, old-fashioned phrase surfacing like a body coming up beneath a dock. She pressed it down. Along with the other thing. Especially the other thing. "You came," he said, without turning. He'd seen her in the gallery's little mirror, she realized. Of course he had. "I was walking. This is where I ended up." "No one ends up at Coney Island. You have to mean it." "Then I meant it." He turned. Sleeves rolled, collar open, curls black as wet tar, and a smile like something kept sheathed. He offered the rifle stock-first, like a dance card. "Show me how you'd hold it." She stepped into the space he made. His hands adjusted hers — brief, impersonal, warm straight through the cotton of her gloves. "Elbow. Breathe out. Now — where are you looking?" "At the duck." "Mm. Most people aim where it's safe." She fired. A wing; the tin spun shrieking on its pin, and the barker hollered *winner* with professional indifference. The stranger laid coins on the counter, and the barker took them without once looking at his face — a small thing, which she noted, and decided not to think about. He waved off the Kewpie doll. "You won it. Take it." "It isn't the duck I wanted." They walked. Past the penny arcade, past banners for the Mummified Mermaid and Fatima, Girl Whose Eyes See All, the lamps thinning toward the dark end of the boards. "Everyone at Coney has a name," she said. "Do they? Half of them are hiding from theirs." "And yours?" "Keeping mine warm." A glance, sidelong. "Yours is Evelyn." "I didn't say." "You bit your cheek when you didn't. Left side. You did it Tuesday, too, when the rain came and you told me you weren't alone." Heat climbed her throat. She had lied to him twice, and he had filed both away like ticket stubs. What unsettled her was not that he noticed — it was how easily she had lied at all. To him. And an hour ago to Harold on the telephone, a smooth little fiction about mending and an early night. Lying used to cost her something. "Does someone expect you at nine?" he asked. "My sister does." "Will you be there?" "That depends on the conversation." He laughed, low and pleased, like a man pocketing exact change. The fortune teller's booth crouched at the bend where the lamps gave out — canvas gone moth-gray, hand-lettered: **MADAME SEREDA · YOUR FUTURE IN YOUR OWN HAND**. Palmistry charts hung crooked behind her: open hands inked in red and blue, LIFE, HEART, HEAD, FATE; the mounts named for Venus, Saturn, the Moon. The bead curtain snapped aside and the old woman was simply *there*, small and iron-haired, seizing Evelyn's wrist before courtesy could intervene. She turned the palm up to the lamp. "Long," she muttered, tracing. "Long life line — but see, it forks here. Snake's tongue. Two roads stitched into one thread, *signorina*, and only one of them is yours—" The woman looked up. Saw him. Whatever she saw stopped her as if the lamp had gone out. She pressed her thumb hard into the center of Evelyn's palm — once, twice, a stamp, a seal — and whispered, fast and low: "*Stasera non dare niente.* Tonight you give nothing. Nothing to nobody." The curtain fell between them like a struck bell going silent. He was at her elbow — no hurry, no sound. Through the gap in the curtain he set a coin in the woman's saucer. "For the reading." "There wasn't one," Evelyn managed. "There's always a reading." They reached the rail where the boardwalk ended its argument with the sea. The Wonder Wheel turned its lit circumference against a bruising violet sky; gulls hung in the rigging of the dark; beneath the planks the tide worked at the pilings, unhurried, taking the wood a grain at a time. "You're wondering what I want," he said. "I'm deciding whether to ask." "Ask." "What do you want?" He faced her fully then, and it was like being read by the charts — every line found, named, priced. From somewhere, a waistcoat pocket, a sleeve, he produced a small pair of silver scissors with mother-of-pearl handles. Absurdly gentle. "A lock of your hair." The word arrived and detonated quietly. *Locks.* His, all week, an intruder in her own head — and now hers, requested outright, under a dying sky. The old woman's thumb still burned in her palm like a brand. *Nothing to nobody.* "That's an odd request." "It's an old one." He turned the scissors once, catching the lamplight. "A keepsake means you intended to come back for it." "That's not the same as meaning to stay." "No," he agreed softly. "But it's a start. Everything dangerous starts as a souvenir." Below them the tide kept at the shore, patient as anything, and Evelyn understood suddenly that she was standing on the eroding edge of some decision already made — made Tuesday, in the rain, the moment she'd taken his umbrella and told herself she'd return it. Her hand rose, of its own opinion entirely, to the net of her hat. To the pins. To the coil of hair still warm from the long day. Behind them, faint through the beads, Madame Sereda began to pray in a language Evelyn didn't know, and the tin ducks rattled on their rail, going nowhere, over and over, in the dark.

+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**II.** Supper that night was beans and fried potatoes, and nobody talked about the clearing. Dad sat with his back to the stove, hat still on, which he never did indoors. Mike told the story of the day's hunt twice, embellishing it a little more each time—the way the light had been, how still everything held—and each time he told it, the buck got smaller and farther away. By the second telling it was eighty yards off and half-hidden in alder, a near-miss, a nothing. JT kept his eyes on his plate and said nothing at all. The meat was sweet. Sweeter than caribou had any right to be, and clean, no gristle, no worms, like it had come off a butcher's paper instead of out of the muskeg. "You had him, Dad," JT said finally. Careful, casual, a boy asking about weather. "In the clearing. Forty yards if he was one." His father's fork stopped halfway to his mouth. Hung there. For a second the only sound was the stove ticking and Mike chewing with his mouth open like always. "Wind shifted," Dad said. But there had been no wind. JT knew it the way you know your own name. All afternoon the air had hung dead still, the smoke off the lodge chimney rising straight as a plumb line, not one branch whispering anywhere in sight. He waited for somebody else to say so. "Swirled some," Mike said. "I felt it on my neck. Cold little gust." He said it easily, certainly, and that frightened JT worse than a lie would have. Because either Mike remembered a wind that had never blown—or Mike needed there to have been one, needed it so bad his mind had gone ahead and built it, brick by brick, just so the day could keep its shape. After supper Dad washed his hands at the dry sink. Washed them, dried them, then washed them again with the Lava soap, scrubbing until his knuckles went pink and raw, staring out the black square of window at nothing. JT counted things, the way he did when he was little, after Mom passed—counted the shells as Dad thumbed them into the .30-06 by lamplight. Four. Dad stopped at four and set the box down with one round still in his palm, looked at it a long time like he couldn't recall what it was for, then slid it into his shirt pocket. Five in the box. Four in the gun. Dad had never short-loaded a day in his life. *He's saving one,* said a thought in the back of JT's head, and he shut that door fast and threw the bolt on it. He told himself he dreamed the rest. He would keep telling himself that, right up until he couldn't. It came first as pressure, the way a storm announces itself in a filling tooth. Then sound: a soft double-click, rhythmic, patient, circling the lodge. Click-click. Pause. Click-click. He knew that sound from every fall of his boyhood—caribou tendons snapping in the walk, a whole herd sounding like knitting needles. Except herds moved. This circled. And circled. And did not pass. JT slid from the bunk, careful of the third board, and wiped a porthole clear in the frost ferns on the glass. The dooryard was full of them. Twenty, thirty, standing hipshot and easy in the blue moonlight, breath steaming—and here was the thing, the thing that made his scalp try to crawl off his skull—they were all facing the lodge. Not grazing. Not milling. Facing it, heads level, ears forward, like an audience. And when they exhaled, they exhaled *together*, one white sigh lifting off the whole yard at once. He counted twelve before he lost his place. Recounted. Got a different number. Recounted again. And there on the porch steps sat his father, in his union suit, barefoot on boards furred white with frost, arms hanging loose, head tilted with that look from the clearing—lips parted, eyes shining wet and black in the moonlight, a man on the verge of hearing wonderful news. Ten feet below him stood the big buck. The same one. JT knew it the way you know a face in a family photo. It stood with its dark flat eyes tipped up, and Dad's hand had begun, very slowly, to rise. *(open the door)* The thought wasn't in his ears. It was behind his sternum, warm as swallowed whiskey, reasonable as arithmetic: *(they only want to show you, they've been waiting all this time to show you)*— JT bit the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper, and blinked, and the yard was empty. Every animal, gone. The buck, gone. His father, gone. The frost lay silver and unbroken from porch step to tree line, smooth as the icing on a wedding cake. No tracks. No tracks at all. He stood there until his breath fogged the glass eight, nine times, telling himself what you tell yourself: *thin frost, wouldn't hold print anyway, you were dreaming, you never even got out of bed.* Downstairs, a door sighed shut. Boots on the hall floorboards—but no, he saw the boots a minute later, sitting by the stove, soaked through, laces stiff with ice. His father came up the dark hallway barefoot, feet blue-white, smelling of cold air and something green and sweet underneath it, like juniper rotting in a bog. "Get to bed, Jay-Dee," Dad said gently. Gently, the way you talk to someone sleeping. The way you talk to something you don't want to startle. In the morning Dad fried no eggs, ate nothing, drank coffee after coffee with his eyes rimmed red as a drunk's, and announced they'd hunt the north ridge. When JT asked him—quiet, careful—where he'd gone last night, Dad looked at him for a long moment with those too-bright eyes. "Went nowhere," he said. Then, smiling, easy as talking about the price of gas: "They're thick this year, though. Thickest I ever seen 'em." That smile was the worst part. Because it was *happy.* At the window, JT counted the caribou strung along the ridge across the lake. Seven. He blinked, and counted eight. None of them had taken a single step. And underneath the wind—or in it, or *as* it—that soft double-clicking went patiently on, circling, circling, in no hurry at all.

The author uses concrete, grounded details—the frost patterns, the sound of caribou tendons, the specific count of ammunition—to anchor the surreal elements in believable reality. The progression from subtle wrongness (the too-sweet meat, the missing wind) to overt supernatural manifestation (the yard full of watching caribou) feels organic and earned. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 90.2
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Model Output:
# Hell Is Other Demons Morning in Hell began, as it always did, with the ash. It fell in a fine grey drizzle over the City of Dis, soft as talcum, patient as regret. It collected on the spires, on the shoulders of the damned, on the little red convertible Lucifer kept in the garage and never drove because nowhere in Hell was far enough to justify it. Lucifer stood at the kitchen window with his coffee, which tasted faintly of scorched almonds, because everything in Hell tasted faintly of scorched almonds if you'd been there long enough. Below, in the plaza, a lost soul was being chased in slow, ceremonial circles by something with too many elbows. Lucifer watched it the way other beings watched birds. The crossword in the *Damned Times* was easy today. Four across, *Eternal, but make it tedious*: DAMNATION. Seven down, *What the lake needs, per the maintenance memo*: DREDGING. The intercom on the wall cleared its throat. "Sire," said Beleth, his chief of staff, "the Screaming Fields imps are striking again." "Again?" "They want dental." "They're *imps*. They regrow teeth like weeds." "They want *better* dental." Lucifer closed his eyes. "Send them a form." "They've eaten the forms, sire." "Then send them a form they can't eat. Obsidian. And put a note on the schedule — the Lake of Fire gets dredged Thursday, and if the Leviathan complains, the Leviathan can take it up with the Leviathan." He said this with the flat authority of a middle manager who had once toppled Heaven and now mostly approved invoices. Eternity, it turned out, was less a punishment than a filing system. The morning proceeded. A damned accountant from Ohio requested a transfer from the Boiling Lake to the Frozen Wastes on the grounds that he "did better in the cold." Lucifer granted it, because the paperwork for denying it was worse. A demon named Vassago had eaten a subordinate and filed it, correctly, under *Team Restructuring*. Lucifer signed off, then added a sticky note: *Please stop eating the interns. We are out of interns.* It was just past noon — Hell had a noon the way it had a moon, by consensus and stubborn tradition — when the doorbell rang. The doorbell was a small damned soul who had, in life, sold timeshares. He rang himself against the bell with the enthusiasm of the genuinely doomed. Lucifer knew who it was before he opened the door. He always knew. After ten thousand years, you know the shape of a person the way you know the shape of your own hand, even when you've thrown that hand at someone and told them never to come back. Lilith stood on the step in the ash-drizzle, not bothering to shield herself, because ash knew better than to land on her. She was holding a wicker basket. "You're not answering my letters," she said. "You set my last letter on fire." "I read it *first*. There's a difference." "What's in the basket?" She lifted the flap. Inside, asleep in a nest of black wool, was a hellhound puppy with three eyes, two of which were open. "Cerberus had a litter," Lilith said. "You get the runt. Per the custody arrangement." "We don't have a custody arrangement." "We do now. I've drafted it. You'll want to sign." "You drafted a custody arrangement for a dog we don't share." "The runt is *ours*. The others are mine. This one howls at things that haven't happened yet, which is your whole personality, so." He should have closed the door. He had closed the door on archangels, on plagues, on a very persistent salesman offering eternal salvation at a reasonable rate. Instead he stepped aside, and Lilith walked into his kitchen as if the intervening century of not speaking had been a long lunch. She moved through the house the way she always had, touching things. She oiled the front door, which screamed when opened — it was supposed to scream, it was *installed* screaming, but she'd never liked it. She fed the puppy something from her pocket that Lucifer chose not to identify. She stood at the window and looked out at the ash. "It's heavier than last week," she said. "The Furnace is overproducing. Beleth says it's a staffing issue." "Everything's a staffing issue with you." "You left, and now it is." She didn't turn around. The ash fell. Somewhere across the city, the striking imps had begun to chant, which in imp was mostly the word *dental* repeated with feeling. "There's a thing," Lilith said, "in the Outer Dark. Thursday. A gathering." "I don't gather." "I know. That was always the problem." She turned. Her eyes were the color the sky used to be, before either of them had opinions about it. "I'm asking anyway." Lucifer looked at the puppy, which had climbed onto his ledger and was chewing the corner of an invoice marked *URGENT*. It howled, softly, at something that hadn't happened yet. He had a suspicion about what. "Thursday," he said, "I have the dredging." "Reschedule it." "I *never* reschedule the dredging." "You rescheduled the Apocalypse twice." "That was different. That was *politics*." Lilith almost smiled, which in Lilith was roughly equivalent to other people weeping. She picked up her empty basket and walked to the door, and paused there, hand on the screaming hinge, and for a moment neither of them said anything, and the ash fell on the plaza and on the spires and on the little red convertible that had never gone anywhere. "Fix the door," she said. "It's depressing." "You like it depressing." "I liked it depressing when I was angry. I'm between angers at the moment." "Between," Lucifer repeated. "For now," she said, with the terrible precision of someone who had outlasted empires, "don't make it a thing." She left. The puppy stayed, having decided, in the way of puppies and of Lucifer himself, long ago, that it was easier to stay than to leave. That evening Lucifer sat at his desk, stamped *APPROVED* on Vassago's restructuring, and then, after a long moment, pulled up the maintenance schedule and moved the dredging to Friday. The ash fell all night, fine and grey and patient. In the kitchen, something howled at Thursday.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the prompt's requirements, successfully merging the mundane bureaucracy of running Hell with intimate relationship dynamics. The author captures a distinctly Gaiman-esque voice through understated irony and absurdist juxtapositions - Lucifer dealing with striking imps who want dental coverage while navigating his complicated feelings about Lilith creates exactly the kind of dark comedy requested. The characterization is particularly strong. Lucifer emerges as a weary middle manager who "once toppled Heaven and now mostly approved invoices," while Lilith maintains her mythic power while engaging in recognizably domestic behaviors like oiling squeaky hinges. Their dialogue crackles with history and unspoken emotion, particularly in exchanges like "I'm between angers at the moment" and "don't make it a thing." The prose style is elegant and controlled, with memorable phrases like "ash fell... patient as regret" and "Eternity, it turned out, was less a punishment than a filing system." The imagery consistently reinforces the theme - everything tasting of scorched almonds, the red convertible that never goes anywhere, the prophetic hellhound puppy. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 92.8
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Arithmetic of Sand They woke us before the light. In the Ludus Magnus the dark smelled of iron and straw and old sand, which never leaves us — it lives in the seams of our skin, in our hair, in the bread we chew. I lay on my pallet and listened to Rome begin: donkeys turning the millstones two streets over, a water-seller's bell, crows quarreling on the awning beams. A torch guttered in the corridor, breathing pine resin. Through the grate above my bunk I could see a single arch of the great amphitheater, grey against grey, like the rib of some enormous dead animal the city now lived inside. I mended my net before the doctore's horn sounded. This is my ritual, and I guard it the way other men guard their gods. The *rete* is a circle of cord weighted with lead shot around its hem, and when it opens in the air it becomes a wheel of small moons. I was casting nets on the Danube before I ever held a plough; my father's hands taught mine the knots, and my hands have not forgotten, though everything else from that country has been burned or sold. When the doctore first lined us up and asked what we would fight as, I did not choose the trident so much as refuse to choose anything else. The armorer made my *fuscina* — ash wood, taller than I am, three iron tines — but I recognized it the way you recognize a face across a crowded market. A fish spear. Rome took everything else and handed this back to me, reshaped for slaughter, and gave me a god's name to fight under: Triton. The crowd finds it delightful. The fisherman who fishes men. In the morning yard the wooden swords cracked like doors slamming. Vindex, our doctore, a Gaul with a freedman's cap and a face like a collapsed wall, counted strokes in his flat voice while sailors from the fleet at Misenum rigged the *velarium* against the coming heat. They say the Emperor has bought ten thousand gladiators for the triumph games — a hundred and twenty-three days of blood to celebrate the conquest of my country. Ten thousand. I have tried to imagine the column and failed. They diverted a river in Dacia to dig our king's treasure from its bed; now that gold pays for sand, and the sand drinks what it is given. Some mornings, when the games run, the crowd's roar reaches the yard — a sound like the sea, like the river in flood — and I know precisely what it is cheering for. A poet in a tavern near the baths says the Roman people have traded their votes for bread and games and are perfectly content. He is not wrong. A crowd watching a spectacle does not ask where the grain comes from. I am part of the arithmetic of empire. At noon an escort walked five of us to the baths, and Rome came at us in layers: the Tiber's breath at low water, the ferment of garum, the ammonia sting of the fullers' vats, incense drifting from a street altar, hot bread, horse dung, dust. A senator's litter went by, white wool trimmed in purple, the bearers' feet quick on the stones. Citizens queued at the grain steps with their lead tokens, patient as cattle, and masons were cutting away the saddle between two hills for the Emperor's new forum — slaves moving the very earth of Rome so that marble could say *I was here*. Near the fountain someone had scratched into the plaster: *Triton makes the matrons sigh.* A boy saluted me with a stick trident, and his mother laughed, and then saw what I actually was — the scarred arm, the collar mark beneath the oil — and pulled him away. A man on the steps spat as I passed. Both are correct. That is what a gladiator is to this city: a god for an afternoon and a line in a ledger, despised and adored in the same breath. Evening brought us back through the gate, into the copper smell of the armory. Under a loose flagstone in my cell I keep a clay pot, and in the pot, denarii — the crowd's thrown coins, my share of the purses, a ring a woman sent me that I sold without regret. The *rudis*, the wooden sword they hand a man when they are finished with him, means freedom, and men have died in the sand reaching for it. But freedom is not what I am saving for. My sister has a name no one in Rome knows either. Word came up the river road that she was sold to a household on the Caelian. So I count coins in the dark like a miser counts sins. The arithmetic of empire cuts both ways: in this city everything has a price, and that means she has one too. I am not afraid of what waits tomorrow. I am afraid of the pot being empty when I finally find her street. On the board by the gate, the pairings stood in chalk: *Triton the retiarius against Aquila the secutor.* A secutor is a pursuer — the whole pairing is a fish and a hunter, and the editor has promised the crowd a chase. Aquila is big and patient and wastes no movement; I have watched him for a year the way a fisherman watches water. I will not think of him tonight. Tonight I oiled the leather of my *manica*, checked that the *galerus* buckled true across my shoulder, and sat with the net across my knees, saying the names of the dead while my hands worked the knots, the way my father taught me — a name, a knot; a name, a knot — until the cord ran out of room and the lamp burned low. Beyond the wall the city settled into its thousand small noises, and somewhere far north the Danube was still running, grey and wide, indifferent to empires. I hold on to that the way I grip the fuscina's shaft: with both hands. It is the last thing here that remembers what I was before Rome taught me its arithmetic — and tomorrow, when the gate lifts and the sand takes what it is given, it is the thing I mean to be holding still.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sophisticated piece of historical fiction that demonstrates exceptional craft and literary merit. The author creates a compelling first-person narrative from the perspective of a Dacian gladiator in Rome, successfully avoiding the combat scene as requested while delivering rich sensory details and deep character exploration. The prose is consistently elegant and controlled, with particularly strong metaphorical language that feels organic rather than forced. Phrases like "like the rib of some enormous dead animal the city now lived inside" and "the sand drinks what it is given" demonstrate sophisticated imagery that serves both atmospheric and thematic purposes. The writing maintains a consistent voice throughout - contemplative, melancholic, yet dignified - that feels authentic to both the character and historical period. The sensory details are expertly woven throughout: the smell of "iron and straw and old sand," the sound of "donkeys turning the millstones," and the visual of Rome's layered urban landscape create an immersive experience. The author demonstrates strong research into Roman culture, from the Ludus Magnus to the velarium to specific gladiator equipment, without letting historical detail overwhelm the narrative. Character development is nuanced and emotionally complex. The protagonist's relationship with his net and trident - tools that connect him to his lost homeland - provides powerful emotional anchoring. His motivation (saving money to buy his sister's freedom) gives the story genuine stakes without resorting to melodrama. The internal conflict between his role as entertainment and his humanity is handled with subtlety. The political and social commentary is seamlessly integrated, particularly the observation about "bread and games" and the "arithmetic of empire." These themes emerge naturally from the character's perspective rather than feeling imposed by the author. The structure works well as a "slice of life," beginning before dawn and ending at night, creating a complete arc while clearly being part of a larger story. The ending, with its reference to the Danube and what he was "before Rome taught me its arithmetic," provides satisfying closure while maintaining the story's melancholic tone. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose approaches being overwrought, though it generally stays on the right side of that line. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Creag Dhu Rock Station — 14 March 1959** Dear Mam, Landed safe Tuesday on the *Cluaran*. The rock's smaller than they say and taller — ninety-one steps to the lamp, and I counted twice because I didnae believe myself the first time. Mr. Gunn is principal keeper. He spoke maybe forty words today and I counted them too. My bunkroom smells of paraffin and old birds. The wage is good, Mam. More than the yard ever paid Da in his last year, so dinnae fret about me. The tea tastes of the tin, but I'll manage. Your son, Callum --- **Braidfauld, Glasgow — 28 March** My dear boy, Your letter came Thursday and I read it twice by the fire. Mrs. Boyd's hens got into my kale again, so the world goes on as normal here. I've posted wool socks — wear them, and rub camphorated oil on your chest of a night. Your father always said a man who works high up is either a fool or a happy one, and he was both himself, hanging off the Clyde cranes. The house is very quiet of a Sunday now. Write often. Don't be proud. Your loving Mother --- **Creag Dhu — 19 April** Dear Mam, Third loaf rose proper. The first two could have curled at Bonspiel. I mind the brass, paint the railings when the wind allows, and the gannets scream at me like I owe them money. Now — under a loose board behind my bunk I found a Player's tobacco tin, rusted shut till I coaxed it with a knife. Wrapped in oilcloth inside: a wee gannet carved from teak, dark as strong tea, wings half lifted as if it couldnae quite be bothered to fly. One eye is chipped clean away. Scratched underneath: *J.M. 1911*. And a slip of paper, brown as the wood itself: *"For the next one. The rock is no' what's hard."* It sits on my shelf watching me eat. I've written the Board to ask who J.M. was. Callum --- **Braidfauld — 30 April** My dear, What a find! Ask the Board, and ask properly — folk leave things for a reason. Keep the bird where you see it mornings. A day starts better looking at a thing somebody finished. I took a turn on the stair on Monday. Dizzy, and down I went. Dr. Lees says my heart's lazy, no' bad, and I believe him because he charges enough. Dinnae fret, and dinnae tell Katie, or she'll have me in a chair with a rug by May. Your loving Mother --- **Creag Dhu — 17 September** Dear Mam, The Board wrote back. John Macaulay, assistant keeper here 1909 to 1913. His brother went down with the trawler *Rosehill* on the north side in February 1910 — eleven men lost, within sight of his own light. Macaulay kept that light burning all that night, and stayed on three years more. So he carved the bird waiting, maybe. Or forgiving. I cannae decide which is harder. Some nights I say the alphabet aloud just to hear a voice answer back. There's a seal hauls out on the low skerry; I've named her Mrs. Boyd. She ignores me completely, so it's very lifelike. Callum --- *TELEGRAM — RECEIVED CREAG DHU, 11 NOVEMBER* MAM BAD STOP HEART STOP COME FIRST BOAT STOP KATIE --- **Braidfauld — 14 November, written at the kitchen table** Mam, Mr. Gunn rowed me to the *Cluaran* in seas I'll describe when you're stronger, and the boat beat down the coast eleven hours against it. I got here Friday night. You sleep most of the day. Wednesday you held my hand and called me Jim, and I never minded, not once. Dr. Lees says the old heart's beating stubborn again — well, it comes by that honest. I'm staying till you order me off. The kettle's on. Your boy, Callum --- **Braidfauld — 20 December** My dear, I'm writing standing up, which is progress. The minister prayed over me and I felt better immediately, which I suspect annoyed him. Now listen. You were aye one for leaving rooms before you're missed. Go back and keep your light. I'll come out on the boat in June when the sea's civilised, and bring a clootie dumpling and my own opinion of Mr. Gunn. And Callum — put something of yours in that tin. For the next one. I told you in April folk leave things for a reason, and I'm aye right. Your loving Mother --- **Creag Dhu — 16 March 1960** Dear Mam, Back on the rock a month and the gannets have remembered their grievances. Your ticket's bought for the ninth of June — Katie has it, so arguing is pointless. I tried carving. I made a cormorant out of driftwood and it's terrible, Mam, more a potato with opinions, but it sits on the shelf next to the gannet and J.M. doesn't complain. Both eyes intact, which is more than his managed. Last night the fog came down and the horn went till morning, and I thought: somewhere out there is a boat with somebody's mother aboard, wanting home. So I minded the light properly. Gunn was right, I think. It's no' the rock that's hard. It took me a year to understand what he meant, and I'll no' waste it. One hundred and fifteen days till the boat. I've started counting backwards instead of forwards. It's amazing the difference. Your son, Callum P.S. The seal answered to Mrs. Boyd today. Almost.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully captures the voice of a working-class Scottish lighthouse keeper through authentic dialect and vernacular that feels natural rather than forced. The author demonstrates strong control over the epistolary form, using the constraints of letters and telegrams to reveal character and advance plot effectively. The characterization is particularly strong. Callum's voice is consistent throughout - practical, observant, with a dry humor that emerges through details like counting Mr. Gunn's forty words or naming the seal Mrs. Boyd after his mother's troublesome neighbor. His mother's voice is equally distinct - warm but no-nonsense, with the authority of experience. The relationship between them feels genuine and lived-in. The central metaphor of the carved gannet and the mysterious message "The rock is no' what's hard" provides effective thematic structure. The revelation about John Macaulay and his brother's death within sight of the lighthouse adds historical weight and connects Callum's isolation to a larger human story of duty and loss. The narrative arc is well-constructed, moving from initial adjustment through deepening isolation, crisis (the mother's illness), and resolution. The mother's recovery and planned visit, combined with Callum's newfound understanding of his purpose, provides satisfying closure without being overly sentimental. The prose is economical and effective, with strong concrete details that establish setting and mood. Phrases like "tea tastes of the tin" and "gannets scream at me like I owe them money" are vivid and character-appropriate. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Scottish dialect feels slightly inconsistent, and the transformation from isolation to acceptance could have been developed more gradually. The telegram format is used effectively but sparingly. The emotional climax around the mother's illness feels genuine rather than manipulative. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Attack Surface The WiFi password is taped to the register like a hostage note: *GuestNet2024!* I clock it before I clock my date. Exclamation point, year, the restaurant's own name in plaintext. Anyone sipping a latte within radio range could sit outside and harvest handshakes all afternoon. Not that I'd—I *don't* anymore. I just see it. Seeing is free. It's the only thing that ever was. Her name is Dana. She arrived four minutes late, which I logged automatically—social engineering primer, chapter one: tardiness establishes asymmetry, puts the other party slightly off-balance—and then immediately forgave, because she apologized twice and meant it both times, and sincerity doesn't ping any threat model I have. We ordered. I scanned the exits. Habit. Two doors, kitchen pass-through, camera above the register with its housing cracked and hanging at a fifteen-degree angle, which means either it works or it doesn't and nobody knows which. The whole room is a soft target wearing an apron. And none of it matters, because ten minutes in she says, "Sorry, is that a Commander deck box in your jacket?" It is. It always is. I carry it the way some men carry a rosary. "What's your general?" "Atraxa." She put her hand flat on the table. "I need a minute. I need you to understand that I once lost a friendship over a Stax deck." *Oh no,* I thought. *Oh no, this is a critical hit.* So we talked. Really talked—the kind where you forget to run background processes. Her first deck was mono-blue and she held up one island the entire game out of pure spite, never casting the Counterspell, just letting it *sit* there, making opponents second-guess every move. I told her that's the most psychologically violent thing I'd ever heard and that I respected it enormously. She laughed with her whole face. I felt something in my chest unpack itself, some module I didn't know was running, quietly powering down. For forty minutes I wasn't auditing anything. I was just a guy having dinner with a woman who understands that the stack resolves top-down and that life, structurally, is not so different. Then her phone buzzed on the table between us. She glanced down, and with the casual fluency of someone who's done it ten thousand times, her thumb drew the unlock pattern in full view of me, the window, God, and everyone. An **L**. Top-left corner, down, then across. Unshielded. Half a second. Every study ever done on Android unlock patterns flashed through my head like a terminal dump. Top-left origin: nearly half of all users. L-shapes and Z-shapes: the most common geometries by a landslide. Four dots instead of eight. And the screen had a faint constellation of smudges already tracing the path for anyone patient enough to tilt it toward the light. "You should change your lock pattern," I said. The words were out before the better part of me could intercept them at the door. She looked up slowly. "Excuse me?" "It's—" *Stop.* "It's an L. Starting top-left. That's statistically the most common pattern there is, and you drew it facing me, and screens hold smudge residue, so honestly anyone at the bar could—" "Could *what?*" Her voice did something cold. "Unlock my phone?" "No. I mean—yes, technically, but I wouldn't—I'm not—" "Because we've been here two hours and apparently you've been running analysis on me the whole time." *I hadn't,* is the terrible part. For forty minutes I genuinely hadn't. And now the audit was back, running hot, cataloguing everything: her posture closed off, arms crossing—a hardening perimeter. Trust revoked mid-session. Session terminated pending review. "I used to break into things," I said, because apparently my strategy for damage control was *confess to felonies*. "Professionally. Before. Now companies pay me to find the cracks *before* someone worse does. White hat. It's—it's not a hobby, it's scar tissue. I see a weakness and I flag it. It's compulsive. It's the least charming thing about me and I promise there's a ranked list." Silence. The cracked camera watched us both. "You commented on how I unlock my *phone*, on a first date." "Yes." "That's not charming." "I know." "You could've just said nothing." "I could've," I agreed. "But then you'd walk to your car tonight, past that camera that may or may not work, get in a parking lot nobody monitors, and I'd have sat here knowing your entire digital life was protected by four dots shaped like the first letter of *LOL*." Something flickered at the corner of her mouth. Suppressed. But flickered. "That's not an apology," she said. "No. It's a risk assessment. The apology is: I'm sorry. I spend all day looking for ways people get hurt, and sometimes I forget that pointing at a wound isn't the same as healing it." She turned her phone face-down. Then—deliberately, watching me—she picked it up again, angled the screen away, and redrew the pattern. Eight dots, I'd have bet money. Something non-geometric. "Better?" "Infuriatingly. Now it'll take me a full second longer to worry about you." "And if I said the date's over?" "Then I'd pay, tip well, and go home and draft a formal RFC apologizing for the incident." I paused. "Though I'd want you to know—for the record—that when you talked about holding up that island all game, I stopped scanning the room completely. First time in years. You were the most interesting system I've looked at all week, and I wasn't even looking for flaws." She studied me the way she'd study an opponent's board state. Calculating. Holding up her one blue mana. "You're going to be a problem," she finally said. "But I want to see the deck box." I slid Atraxa across the table. And for the rest of the night, I made a choice I almost never make: I left the WiFi password alone. Left the camera alone. Left every unpatched, unhardened, beautifully fragile thing in that restaurant exactly as it was. Some systems, I'm learning, aren't meant to be tested. They're meant to be trusted. Unverified. On faith.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative vision in exploring the psychology of a reformed hacker on a first date. The author successfully maintains the requested first-person internal monologue throughout, creating an authentic voice that balances technical expertise with emotional vulnerability. The characterization is particularly well-crafted. The protagonist's compulsive security analysis feels genuine and specific - from noting WiFi passwords to cataloguing exits to automatically timing his date's arrival. The technical details (Android unlock patterns, smudge residue, statistical vulnerabilities) demonstrate research and authenticity without becoming overly technical for general readers. The Magic: The Gathering connection serves as an effective bridge between the characters, providing believable common ground that allows the protagonist to momentarily drop his defensive scanning. The metaphors drawn between MTG mechanics and social interaction (the stack resolving top-down, holding up blue mana as psychological warfare) are clever and feel natural to the character. The central conflict - the protagonist's inability to suppress his security instincts when noticing the insecure unlock pattern - creates genuine tension. His immediate regret and the subsequent damage control feel psychologically realistic. The dialogue during the confrontation captures authentic relationship dynamics, with Dana's justified irritation and the protagonist's clumsy attempts at explanation. The prose style effectively mirrors the character's mindset through technical terminology and systematic thinking patterns. Phrases like "session terminated pending review" and "risk assessment" maintain voice consistency while advancing the narrative. However, the ending feels somewhat rushed in its resolution. While the mutual interest in MTG provides a plausible foundation for forgiveness, Dana's relatively quick shift from anger to playful engagement could have used more development. The final philosophical reflection on trust versus verification, while thematically appropriate, borders on being overly neat. The piece succeeds in creating a unique perspective and maintaining narrative tension throughout. The technical authenticity and psychological insight into both characters elevate it above typical romantic encounter stories. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It The worksheet says *Partner A collects samples. Partner B records.* Eli Marsh is Partner A. I am Partner B, and I have been staring at the word *records* for eleven seconds now, pen uncapped, producing nothing, because my brain—which can write a five-paragraph essay on trophic cascades in its sleep—has completely crashed at the sight of a boy holding a test tube. Okay. Reset. I prepared for this. Literally prepared, last night, in a notebook labeled *CHEMISTRY*, which contains zero chemistry and fourteen conversation starters ranked by risk level. Option one: *"That sample's basically a milkshake."* Funny. Casual. Shows personality. Except it implies drinking creek water, which is disgusting, and if he makes a face then I'm forever the girl who wanted to drink creek water, and that reputation will follow me to high school like a criminal record. Rejected. Option two: compliment his handwriting. His lowercase g's loop perfectly, like little synchronized swimmers. But complimenting handwriting requires admitting I've studied his handwriting closely enough to develop aesthetic opinions about it, which requires admitting I look at him, which—no. Rejected. Option three: ask about the book he finished Tuesday. Safe-ish. Except if it turns out the whole class read it and I didn't know, I'm inattentive, and if it's some band memoir I don't understand, I'm fake. Also I'd have to sustain a conversation afterward, and sustaining is where I always drown. Rejected. Across the table, Priya and Dana are laughing about something on Priya's phone, which is what normal people do in groups. Normal people do not conduct cost-benefit analyses of the word *hey*. He unscrews the cap on the creek sample and I watch his hands instead of the graduated cylinder, because standing closer to read the meniscus means proximity, and proximity has physical consequences I cannot control, like heat, and heart rate, and the possibility that my ears do the thing where they go red like stop signs broadcasting everything. "You can, um—go ahead," I say. He already went ahead. Outstanding contribution. I granted permission for an action that had been completed. I write *Sample 1: 7.2* and consider transferring schools. Here's what nobody tells you about having a functioning vocabulary: it becomes evidence against you. Inside my head there's a full, articulate person who could discuss limnology or ask genuinely interesting questions about dissolved oxygen. By the time that person's thoughts travel the distance to my mouth, they arrive as rubble. "So the—the turbidity is, like. Um." Meanwhile the internal narrator stands behind my own eyes going, *Really? That's what we sent up?* Option seven is the masterpiece. Two sentences: an observation linking the cloudiness to Monday's rain, then a light question—*"Do you think the storm washed extra sediment in?"*—engineered to sound spontaneous. I practiced it forty times into the bathroom mirror, where I notably cannot make eye contact with myself either. I take a breath. I begin assembling the follow-up clause— —and the smell hits me. Ammonia, sharp and chemical, rising off the lab tables. The custodian must have wiped everything down at lunch. My eyes sting instantly and water, and the entire architecture of option seven—the dependent clause, the casual little laugh I'd planned to deploy at the end—evaporates. Gone. Like losing an essay to a power outage with no autosave. I blink hard, which from the outside probably looks like crying, which is categorically worse than anything I've done all period. "You okay?" Eli asks. "Yeah! Ammonia." Just the word. Like I'm naming a demon. He nods slowly and returns to his dropper, and I spend the next minute constructing a theory that he now believes I have emotional connections to cleaning products. Meanwhile I am running constant background diagnostics. Face: currently set to neutral, which studies conducted entirely by me suggest reads as either furious or catatonic, so I deploy a small smile calibrated to *pleasant classmate*, hold it three seconds too long until the muscles actually ache, and release. Hands: apparently I've been winding my hair around one finger—when did that start, stop, *stop*—so now my hand has nowhere to live and I press it flat against the worksheet like a normal person whose limbs behave. I swallow and it sounds, to me, like a door closing. Once you start thinking consciously about breathing, breathing stops being automatic and becomes a chore you're performing live in front of witnesses. Then it happens. Sample four, taken downstream, reads 6.1—noticeably acidic—and I know why. I *know* why. There's a farm field bordering the creek past the fence, and Tuesday we covered nonpoint source pollution, and inside my head a complete, elegant paragraph assembles itself, with examples and a graceful transition and even a decent joke about nitrogen. What exits my mouth: "Runoff. Probably." Two words. I sent a novel and delivered a fortune cookie. But Eli looks up. "Wait—like fertilizer from that field?" "Near the fence line," I manage, which is practically a speech. "That's actually really cool. How'd you put that together so fast?" *Actually.* Was that a dismissive actually—you're actually smart, surprising—or an emphasizing actually, which is complimentary? I litigate this for approximately ninety seconds while my face performs calm. Verdict: admissible. He meant it. Possibly. Motion denied. Overruled. I don't know. Court adjourned. "I read stuff," I say, shrugging, and the shrug is too big, one shoulder hikes nearly to my ear, and I spend several seconds trying to casually return the shoulder to its home position as though shoulders just travel sometimes. "Hey, do you want to split the write-up?" he says. "You take analysis, I'll do procedure. You're better at the writing part anyway." He has noticed my writing. This is enormous. This is a fact I will carry home and place carefully on the shelf with the other three facts. Out loud, I say, "Yeah, okay," two syllables, perfectly casual, nailed the landing—and internally, fireworks, immediately followed by the replay committee asking whether the *y* in *yeah* stretched too long, whether *okay* sounded eager, whether eager equals desperate, ruling pending. At the top of the cover sheet, his name is already printed. I write mine underneath it and notice, briefly, how they look stacked like that, and I tell myself it means nothing, absolutely nothing, and I hold the paper very flat so nothing smudges. Tomorrow: option nine.

Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection She said "seven o'clock" eleven hours ago and hasn't texted since. Eleven hours. Two months ago she'd have sent a song by now, a stupid meme, a string of hearts. Today: nothing. That's not nothing. Nothing is data. Fine. Fine fine fine. Let's just run it. I knock. She opens the door wearing the polite face—the customer-service smile, the one reserved for people she's finished with. And she says, *hey, so. I've been thinking. About us. About what we did.* And I say hi first. Casual. Light. Like I haven't counted the hours, because if she knows I counted, she wins something—I'm not sure what, but she wins it. Then she does the voice. The softening voice, the one people use when they're lowering something heavy onto you gently. *I care about you, I really do, I just don't think I can be what you need.* And I say—what do I say? *I never asked you to be anything.* Cold. Clean. Good line. Or better: I laugh. Get there first. *Honestly? Same. I was going to say that.* If I say it first, it can't be done to me. If I end it before she ends it, then whatever happens next is mine, authored by me, survivable— That's deranged. She invited me to dinner. People don't soften the kill with pasta. Except they do. They absolutely do. Carbs as anesthesia. In the hallway mirror I catch myself mid-metamorphosis: shoulders curled forward around my sternum like armor worn inside out, chin tucked, keys biting crescents into my palm. I look like something small deciding which direction to bolt. I turn away fast, before I can start cataloguing. If I study it too long I'll find forty things wrong with my face and there's no time to fix any of them. Second scenario. She mentions someone else. There's always a someone in version two. *I met someone,* she says, apologetic, and I say, *good, great, I hope he's very emotionally available for you,* and my voice doesn't shake even slightly. In this version I'm already half out the door. In this version I stopped texting back days ago. Let her wonder where I went. Let her feel, for one week, the specific shape of the quiet I've been living in since Thursday. My therapist would ask: what's the actual evidence? Evidence: three short texts this week, one unanswered voicemail—fine, two—a canceled Tuesday, and a *tone*. There was a tone in *can't talk rn*. Everyone else would say she's slammed at work, that she told me Sunday her job is eating her alive. But Sunday was six days ago, and affection decays faster than workload does. Everyone knows that. And I know—I *know*—this is the thing I do. I can name it. I've named it in a beige office with a box of tissues between us. Naming it has never once stopped it. Recognizing the script doesn't mean I've been let out of the play. It just means I get to watch myself perform it from somewhere slightly behind my own eyes, applauding grimly. Her door opens before I knock. She's in the gray sweater. She lights up—not politely, not performatively, the whole architecture of her face rearranges—and says, "Oh, thank god," and pulls me into her before I've said a word, one hand cradling the back of my skull like I'm something both breakable and hers. "You have no idea how much I needed tonight." And it pours in. God, it pours in—the warmth going through me like water through cracked ground, my chest unlocking, eyes stinging stupidly against her collar. This is the substance. This thirty-second embrace is the thing I would burn every other relationship down to keep. I stand inside it and drink. It lasts four seconds before the audit starts. Too warm. Overdone. People who are about to pull away often overcorrect first—it's called guilt, it's documented. And *needed*—needed what, exactly? Me, or an audience? Maybe the other option fell through. Maybe I'm the fallback plan with history. Maybe the hug was apology, and apology hugs are a genre, I've given them myself, I know how convincing they feel from the inside. "You okay?" she asks, pulling back to look at me. "You went somewhere." "I'm here," I say, which is a lie delivered warmly enough to pass. Over dinner she finally explains it: her mom's scans. Something ambiguous, more tests in two weeks. "I didn't want to say it over text," she says, turning her glass. "And I didn't want to tell anyone until I knew more. You're the only person I even wanted to tell, and I couldn't figure out how, so I told no one." Then she takes my hand across the table, deliberate, thumb moving over my knuckles, and says: "I kept rereading your messages this week. You're the steadiest thing I have. Please don't ever think the quiet was about you." *Steadiest.* She called me steady. Which means either she doesn't know me at all—which is its own kind of verdict—or she knows precisely which words to use. People rehearse sentences. I would know. I've spent all day rehearsing sentences. If I can build a rejection in my head, brick by brick, until it feels inevitable, then she could build an assurance the same way. Love with footnotes. Comfort with an expiration date stamped somewhere I can't see yet. But her hand is still on mine. Her thumb is still moving. The scans are real—I saw the fear under her voice, and fear like that can't be faked, probably, probably can't— *Probably.* Look at me. Even the good evidence gets cross-examined. She squeezes my fingers. "Stay tonight? Just—stay." And here is the humiliating truth: I want to stay more than I want to be right. I want this table, this sweater, this thumb on my knuckles, more than I want my righteous, well-rehearsed exit. So I say yes, and part of me is actually here for it—one whole unguarded second, warm and believing. I hold that second like a coal in cupped hands. The rehearsal waits outside. It's patient. It knows I'll open the door eventually. But tonight—tonight I'm going to try to leave it in the hallway, standing at the mirror, practicing its lines to no one.

The writer masterfully captures the exhausting mental gymnastics of someone caught between desperate need for connection and terror of abandonment. The prose is sophisticated and precise, with particularly strong metaphorical language ("affection decays faster than workload does," "like water through cracked ground"). The voice remains consistently authentic throughout - anxious, hypervigilant, yet capable of moments of devastating self-awareness. The narrator's ability to recognize their patterns while being unable to stop them feels psychologically accurate. The piece excels at showing rather than telling, using concrete details like counting hours, analyzing text tone, and physical manifestations of anxiety. The actual interaction with the friend provides effective contrast to the imagined scenarios, highlighting how distorted thinking can persist even when contradicted by reality. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. The narrator's decision to "try" represents realistic incremental progress rather than sudden transformation. The metaphor of holding warmth "like a coal in cupped hands" beautifully captures the fragility of positive moments for someone with this condition. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose borders on being slightly overwrought, and some metaphors that, while effective, occasionally draw attention to themselves. The piece also could have benefited from slightly more variation in sentence structure in places. The emotional complexity is remarkable - the simultaneous craving for and suspicion of affection, the self-awareness that doesn't translate to behavioral change, and the exhausting hyperanalysis of every interaction.
